World.title: Osun Election: Reps minority caucus accuses Tinubu of using federal agencies to intimidate state
World.content:
The House of Representatives Minority Caucus has accused President Bola Tinubu of attempting to use federal institutions to intimidate the Osun State Government ahead of next week’s governorship election.

It described his directive to the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) to vacate the court order freezing the state’s bank accounts as a “panicky, belated afterthought.”

It alleged that the president’s intervention was prompted by widespread public criticism rather than a commitment to the rule of law, arguing that the directive exposed contradictions within the federal government and raised fresh questions about the legality of the anti-graft agency’s actions.

The position of the opposition lawmakers was contained in a statement jointly signed by the Minority Leader, Fredrick Agbedi, and the caucus spokesperson, Afam Ogene, on Friday.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The statement comes amid heightened political tension in Osun State as preparations intensify for the governorship election scheduled for next week. The election is expected to be closely contested and has attracted significant attention following recent disputes involving security agencies, the EFCC and the state government.

The controversy began after the EFCC moved to freeze Osun State’s bank accounts as part of an investigation, a development that sparked criticism from opposition politicians and the state government, which described the action as politically motivated.

Mr Tinubu subsequently directed the anti-corruption agency to take immediate steps to vacate the court order freezing the accounts, saying democratic governance requires that elected governments continue to function without unnecessary disruption while investigations continue through lawful means.

However, the minority caucus argued that the president’s intervention only highlighted inconsistencies within his administration.

Contradictions over court order

According to the lawmakers, there were conflicting accounts from the EFCC and the Presidency regarding the legal basis for freezing the accounts.

They noted that while the EFCC spokesperson, Wilson Uwujaren, reportedly stated during a television interview that the accounts were frozen “without a valid court order,” the president’s directive later instructed the commission to approach the court to vacate the order.

The lawmakers questioned how both positions could be correct.

“So, which is it? Was there a court order or not?” the statement asked.

The caucus also questioned whether the President was fully aware of the actions and public statements of officials under his administration.

“Is the President not aware of what his own appointees are saying and doing? Has the President lost control to his army of sycophants who behave like lords over the people? Or are they simply trying to hide an illegality that has already been exposed?” the statement added.

The lawmakers further alleged that senior presidential aides were among the first to circulate and defend the EFCC’s initial statement supporting the freezing of the state’s accounts.

“It is, therefore, insulting for the president to pretend ignorance. Nigerians are not fools,” the caucus said.

Allegations of intimidation

Beyond the account-freezing controversy, the opposition lawmakers accused the federal government of pursuing what they described as a sustained campaign of intimidation against the Osun State Government ahead of the election.

According to the caucus, the latest EFCC action forms part of a broader pattern aimed at weakening the opposition administration in the state.

The lawmakers alleged that statutory allocations meant for local government councils in Osun had been withheld for months, describing the development as “economic strangulation” intended to cripple governance at the grassroots before the election.

They also alleged that the state had witnessed persistent violence allegedly involving members of the All Progressives Congress (APC) and imported political thugs, while accusing the Nigeria Police Force of failing to respond appropriately.

The caucus further criticised what it described as the “Gestapo-style arrest and detention” of the Secretary to the Osun State Government, Teslim Igbalaiye, and other officials over what it called flimsy allegations, arguing that the arrests amounted to an attack on the state government.

It also faulted the conduct of the Osun State Commissioner of Police and criticised comments made following a recent visit by the Inspector-General of Police, alleging that accusations that the Osun Government was harbouring hoodlums in the Government House were politically motivated.

“This is not policing. It is partisan propaganda in uniform,” the lawmakers said.

Warning against abuse of institutions

The minority caucus warned that actions and public comments by some presidential appointees were capable of damaging the administration’s credibility and deepening public distrust.

According to the lawmakers, the latest developments suggest that federal institutions are being deployed against opposition-controlled states.

“The mask is off. Nigerians can now see clearly that the APC has weaponised federal institutions against opposition states – a dress rehearsal of what is to come in the 2027 general elections,” the statement said.

While acknowledging that Mr Tinubu is from Osun State, the caucus insisted that he should allow residents to freely choose their governor without interference.

“Yes, Mr President hails from Osun, but the state cannot be a personal fiefdom. He must therefore allow the people to freely choose who governs them,” the lawmakers stated.

They called for an atmosphere that would allow voters to participate freely without fear, intimidation or coercion.

“Violence, intimidation, economic sabotage and the misuse of federal agencies have no place in a democracy,” the caucus added, warning that Osun “is not a conquered territory.”

The lawmakers also urged civil society organisations, election observers and the international community to closely monitor developments before, during and after the election, saying both the APC and the federal government should be held responsible for any breakdown of law and order.

“Osun people will vote. Osun people will be protected. And democracy will prevail,” the statement said.

World.title: EFCC returns recovered N125 million to Lagos land fraud victim
World.content:
The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) has handed over N125 million recovered from an alleged land fraud suspect to a Lagos businessman, Akinsewa Akiode.

According to a statement on Friday by EFCC spokesperson Dele Oyewale, the money was presented to Mr Akiode on Thursday by the commission’s Lagos Zonal Directorate 2 in Ikoyi after an investigation into a petition he filed over the disputed property transaction.

The statement stated that Mr Akiode alleged that Olufemi Fashehun collected N125 million from him for the sale of a 550-square-metre parcel of land at No. 10, Kudirat Abiola Way, Oregun, Lagos.

He later discovered, however, that the property had been the subject of litigation since 2011, a fact the seller allegedly failed to disclose before collecting the money.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The EFCC said its investigation showed that Mr Fashehun had been served with several court processes, including injunctions restraining him from carrying out any construction on the property, but did not disclose the pending litigation before completing the transaction.

The commission noted that Mr Akiode eventually lost both the property and the structures he had begun putting up on the land, prompting him to seek its intervention.

After concluding its investigation, the EFCC said it recovered the full N125 million from the suspect and returned the money to the petitioner through Sterling Bank drafts.

The handover is the latest in a string of restitutions by the anti-graft agency. Just over two weeks ago, the commission returned N108 million recovered during an investigation into an alleged fraud involving two former employees of Greenwich Planet Sun King Nigeria Limited.

In October 2025, it also handed over three houses, two vehicles and N1.1 million recovered from a convicted fraudster to one of his victims in Ibadan after a Federal High Court ordered the assets forfeited.

Speaking at Thursday’s ceremony, the Acting Zonal Director of the EFCC’s Lagos Zonal Directorate 2, Bawa Kaltungo, said the commission would continue to investigate economic and financial crimes, recover illicit proceeds and ensure victims receive restitution where possible.

The EFCC did not state whether criminal charges have been filed against Mr Fashehun over the alleged fraud.

World.title: EFCC’s over-sabi and 2027 question: Is Tinubu being misled by his inner circle?, By Yushau A. Shuaib
World.content:
After the bishops’ recent closed‑door meeting with President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, Cardinal John Onaiyekan made a striking claim: that presidential aides are shielding the President from the true suffering in the country, presenting a false “rosy picture,” and that Tinubu already appears desperate about winning the 2027 election.

As a writer and observer of governance, I share that concern. A president who controls the instruments of state, commands a united party, and faces a divided opposition has little rational cause for electoral anxiety — unless overzealous handlers are manufacturing threats where few exist.

The question therefore deserves to be asked plainly: what exactly is President Bola Ahmed Tinubu afraid of?

The EFCC’s freezing of the Osun State Government’s accounts barely a week before the July 2025 governorship election — citing a court order later reversed by the President himself — was not merely a legal misstep. It was a political signal of ‘over‑sabi’ — that familiar Yoruba expression for excessive, misdirected overzealousness — gone disastrously wrong. It also raised a question that goes beyond Osun’s finances and cuts to the heart of governance in Abuja: are these the deliberate choices of a confident presidency, or the panicked manoeuvres of handlers who have convinced the President that 2027 is a battle he might lose?

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Because by any honest reading of Nigeria’s political landscape, the evidence for such fear is astonishingly thin.

Tinubu enters the 2027 cycle with structural advantages unmatched in recent democratic history.

He controls the executive machinery of the Federal Government with unusual cohesion. The CBN and FIRS — custodians of national treasury and revenue — and the full architecture of anti‑corruption agencies operate within a presidency facing no internal rebellion. The security services — police, DSS, and the military — answer to the Commander‑in‑Chief. INEC operates within a constitutional framework that any well‑resourced incumbent can navigate with relative ease.

Why should he entertain fear? His party, the APC, has absorbed opposition defections at a rate that has reshaped the electoral map. Several governors elected on opposition platforms in 2023 have since crossed over, weakening the institutional backbone of any credible challenge. The PDP, Labour Party, and other formations remain fractured — much like 2023, when the split between Atiku Abubakar, Peter Obi, and Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso arguably delivered the presidency to Tinubu on the platter of gold. Has he forgotten that blessing in disguise?

Tinubu won the 2023 election under conditions far more hostile than anything he faces today. President Muhammadu Buhari was not enthusiastic about his candidacy. Vice President Yemi Osinbajo, Senate President Ahmed Lawan, ministers, and other APC heavyweights were either rivals or reluctant supporters. Yet Tinubu prevailed.

He now enters 2027 with those internal rivals neutralised and with the incumbency advantage he lacked in 2023.

So why are his handlers suddenly desperate — even flirting with anti‑democratic impulses?

Should a president who survived 2023’s turbulence now need anti‑corruption agencies freezing a state’s accounts one week before an election to prove loyalty?

Governance under Tinubu is mixed — but not devoid of genuine achievements. Abuja, under the politically abrasive but undeniably effective Nyesom Wike, has witnessed accelerated infrastructural development: roads, housing schemes, and urban renewal projects visible to anyone who drives through the city. One may dislike his crude politics, but his performance as minister rivals the El‑Rufai era. Had these — and other ministerial achievements — been properly documented and consistently communicated, wouldn’t they have formed a persuasive counter‑narrative to critics?

The Ministry of Information and National Orientation has also done strategic work in countering the internationally amplified “Christian genocide” narrative — a framing that ignored the Muslim communities devastated by banditry and terrorism in the North‑West and North‑East. Doesn’t the lobbying that produced a more balanced posture from Washington — including under President Donald Trump — reflect a sophistication in foreign‑policy communication that deserves amplification?

The administration has increased military remuneration, strengthening loyalty to civilian command. The foiling of a reported coup attempt further consolidates military alignment with the presidency.Do these achievements justify political panic?

One under‑analysed dimension of Tinubu’s political arithmetic is the legacy of the Muslim–Muslim ticket. The Tinubu–Shettima pairing was controversial in 2023, with critics warning it would alienate Christian voters. Yet, paradoxically after the victory, the administration has appointed Christian technocrats to some of the most economically sensitive ministries and key security portfolios — alongside many Yoruba appointees. Whether by design or necessity, hasn’t the Muslim–Muslim ticket ended up delivering significant Christian representation at the apex of federal governance?

Retaining Shettima for 2027 follows the same logic: consolidate the Muslim North — especially the core North that delivered decisive margins — while Christian appointments counterbalance the optics. It is a defensible strategy. But doesn’t it require sophisticated communication — which has not always been forthcoming?

Back to Osun: The real danger. The EFCC’s freezing of Osun’s accounts days before an election was legally arguable but politically indefensible. The timing made it impossible to interpret as anything other than partisan interference. The President‑ordered reversal after the alleged court order only confirmed what the optics had already declared.

The damage is not to Governor Ademola Adeleke or the opposition party. The damage is to President Tinubu. It invites the central question every overzealous enforcement action provokes: did the President authorise this — and other similar actions, including judicial manoeuvres?

If yes, it suggests a president anxious about 2027 despite overwhelming structural advantages — or one willing to compromise institutional integrity for marginal electoral gain. If no, it suggests something equally dangerous: that agencies are acting in his name without his knowledge, and that the presidency is unable to control institutions under its authority.

Neither interpretation flatters the presidency. Both are politically corrosive.

Nigeria has seen this pattern before. Weaponising anti‑corruption agencies does not strengthen incumbents. It delegitimises institutions, hardens opposition resolve, generates sympathy for targeted figures, and provides ammunition to international observers already sceptical of Nigeria’s democratic governance.

Does the arithmetic of intimidation ever favour the intimidator?

Tinubu is not a political novice. He is one of the most strategically sophisticated political minds Nigeria has produced. The Lagos model — whatever its imperfections — demonstrates his ability to build and sustain political structures over decades.

Which makes the question more urgent: who is advising him that these manoeuvres are necessary? Are they genuinely trying to secure his re‑election? Or are some exploiting his perceived anxiety for their own selfish interests?

Because the greatest threat to a Tinubu second term is not Atiku Abubakar, Peter Obi, or Kwankwaso. It is the growing perception that a confident presidency is behaving like one that is not.

Yushau A. Shuaib is the author of MNI Versus MNIPR in NIPSS on Tackling Institutional Bullying. [email protected]

World.title: Osun funds: CISLAC backs EFCC account restriction
World.content:
By Innocent Anaba

The Civil Society Legislative Advocacy Centre, CISLAC, and Transparency International Nigeria have defended the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission, EFCC, over its decision to restrict accounts belonging to the Osun State Government, saying protection of public funds should take precedence where there are credible concerns over their possible diversion or misuse.



CISLAC, through its Executive Director and Head of Transparency International Nigeria, Auwal Rafsanjani, said the controversy surrounding the restriction had overlooked a fundamental question: “Who protects the money of the people of Osun when alarm bells ring?”



The organisation, in a statement, maintained that public funds belonged to the people and not to governors, political parties or administrations.



It said salaries, pensions, healthcare, road projects and school feeding programmes depended on the protection of public resources and ensuring that such funds remained available for their intended purposes.



According to CISLAC, once public funds are moved into questionable channels, recovering them could become difficult.



It, therefore, defended the EFCC’s use of account restrictions as a preventive measure aimed at preserving funds and evidence while investigations are ongoing.



“The intent is simple: pause first, audit second, prosecute third if necessary,” the organisation said.



CISLAC rejected the argument that restricting state government accounts necessarily amounted to paralysing governance, asking whether a temporary restriction to facilitate an investigation was more damaging than the possible disappearance of billions of naira meant for public services.



“What paralyses governance more — a temporary audit, or the disappearance of billions meant for public good?” it asked.



The organisation stressed that allocations and other public funds at the federal, state and local government levels were meant to finance government operations and public services, including education, healthcare, security, infrastructure and the general welfare of citizens.



It said the EFCC’s intervention should be viewed within the context of the commission’s statutory responsibility to prevent economic and financial crimes and preserve assets that may be at risk during an investigation.



CISLAC also cited previous interventions by the EFCC involving state government funds, including cases involving Edo, Benue and Kogi states.



It said that during the last governorship election in Edo State, the EFCC restricted state government accounts following petitions and intelligence reports concerning alleged contract inflation and diversion of federal allocations.



According to the group, about N12 billion was preserved through the intervention, which it said was aimed at preventing the funds from being moved beyond the reach of investigators before a forensic audit could be conducted.



CISLAC also referred to the EFCC’s action in Kogi State in August 2021, when the commission obtained a Federal High Court order restricting a salary bailout account containing more than N20 billion.



The money, according to the organisation, was a loan intended to augment salary payments and meet the running costs of the Kogi State Government.



It said the EFCC had approached the Federal High Court in Lagos pursuant to Section 44(2) of the Constitution and Section 34(1) of the EFCC Act, arguing that the restriction was necessary to preserve the funds.



CISLAC said the court accepted the principle that the EFCC could take such steps in the public interest.

It argued that the same principle applied to the Osun controversy, stressing that investigations should not be defeated by the dissipation of funds.



“You cannot investigate a moving target,” it said.



The organisation urged the EFCC to act swiftly where credible petitions, intelligence reports or audit queries indicate a risk of large-scale movement of public funds.



“A state account can be emptied in 24 hours. A court case can take five years,” it stated, arguing that waiting until the conclusion of a criminal trial before taking preventive action could leave little or nothing to recover.



CISLAC, however, said EFCC account restrictions should be accompanied by safeguards, including clear timelines and judicial oversight.



It proposed that restrictions should ordinarily have a 30-to-60-day window within which the EFCC should conclude its preliminary investigation and approach the court where further action was required.



The organisation also urged the EFCC to clearly communicate that an account restriction was not a declaration of guilt but a preventive investigative measure.



CISLAC commended EFCC Chairman, Ola Olukoyede, and his team for what it described as an effort to protect the Osun State treasury.



According to the organisation, the central issue should not be whether the funds belonged to a government controlled by a particular political party, but whether public resources were being adequately protected.



“The treasury does not belong to you; it belongs to the people,” CISLAC said.



It urged Nigerians to support anti-corruption efforts aimed at protecting public resources and strengthening democracy.

World.title: Terrorism: US vows continuous action against ISIL, al-Qa’ida
World.content:
… Warns groups exploiting instability in Sahel, Africa, others

By Nkiruka Nnorom

The United States has said that countering ISIL, al-Qa’ida and their affiliates remained a key priority of its counterterrorism efforts, as the groups continue to exploit instability across Africa and Asia.

Speaking at a UN Security Council briefing on Wednesday, U.S Deputy Representative to the UN, Ambassador Tammy Bruce, said the groups were expanding operations in new theatres.

“Since the Council’s last briefing on this issue in February, the United States released its new national Counterterrorism Strategy on May 6, identifying three priority threats: narco-terrorists and transnational gangs, legacy Islamist terrorists, and violent left-wing extremists.

“Countering ISIL, al-Qa’ida, and their affiliates remains a key priority. These groups continue to exploit instability as evidenced by al-Qa’ida’s gains in the Sahel, ISIL’s growing focus on Africa, and the persistent threat from ISIL-K in Afghanistan,” she said in her remarks shared with the press.

The US envoy called for expanded intelligence coordination among member states, saying that information sharing must be strengthened to tackle both jihadist groups and Iran-backed proxies.

“Beyond the jihadist threat, Iran and its proxies and partners, including the Houthis, Hizballah, Hamas, and Iran-aligned militias in Iraq, continue destabilizing the Middle East and seeking broader reach. Expanded information sharing is vital to prevent them from acquiring critical weapons and to constrain their actions,” Bruce said.

She added that the same approach was needed to confront emerging threats, including violent far-left groups recently designated by Washington.

“Designations alone are insufficient. We must strengthen information sharing on the tactics, networks, funding, and malign state actors enabling this violence,” she said.

Bruce also noted the growing use of satellite communications, artificial intelligence, drones and cryptocurrencies by terrorist groups, saying it “demands vigilance from member states and the private sector.”

Bruce commended Member States whose operations and financial disruption efforts have constrained ISIL and al-Qa’ida in Iraq, Syria, and Somalia.

She also recognized Iraq’s leadership in repatriating detained and displaced persons from northeast Syria, and urged other countries to follow suit.

“We encourage efforts to follow suit, prosecute ISIL-affiliated nationals, and prevent returning foreign terrorist fighters from evading detection.

“It is critical that we work together to disrupt the production and movement of synthetic drugs, eradicate transnational organized crime, and combat terrorist travel,” she stated

She stressed that as the 25th anniversary of September 11 approaches, the UN and Member States must “refocus on core, actionable priorities and deliver measurable results” to protect citizens and borders.

Since November 2025, US-Nigeria security cooperation has shifted from dialogue to direct operational action, centered around intelligence sharing, joint strikes, and equipment support.

U.S Tomahawk missile strikes were conducted in Sokoto State on Christmas Day 2025 targeting Islamic State Sahel Province camps. Nigerian authorities described the strikes as precision hits following credible intelligence and careful operational planning. Casualties were put at 155-200+ fighters.

Again, a joint operation in the Lake Chad Basin in May 2026 resulted in the death of Abu-Bilal al-Minuki, the second-in-command of ISIS globally, along with 175 fighters.

Another reported joint operation killed more than 20 terrorists in the North-East, including ISWAP commander, Abubakar Mainok.



In February 2026, the U.S. deployed up to 200 troops to train and advise Nigerian forces, not in direct combat. Most of those forces were later withdrawn after the May operation, with the U.S. reverting to intelligence support at Nigeria’s request.

World.title: US to bar, deport birth tourists as Trump orders fresh crackdown
World.content:
US President Donald Trump speaks after signing executive orders in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, on August 7, 2026. (Photo by Jim WATSON / AFP)

By Nkiruka Nnorom

The United States has ordered a major crackdown on birth tourism, with President Donald Trump signing an Executive Order directing federal agencies to deny visas, revoke travel authorizations and deport foreign nationals who enter the country to give birth.

The order, signed on August 6, 2026, described U.S citizenship as “among the greatest inheritances the nation can bestow” and warned that it was being treated “as a commodity to be acquired through calculated exploitation and evasion of the immigration laws.”

According to the White House, the measure was aimed at closing loopholes that have allowed foreign nationals to exploit non-immigrant visas to secure citizenship for children born on American soil.

Under the directive, the Secretaries of State and Homeland Security were given authority to implement the new policy, while all other executive departments and agencies were directed to provide records and information necessary for implementation of the new policy.

Specifically, the Secretary of State and Secretary of Homeland Security, were directed to prevent the entry of any foreign national attempting to enter the United States for the purpose of birth tourism. The agencies were also mandated to revoke visas and travel authorizations and to permanently bar entry of anyone found to have engaged in the practice.

In addition, the order empowers both departments to deny entry or remove any ‘alien’ who previously engaged in or plans to engage in birth tourism.

The Secretaries were further instructed to take action against entities and individuals within and outside the United States responsible for facilitating or enabling birth tourism.

The directive covers operators, organisations and middlemen accused of coaching clients to misrepresent their travel purpose to consular and border officials.

The Secretaries were also mandated to update rules, policies and operational guidance to effectuate the policy.

The White House noted that the policy would promote the integrity of the immigration system and ensure non-immigrant visa classifications were not exploited for permanent immigration benefits.

President Trump accused birth tourism operators of using deceptive s and inducements and coaching clients to misrepresent their travel purpose to consular and border officials.

According to the White House, birth tourism undermines the integrity of the US’ immigration system, diverts consular resources from legitimate applicants, erodes public confidence, and impairs national security.

“The United States has a compelling interest in ensuring that each visa category is used only for the purpose for which it was established,” the order stated.

The order, however, provides that the Secretary of State or Homeland Security may grant exemptions “on humanitarian grounds or when the foreign national’s entry is in the national interest.”

President Trump’s effort to end birth tourism is not the first time his administration has moved to restrict birthright citizenship and immigration benefits.

Since returning to office in January 2025, Trump has made immigration enforcement a central focus of his second term.

His attempt to end automatic citizenship for children born on US soil received a final blow in the June 2026 ruling that saw the Supreme Court struck down the executive order seeking to end birthright citizenship.

Despite the Supreme Court ruling, the administration has continued to pursue related enforcement steps.

The administration has added birth tourism as a specific ground for visa refusal in the Foreign Affairs Manual, and instructed Customs and Border Protection, CBP, officers at airports to question pregnant travelers on tourist visas with the intention of denying them visas.

The August 6, 2026 order represents the administration’s latest attempt to enforce the policy by focusing not on birthright citizenship itself, but on the method of entry using existing visa and immigration authorities to block and remove those deemed to be engaging in birth tourism.

World.title: Alausa to education officials: No more ‘half-done’ deliverables
World.content:
•Dr Tunji Alausa, Minister of Education

…demands measurable results

By Joseph Erunke, Abuja

ABUJA — The Federal Government has moved to strengthen accountability in the implementation of education reforms, with the Minister of Education, Dr Tunji Alausa, warning officials handling the Nigeria Education Sector Renewal Initiative (NESRI) that commencing a programme would no longer be enough to qualify it as completed.

Alausa gave the warning on Friday in Abuja at a Ministerial Deliverables Meeting on NESRI, where the Ministry undertook a six-month review of progress on education sector reforms and subjected reported achievements to scrutiny to determine whether they had been fully delivered.

The minister said the meeting was not convened to celebrate achievements, but to establish what had actually been accomplished, identify outstanding commitments and determine what must be done to complete ongoing assignments.

“Today is not about celebrating what we have done and going home. It is about looking at what we have done, what remains to be done and how we can finish what we have started,” Alausa said.

The review, coming six months after the last NESRI retreat in February, focused on verifying completed deliverables, identifying bottlenecks affecting pending assignments, setting realistic deadlines for completion and considering new priorities emerging within the education sector.

Officials were required to defend assignments listed as completed and establish whether they had achieved their full scope, rather than being declared successful merely because activities had commenced or partial milestones had been reached.

The minister also directed programme coordinators and responsible officials to take full ownership of outstanding deliverables, identify specific obstacles delaying implementation and agree on practical measures and timelines for resolving them.

Alausa said the administration of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu had demonstrated strong political commitment to education and provided the necessary support for reforms aimed at expanding access, improving quality and making education more relevant to the needs of Nigerians.

He stressed that the mandate given to him and the Minister of State for Education was to do everything possible to ensure that every Nigerian child had access to quality education capable of providing the knowledge, skills and opportunities required to succeed.

The minister, however, warned against complacency, saying achievements already recorded must serve as a springboard for the next phase of delivery rather than an excuse for officials to slow down.

According to him, the NESRI reform agenda cuts across critical areas, including Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET), Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM), the out-of-school children crisis, girl-child education, quality assurance, education data and digitalisation.

He said the success of the Ministry would ultimately be measured not by the number of programmes launched, meetings conducted or activities recorded in official documents, but by the tangible changes experienced by Nigerians in schools and throughout the education system.

Alausa therefore tasked programme coordinators, directors and other officials with strengthening collaboration, maintaining clear responsibility for their respective assignments and focusing relentlessly on measurable outcomes.

He assured Nigerians that the Ministry would continue to pursue the President’s education agenda with determination, sustain reforms already initiated and respond to emerging challenges, with the ultimate goal of building an education system in which every Nigerian child has a genuine opportunity to learn, acquire relevant skills and fulfil their potential.

World.title: NAUB student develops autonomous robot to fight indoor fires
World.content:
By Ibrahim Hassan-Wuyo

A final-year Information Technology student of the Nigerian Army University Biu (NAUB), Muhammad Inuwa Abdullahi, has developed an autonomous firefighting robot designed to detect and suppress small indoor fires without direct human intervention.

Abdullahi, an indigene of Pantami in Gombe State, developed the robotic system as his final-year project using an Arduino Uno microcontroller platform.

The robot is designed to detect flames, navigate autonomously towards the source of a fire and activate a water pump to suppress it before it spreads.

The project demonstrates the practical application of robotics, embedded systems and automation to fire detection and emergency response.

Abdullahi said the project was inspired by the need to explore how technology could be deployed to protect lives and property through early detection and rapid intervention.

“I built this robot to show how technology can help save lives and property before fire spreads. It’s my contribution to solving real problems in our society,” he said.

According to him, the technology could potentially be adapted for use in homes, schools, offices, hospitals, laboratories, libraries, warehouses and other enclosed facilities where early detection and intervention could help minimise fire-related losses.

The project has attracted attention as an example of practical innovation emerging from Nigerian universities, particularly at a time when there is growing emphasis on developing indigenous technological solutions to local challenges.

The development also highlights the potential of university-based research to produce practical applications in areas such as public safety, automation and emergency response.

NAUB was established during the tenure of former Chief of Army Staff, Lt. Gen. Tukur Yusuf Buratai, as part of efforts to strengthen the relationship between military operations, academic research, science, technology and national development.

The university was conceived as an institution capable of producing skilled professionals, promoting research and developing technological solutions to Nigeria’s security and socio-economic challenges.

Abdullahi’s project reflects some of those objectives, particularly in the application of technology to a practical safety challenge.

The firefighting robot could also serve as a foundation for further research into more sophisticated emergency response systems incorporating artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things (IoT), sensors and smart-building technologies.

As Nigeria continues to promote indigenous research and reduce reliance on imported technologies, the project underscores the capacity of young Nigerian innovators to develop technology-based responses to everyday challenges.

Abdullahi expressed hope that his project would encourage other young Nigerians to pursue research, innovation and technology-driven solutions that could contribute to community development and national progress.

World.title: 2027: Ortom denies plot to replace Aondoakaa as Benue PDP candidate
World.content:
Ortom

By Peter Duru, Makurdi

MAKURDI — Former Benue State Governor and leader of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in the state, Chief Samuel Ortom, has dismissed reports alleging that he and other party leaders are planning to replace the party’s 2027 governorship candidate, Chief Michael Aondoakaa, SAN, with the Executive Secretary of the Nigerian Shippers’ Council, Dr Pius Akutah.

Ortom, in a statement issued by his Media Assistant, Zege Terhide, described the report circulating on social media as a “mischievous” distortion of a recent meeting involving prominent Benue stakeholders.

The former governor explained that he, alongside the Senate Minority Leader, Senator Abba Moro, and the PDP governorship candidate, Aondoakaa, met with prominent Benue indigenes, including Chief Simon Shango, Prof Iyorwuese Hagher, Dr Pius Akutah, Emmanuel Ameh and Dr Matthias Byuan.

According to him, the meeting was part of ongoing consultations aimed at building a broad strategic alliance among Benue stakeholders in the overall interest of the state.

“At no time during the meeting was the replacement of Chief Aondoakaa as the PDP governorship candidate discussed, contemplated or placed on the agenda,” Ortom said.

He described attempts to give the meeting a different interpretation as mischievous, stressing that political consultations across party lines were normal in a democratic environment.

“It is therefore mischievous for anyone to take a legitimate meeting of Benue leaders and manufacture an entirely different motive for it,” he said.

Ortom maintained that consultations and engagements involving political actors and stakeholders should not automatically be interpreted as secret conspiracies, particularly when such engagements were motivated by the larger interest of the people.

“Political consultations and engagements across party lines are neither strange nor secret conspiracies, particularly when they are driven by the larger interest of the people,” he stated.

The former governor also dismissed speculation over the PDP governorship ticket, declaring that Aondoakaa remained the party’s duly nominated candidate for the 2027 governorship election in the state.

“Chief Michael Aondoakaa, SAN, remains the duly nominated governorship candidate of the PDP in Benue State for the 2027 election,” Ortom declared.

He said the former Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice enjoyed the confidence and support of the PDP leadership and members across the state.

Ortom also expressed confidence in Aondoakaa’s ability to provide effective leadership if elected, citing his experience, competence and understanding of the challenges facing Benue.

He said Aondoakaa had the capacity to reposition the state and provide purposeful leadership, particularly in the areas of security, economic recovery and sustainable development.

The former governor therefore urged those responsible for circulating the alleged replacement story to desist from spreading what he described as fabricated narratives capable of causing confusion within the PDP and among supporters of its governorship candidate.

“Political journalism and commentary must be anchored on facts, not conjecture, deliberate falsehood or the attribution of imaginary motives to legitimate engagements,” he cautioned.

Ortom urged PDP members, supporters of Aondoakaa and the people of Benue State to disregard the report and remain focused on the party’s preparations for the 2027 elections.

He stressed that the alleged misinformation would not distract the PDP leadership from its efforts to build what he described as a formidable coalition of Benue people capable of providing the state with a credible alternative in 2027.

World.title: Naira appreciates to N1,412/$ in parallel market
World.content:
By Elizabeth Adegbesan

The naira appreciated to N1,412 per dollar in the parallel market on Friday, from N1,416 per dollar recorded on Thursday.

Similarly, the local currency strengthened to N1,364 per dollar at the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market (NFEM).

Data from the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) showed that the indicative exchange rate for the naira stood at N1,364 per dollar, compared with N1,365.10 per dollar on Thursday, representing an appreciation of N1.10.

Consequently, the gap between the parallel and official markets narrowed to N48 per dollar from N50.90 per dollar recorded on Thursday.

Meanwhile, interbank turnover at the NFEM increased sharply by 298.2 per cent to $393.5 million on Thursday, from $98.8 million recorded on Wednesday.

World.title: Alaafin: Oyo passport office autonomy’ll boost local economy, ease travel burden
World.content:
By Adeola Badru

IBADAN — The Alaafin of Oyo, Oba Abimbola Owoade, has welcomed the newly granted autonomy to the Oyo Passport Office, describing the development as a significant step towards decentralising government services and stimulating economic activities in the ancient city.

The monarch said the development would bring critical government services closer to residents, particularly those in rural and semi-urban communities who previously had to travel to Ibadan or Ilorin to access passport-related services.

Oba Owoade stated this through a high-powered delegation led by a member of the Oyo Traditional Council (Oyo Mesi), High Chief Asimiyu Atanda, during a visit to the Oyo Passport Office to felicitate with its management on the autonomy recently granted to the facility.

Before the development, the Oyo Passport Office operated as an appendage of the Ibadan Passport Office and was required to refer certain operations to the latter.

With the new status, however, the Oyo Passport Office can operate independently, while international passports processed through the facility will bear the name of the Oyo Passport Office.

The Alaafin said the development was significant because having a local passport office was essential to decentralising government services and improving accessibility.

He noted that the autonomous facility would “eliminate long-distance travel to state capitals” and reduce pressure on major passport processing centres.

According to him, residents would no longer have to bear the additional transportation costs and time associated with travelling outside Oyo for biometric capture, documentation and other passport-related services.

Oba Owoade said the development would “bring biometric capture and documentation services closer to rural or semi-urban residents, saving travel time and transport costs.”

The monarch also linked the development to broader economic benefits for Oyo, arguing that increased movement of applicants and visitors to the city would generate additional patronage for local businesses.

He said the office would “alleviate massive workloads and long queues at Central State or Regional Passport Headquarters” while creating opportunities for businesses operating around the facility.

“It would also increase local commercial activities as travellers from neighbouring towns visit the city for administrative processing, as well as create jobs directly through facility staffing and indirectly via local micro-businesses that support office visitors,” the Alaafin said.

Earlier, the Chief Passport Officer of the Oyo Passport Office, Assistant Controller of Immigration Oladejo Taiwo David, expressed appreciation to the Alaafin and his delegation for the visit.

Oladejo acknowledged the role played by the monarch and other prominent Oyo indigenes in securing the autonomous status for the office.

“This feat wouldn’t have been achieved if not for the efforts of His Imperial Majesty,” he said, while also acknowledging the support of prominent Oyo sons, particularly Alhaji Daud Igi-Ogun.

The Chief Passport Officer appealed to the Alaafin to assist the office in creating awareness among residents about the services now available in Oyo.

He urged residents to take advantage of the development by patronising the Oyo Passport Office instead of travelling to Ibadan or Ilorin for passport-related services.

“We solicit the support of His Imperial Majesty in the creation of awareness for the people to start patronising the Passport Office instead of going to Ibadan and Ilorin,” Oladejo said.

He assured residents that the new autonomous status would lead to more efficient service delivery.

According to him, “Oyo Passport Office would serve the people better as it would be faster to get their passports.”

The Alaafin’s delegation comprised the Director of Administration to the monarch, Prince Adesola Sanda, and renowned Sheikh, Alhaji Daud Igi-Ogun.

World.title: How Access Bank is Nurturing Africa’s Next Generation of Innovators
World.content:
From a local initiative to one of Africa’s biggest STEM learning platforms, STEM Africa Fest has inspired nearly 30,000 young people, driven by Access Bank’s six-year commitment to science and technology education, writes Sunday Ehigiator

On a bright Saturday morning at Landmark Event Centre in Victoria Island, Lagos, the usual sounds of children’s laughter mixed with the whirring of drones, the buzz of 3D printers and animated conversations about artificial intelligence filled the ears.

Instead of spending the long school holiday indoors glued to television screens or mobile phones, more than 3,500 children gathered to immerse themselves in a world where science was exciting, technology was hands-on, engineering was creative, and mathematics became an adventure rather than a classroom obligation.

Across the expansive exhibition halls, children programmed robots, experimented with chemistry, built paper engineering models, flew drones, designed digital animations using artificial intelligence and interacted with more than 50 exhibitors showcasing cutting-edge technologies.

It was the sixth edition of STEM Africa Fest, now regarded as one of Africa’s largest STEM education festivals for children.

Yet beyond the colourful exhibitions and excitement lay a deeper story; not just about education, but about what sustained corporate investment can achieve when it is driven by purpose rather than publicity. That story begins with Access Bank.

Partnership with Belief

Long before the festival became an annual attraction drawing thousands of participants, before it expanded across Africa and before STEM education became fashionable among many organisations, Access Bank made an early decision to support an idea whose impact had not yet been proven.

Six years later, the results speak loudly. The bank has remained the headline sponsor throughout the festival’s journey, helping transform what began as a Nigerian initiative into a continental platform reaching children in Ghana, Rwanda, Kenya, Zambia, Sierra Leone, The Gambia and several Nigerian states.

For co-Convener of the event, Titi Adewusi, Access Bank’s role extends far beyond financial sponsorship. “They were the first people that believed in us. When it was just a dream that nobody was doing, we went around, and nobody understood. They took a chance on us from the very first year.”

That early confidence became the foundation upon which the festival expanded. According to Adewusi, it was Access Bank that encouraged the organisers to think beyond Nigeria.

“When we went to Ghana, it was because Access was in Ghana and they said, ‘Come, we’ll back you up.’ When we went to Gambia, Sierra Leone, Zambia and Kenya, they stood with us.”

Even more importantly, she said, the bank challenged them to dream beyond what they initially imagined possible. “They’ve been a partner everybody prays for. They’re the kind of partner that puts their money there and also helps you dream bigger.

Investing in Tomorrow

Corporate sustainability has evolved significantly over the past decade. Increasingly, companies are recognising that creating lasting value requires investing not only in communities but also in future generations. For Access Bank, STEM Africa Fest fits squarely within that philosophy.

Speaking during the event, Programme Manager, Sustainability at Access Holdings, Ikechukwu Iheagwam, explained why the institution has remained committed to the initiative.

“In Access, we believe in the future, and the future is these children. In some years to come, these children will be the ones to shape the world.”

He noted that supporting STEM education aligns directly with the bank’s sustainability agenda, particularly its focus on education and technology.

Perhaps the most striking aspect of Access Bank’s involvement is its consistency. Many corporate partnerships last only a year or two before priorities change. Access Bank has remained involved throughout all six editions. That consistency has given organisers confidence to plan long-term, expand geographically and continually improve programme quality.

From Lagos to Abuja and Ilorin, and from Nigeria to multiple African countries, the bank’s backing has provided the stability necessary for sustainable growth. Another co-Founder, Jadesola Adediji, believes that commitment made all the difference.

“They probably didn’t fully understand what we were trying to do at the beginning, but irrespective, they put a bet on us. Year after year, Access Bank keeps showing up for us. If it wasn’t for them, especially when we were starting from ground zero, it would have been much harder.”

Learning by Doing

One reason STEM Africa Fest continues attracting thousands is its emphasis on experiential learning. Unlike traditional classroom settings where students often memorise theories, the festival encourages children to touch, build, experiment and create.

Adewusi described the festival as “a STEM wonderland. It has to be engaging. It has to be immersive.

The children need to touch and feel. They don’t just hear about technology. They see it, and they do it; that philosophy is evident everywhere. Instead of reading about drones, children fly them. Instead of watching videos about robotics, they build robots. Instead of merely hearing about AI, they generate animations using artificial intelligence tools. Instead of learning chemistry from textbooks, they conduct real experiments.

AI takes centre stage.

This year’s edition reflected one unmistakable reality. Artificial intelligence has arrived. Masterclasses on AI attracted packed audiences as children learned how AI tools generate videos, solve problems and stimulate creativity. For many participants, it was their first practical exposure to the technology reshaping industries worldwide.

A student, Jason Lawal from Court Hill College, admitted he arrived simply hoping to broaden his knowledge. He left inspired. “I learned about artificial intelligence,” he said. “We worked in groups to create AI animations. It was really exciting.”

Jason believes AI education should become mainstream. “AI is what’s reigning now. So students really need to learn it.”

A Festival for Everyone

One notable aspect of STEM Africa Fest is its commitment to inclusion. While many educational programmes inadvertently cater mainly to privileged schools, STEM Africa Fest deliberately creates opportunities for children from public and low-income schools.

Sponsors, including Access Bank, purchase tickets enabling disadvantaged students to attend free of charge. According to Adewusi, this approach reflects the festival’s commitment to Sustainable Development Goal Four: Quality Education for All.

“We don’t want it to become elitist. We want children of every background to experience quality STEM education.”Each year, between 60 and 100 schools participate. That diversity enriches the learning environment while ensuring access is not determined solely by economic status.

STEM Africa Fest’s greatest achievement lies beyond attendance figures. It has catalysed a growing STEM education movement across Africa. Schools have established STEM clubs after attending. Educators have replicated similar festivals in their own states.

Organisers from other African countries now seek guidance on creating comparable programmes.

For educators, the impact becomes visible long after the festival ends. Tolulope Aleogena, Director of Briarcrest School, Ikeja, attended for the third consecutive year. This year, she brought students.

“It’s been really good,” she said. “The children experience things they ordinarily wouldn’t in school.” She observed that each edition introduces emerging technologies. “Every year you see something new. It tells the children that technology is constantly evolving.”

Such exposure broadens students’ perspectives while complementing classroom instruction.

Some participating students have also become regular attendees. Fatima Namama, now an SS1 student, has attended since junior secondary school.

“I always have fun here,” she said. “I always have something new to tell people when I go back.”

The Private Sector’s Role

While discussions about education often focus on government responsibilities, STEM Africa Fest demonstrates what effective public-private collaboration could achieve. Asked whether the government was doing enough, Iheagwam acknowledged ongoing efforts but emphasised that the government alone cannot meet every need.

“The government cannot do everything. Private sector participation is very important.”

His position reflects growing recognition that addressing educational gaps requires collective action. Businesses possess resources, technology, expertise and networks capable of complementing government interventions. When deployed effectively, those assets accelerate educational development.

Measuring Success Differently

Unlike many events where success is measured by attendance alone, STEM Africa Fest defines impact differently. For Adewusi, success begins with curiosity.

“If one child leaves saying, ‘I can do this,’ then we’ve achieved something.” The organisers equally celebrate when schools establish STEM clubs or teachers adopt more practical teaching methods. Those ripple effects often prove more valuable than the event itself.

From impacting roughly 25,000 children over five years to approaching 30,000 today, STEM Africa Fest continues expanding. Its ambitions are equally growing. Already active across several African countries, organisers believe the platform could eventually become global. That aspiration appears increasingly realistic. The demand exists. The model works. And crucially, strong partnerships continue providing momentum.

A blueprint for Corporate Impact

Access Bank’s involvement offers an important lesson for corporate Nigeria. Meaningful corporate social investment is rarely about one-off donations. Its greatest impact comes through sustained commitment, strategic collaboration and long-term vision.

By remaining invested over six years, Access Bank has helped build an institution rather than merely sponsor an event. Its contribution has enabled thousands of children to discover interests in coding, robotics, engineering, artificial intelligence and scientific inquiry. It has expanded educational opportunities across borders. It has strengthened Africa’s STEM ecosystem.

And perhaps most importantly, it has inspired countless young minds to believe that innovation belongs not only to Silicon Valley or Europe, but also to Africa.

Looking Ahead

As children reluctantly filed out of Landmark Event Centre at the close of the day’s activities, many carried no trophies or certificates. Instead, they left with something potentially far more valuable: curiosity, Confidence, and Imagination.

They also left with the knowledge of a drone successfully flown for the first time, a robot programmed for the first time, an AI animation created for the first time, a scientific experiment completed for the first time, etc.

For some, these may become lifelong memories. For others, they could become the first steps towards careers in engineering, medicine, artificial intelligence, software development or scientific research. Behind each possibility lies a network of educators, innovators, volunteers and corporate partners committed to nurturing Africa’s next generation.

Among those partners, Access Bank stands out; not simply because it funded an event, but because it recognised the power of an idea long before it became a movement.

In an era where Africa’s future competitiveness will depend increasingly on innovation, digital skills and scientific capability, that early investment may ultimately prove to be one of the bank’s most enduring contributions to the continent.

World.title: How Zenith Bank’s Cancer Care Initiative is Giving Nigerians Second Chance at Life
World.content:
Through strategic healthcare investments, Zenith Bank is demonstrating that corporate social responsibility can save lives, restore dignity and give vulnerable Nigerians a second chance, writes Omolabake Fasogbon

For many Nigerians, a cancer diagnosis is often the beginning of a financial, emotional and psychological crisis. Families sell property, exhaust their savings, borrow heavily or simply abandon treatment because they cannot afford the cost of chemotherapy, radiotherapy or surgery. In a country where access to specialist cancer care remains limited and treatment costs are beyond the reach of many households, thousands of lives are lost each year, not only because of the disease itself but because help arrives too late or not at all.

Against this backdrop, Zenith Bank Plc is redefining what corporate social responsibility (CSR) means in Nigeria. Rather than limiting CSR to periodic donations or symbolic community projects, the bank has adopted a long-term approach that addresses one of the country’s most pressing public health challenges.

Through strategic investments in cancer awareness, prevention, early diagnosis and treatment, Zenith Bank is demonstrating that corporate institutions can become powerful partners in saving lives and strengthening healthcare delivery.

Its interventions illustrate a growing recognition that businesses have responsibilities beyond generating profits. Increasingly, they are expected to contribute meaningfully to solving social problems, particularly in areas where public resources alone cannot meet rising demand. For Zenith Bank, healthcare has become one of the defining pillars of its sustainability agenda.

The bank’s approach reflects the philosophy that when businesses invest in healthier communities, they also invest in stronger economies, more productive citizens and a more sustainable future.

Cancer remains one of the leading causes of death globally, and Nigeria continues to face enormous challenges in combating the disease. Delayed diagnosis, inadequate screening facilities, shortage of specialist treatment centres and the high cost of care have combined to make cancer one of the country’s most difficult public health battles.

Recognising this reality, Zenith Bank has deliberately focused its healthcare CSR on removing some of the financial barriers that prevent vulnerable Nigerians from accessing life-saving care. This approach aligns with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly Goal 3 on Good Health and Well-being and Goal 10 on Reducing Inequalities.

Standing with Cancer Patients

Beyond financial assistance, Zenith Bank has worked to create a culture of empathy around cancer. Each year, employees participate in cancer awareness campaigns by wearing cancer awareness lapels, serving as visible reminders that the fight against cancer is everyone’s responsibility. The initiative may appear symbolic, but its impact extends much further. It encourages conversations about early detection, reduces the stigma associated with cancer and reminds patients and survivors that they are not alone.

Within corporate Nigeria, such initiatives help normalise discussions about preventive healthcare while encouraging more people to seek timely medical attention.

One of Zenith Bank’s most impactful interventions has been its partnership with the WinCancer Foundation. Recognising that thousands of Nigerians discontinue treatment simply because they cannot pay, the bank directly funded chemotherapy and radiation therapy for financially disadvantaged cancer patients in Lagos. For beneficiaries, the intervention represented hope and meant another opportunity to fight for life.

Additionally, it meant parents remaining with their children, breadwinners returning to work and families being spared the devastating choice between survival and financial ruin.

The partnership also acknowledges that healing extends beyond medicine. Cancer survivors receive specially designed care packages that provide emotional, psychological and mental support throughout recovery.These initiatives recognise the fact that successful healthcare is not measured only by clinical outcomes but also by the dignity, confidence and emotional resilience restored to patients.

Extending Care Beyond Hospital Walls

Zenith Bank has equally recognised that lasting healthcare transformation cannot be achieved by one institution acting alone. The bank has therefore expanded collaborations with organisations already working within vulnerable communities.

Among the most notable partnerships is its support for the Charly Boy Foundation, an organisation committed to improving men’s health through prostate cancer diagnosis and treatment, diabetes management and mental health advocacy. The bank’s donation funded complete prostate cancer treatment for 40 men requiring urgent medical intervention.

For many beneficiaries, the intervention eliminated costs that would otherwise have placed treatment beyond reach. Beyond the number of beneficiaries, the partnership demonstrates how strategic collaboration between the private sector and civil society can significantly improve healthcare outcomes.

Perhaps the most transformative element of Zenith Bank’s healthcare CSR is its investment in mobile cancer diagnostic and treatment centres. Rather than waiting for patients to travel long distances to urban hospitals, the bank chose to bring specialist healthcare directly to communities.

Its funding of ten Mobile Cancer Diagnostic and Treatment Centres, popularly known as PinkCruise, represents one of the most ambitious healthcare interventions ever undertaken by a Nigerian financial institution. The innovation addresses one of Nigeria’s greatest healthcare challenges—geographical access.

For millions of Nigerians living outside major cities, specialist medical facilities remain hours away. By the time many patients reach hospitals, diseases have often progressed to advanced stages. The PinkCruise initiative changes this narrative. These fully equipped mobile centres travel directly into communities, providing services that many residents would otherwise never access.

Their facilities include cancer screening, mammography, colonoscopy, endoscopy, colposcopy, cryotherapy, laboratory investigations, vaccination services and minor surgical procedures for pre-cancerous conditions and early-stage cancers.

Importantly, the centres extend beyond cancer care. Communities also receive screening for hypertension, diabetes, kidney disease, hepatitis, HIV, obesity, malaria, schistosomiasis and Helicobacter pylori infection.

Eye examinations under the Mission PinkVISION programme further broaden access to preventive healthcare. Every outreach becomes a one-stop health intervention capable of identifying multiple life-threatening conditions before they become critical.

Reaching Communities That Need Help Most

The impact of the mobile programme became evident soon after the arrival of the first pilot centres. Operational units were established across Lagos, Abuja, Asaba and Port Harcourt, extending specialist healthcare to Nigeria’s major regions. Community outreach began in Agbor, Delta State, where residents received free cancer screening, medical examinations, eye care services, nutritional support, treatment and referrals regardless of age or gender.

Subsequent programmes expanded across Lagos and other locations, bringing preventive healthcare directly to thousands of Nigerians.

According to reports from the Cancer Education and Prevention Programme (CECP), more than 5,000 Nigerians benefited during the initiative’s early implementation phase.

For many participants, the screenings represented their first comprehensive health examination. Some discovered underlying conditions early enough for effective treatment. Others received referrals before illnesses progressed into life-threatening emergencies.

Redefining Corporate Citizenship

Zenith Bank’s healthcare interventions reflect a broader shift in how responsible businesses measure success. Corporate value is no longer determined solely by balance sheets and profitability. Increasingly, it is measured by the positive impact companies create within the societies where they operate.

Healthcare represents one of the areas where this impact is most visible. By investing in awareness campaigns, funding treatment, supporting vulnerable patients, strengthening partnerships and introducing innovative mobile healthcare solutions, Zenith Bank has demonstrated that CSR can move beyond philanthropy to become an instrument for national development. Its interventions improve access to healthcare, promote early diagnosis, reduce treatment costs for vulnerable families, strengthen disease awareness and support government efforts to reduce preventable deaths.

Investing in Lives

Zenith Bank has shown that corporate organisations have both the capacity and the responsibility to become active participants in that effort. Its healthcare CSR programme is an investment in people, families and communities.

In demonstrating that responsible banking extends beyond financial services to improving lives, Zenith Bank is setting a compelling example of how corporate social responsibility can become a powerful force for healthcare transformation. In doing so, the bank is proving that some of the most meaningful returns on investment are not measured in financial statements, but in healthier communities, restored hope and lives given a second chance.

Zenith Bank has over the years, continued to restore hope, dignity and confidence to some of Nigeria’s most vulnerable citizens.

For instance, in partnership with the Marymine Mother’s Care Initiative Network (MMCIN), the bank supported the launch of the “Protect the Dignity of Our Females” project, a programme designed to improve menstrual hygiene management while raising awareness about sexual and gender-based violence in IDP camps across Benue State.

More than a corporate social responsibility initiative, the project addressed two issues that often receive little attention during humanitarian emergencies. For many displaced women and girls, the absence of sanitary products and accurate reproductive health information affects their education, health, confidence and participation in community life. At the same time, overcrowded camp conditions expose many to heightened risks of abuse and exploitation.

In April this year, the bank celebrated the Zenith Bank’s 2026 International Women’s Day seminar with the theme, “Take It, You Own It.” The bank also held the inaugural ‘Woman of Power Award,’ in partnership with Ford Foundation. The event was about visibility and bringing into the national consciousness the everyday women who hold communities together, often without acknowledgment or reward.

Sustainability is deeply embedded in the bank’s operations and strategic vision. In commemorating World Environment Day 2026, Zenith Bank chose to move beyond words and demonstrate what responsible corporate citizenship can look like in practice. By cleaning streets, restoring waterways, partnering with public institutions and promoting environmental awareness, the bank transformed a global environmental theme into local action.

As cancer continues to threaten countless Nigerian families, Zenith Bank’s healthcare interventions demonstrate that responsible corporate citizenship can bridge critical gaps in access to life-saving care. By investing in awareness, early diagnosis, treatment and community partnerships, the bank is not only transforming cancer care but also giving thousands of Nigerians what every patient deserves—a genuine second chance at life.

World.title: When Wealth Raises Questions: ‘19’ Explores Nigeria’s Culture of Easy Money
World.content:
Tosin Clegg

In today’s Nigeria, the display of extravagant wealth on social media has become almost routine. Luxury cars worth hundreds of millions of naira line the entrances of exclusive nightclubs, while expensive champagne, cognac and limited-edition whiskies are ordered by the crate, often with little public curiosity about how such fortunes were made.

While legitimate wealth has grown through technology, entertainment, entrepreneurship and the digital economy, the scale of conspicuous consumption has also fuelled difficult conversations about the country’s growing fascination with quick money. Increasingly, many Nigerians are asking whether society has become too comfortable celebrating wealth without questioning its source.

It is this uncomfortable reality that ‘19’, a gripping new crime drama, confronts head-on.

Rather than celebrating cybercrime or reinforcing stereotypes, the film traces the origins of Nigeria’s internet fraud culture through the life of Ndubuisi Madueke, an exceptionally brilliant young man whose search for success gradually draws him into a dangerous world where ambition, desperation and opportunity collide.

Set during the early years of Nigeria’s internet revolution, ‘19’ revisits the emergence of the infamous “419” culture, exploring the economic pressures, social influences and moral compromises that blurred the line between survival and criminality for many young people. More importantly, the film goes beyond the scams themselves.

It examines the devastating consequences that fraudulent lifestyles leave behind—the broken families, fractured friendships, damaged reputations and emotional scars often hidden beneath the glamour of sudden wealth.

At the centre of the production is multiple award-winning actor Stan Nze, whose compelling portrayal of Ndubuisi captures the emotional transformation from an ambitious young dreamer into a man forced to confront the consequences of his choices. His performance anchors a film that combines suspense with powerful social commentary.

The story is further enriched by an accomplished cast that includes Sola Sobowale, Bisola Aiyeola, Deyemi Okanlawon, William Benson, Demola Adedoyin, Enado Odunsi, Tayo Faniran and Boma Akpore. Their performances provide emotional depth, showing how crime rarely affects only the perpetrator but also parents, spouses, friends and entire communities. The title itself carries symbolic weight.

‘19’ draws inspiration from Section 419 of Nigeria’s Criminal Code, the law historically associated with advance-fee fraud. Yet the film deliberately avoids simplistic judgments. Instead, it asks difficult questions about the choices people make, the society that shapes those choices and the true cost of pursuing wealth without integrity.

Writer, producer and director Tola Odunsi describes the project as the culmination of months of extensive research, writing, filming and testing. Reflecting on the journey, Odunsi posed a question that captures the essence of the film:

“You can outsmart the police, the banks and the system. But can you outrun the truth?”

The film opens in cinemas nationwide on September 11, 2026, with distribution by Nile Entertainment. Beyond the cinema release, the producers are also seeking to extend the conversation into society.

In partnership with Aforevo TV’s Build Africa Store, Nile Entertainment has launched the #19TheFilmChallenge, a nationwide awareness campaign designed to stimulate conversations about fraud, cybercrime and ethical decision-making among young Nigerians. Adding further excitement is a N5 million grand prize, encouraging creative participation while reinforcing the campaign’s broader message against internet fraud.

At a time when online scams continue to damage reputations, destroy trust and cost victims billions of naira across the world, ‘19’ arrives as more than another crime thriller.

It is a timely social commentary that challenges audiences to look beyond the glamour of fast money and confront the deeper moral, economic and human consequences of a culture increasingly defined by the pursuit of instant wealth.

World.title: Bola Oyebamiji: Osun  Deserves Business-minded Governor
World.content:
Asiwaju Munirudeen Bola Oyebamiji (AMBO), the All Progressives Congress candidate in the August 15, 2026, Osun State governorship election, believes his years in banking, public finance and public administration have prepared him to lead the state. A former Commissioner for Finance under two administrations and immediate past Managing Director of the National Inland Waterways Authority, Oyebamiji says Osun needs a business-minded leader capable of translating its abundant human and natural resources into shared prosperity. He speaks on his vision for the state, his PROSPERITY Agenda, governance priorities, security concerns and why he believes the APC will reclaim Osun. Sunday Ehigiator brings the excerpts:

Why do you believe you are best qualified to be the next governor of Osun State?

I am running because I believe that I have what it takes to turn around the declining fortune of Osun State. The state has an estimated population of about five million citizens. We are blessed with vast human capital and abundant mineral resources — all tangible assets that can elevate our state to a new level of prosperity. To maximise these assets, Osun requires a focused, credible, knowledgeable manager with proven character and capacity. A leader who can confidently sign their signature and stand by it. I, Bola Oyebamiji, offer myself because I have the managerial competence and experience to reposition Osun State for greatness and deliver the dividends of democracy to our people. I have served as Commissioner for Finance, working directly with two governors, and I also served as Managing Director of the state’s investment arm, OSICOL. The records are there, and my antecedents are clear. I am that manager that Osun State needs to flourish. I became MD of OSICOL, now known as Omoluabi Holdings Limited, and the achievements are there for anyone to verify. From OSICOL, I was appointed Commissioner for Finance under former Governor Rauf Aregbesola, and we delivered excellently. I also served our leader, Adegboyega Oyetola as Finance Commissioner, also without blemish. Later, I was appointed Managing Director of NIWA, and in two years, we recorded unprecedented progress, and the results have never been matched since the establishment of NIWA. These experiences give me confidence that with hard work, competence, and God’s grace, success will always follow. We are in this race to win, to serve, and to deliver value to our party and our people.

Why do you believe the people of Osun should replace the current administration in the August 15 governorship election?

The facts speak for themselves. And to properly situate why Osun deserves a better deal at this time, the last allocation received by the APC administration of Governor Gboyega Oyetola from the Federation Account Allocation Committee (FAAC) stood at approximately N2.6 billion. Today, the average monthly allocation to the state is about N16 billion without commensurate values to the state and her citizens. In fact, few of the infrastructure projects delivered by the current administration were awarded in secrecy to incompetent contractors while many of such projects have failed before commissioning. To arrest the current drift in the state, I therefore seek your support as we approach the August 15, 2026, governorship election in Osun State. I have spent 12 years in the topmost levels of government, working directly with tough, credible managers — two former governors. As Commissioner for Finance, you must thoroughly analyse, review, and recommend every financial decision. I understand government operations deeply. Among all the other candidates, I am the only one with these combinations of high-level experience, proven records, and capacity in both the private and public sectors. I have the experience. I have the records. I have the antecedents. And I am prepared to lead Osun State to a new era. I was shaped in a target-oriented industry: banking, which rewards performance and sanctions inefficiency. This philosophy has guided my professional and personal life for decades. I am committed to a fair reward system, helping everyone reach their potential without bias. My administration will be firmly rooted in fairness and equity. It will be a new dawn for our people. Our people can no longer sit and watch the enormous resources of the state being expended without equal value or meaningful improvement in their daily lives. Osun State cannot afford to be left behind in the current wave of reforms, development and economic transformation being championed by the administration of our great leader, Mr President, His Excellency, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR. We must therefore seize this moment of national transformation and ensure that Osun State becomes an active participant and beneficiary of the Renewed Hope Agenda. This is why I believe Osun State deserves a change in leadership at this point in time.

Can you walk us through your PROSPERITY agenda?

As you may have noticed, our Prosperity Agenda has continued to gain widespread acceptance among the people of Osun. So far, we have taken our campaign to twenty-four local government areas spread across seven federal constituencies in the state. Within the next forty-eight hours, our campaign train will cover the remaining six local government areas across the two outstanding federal constituencies. As a party, our firm belief is that the primary responsibility of any government, as provided in the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, is the security and welfare of its citizens.
