Now San Miguel is widely regarded as one of the top international destinations in Mexico, bringing in over two million visitors each year. There are an abundance of vineyards just outside the city limits, fine dining is around every corner and luxury hotels are found all throughout town.

As more and more foreigners came to San Miguel and as the arts scene continued to grow, the town became increasingly accommodating to American tourists. Americans tend to like to feel comfortable abroad, and the prevalence of English in the town takes away a massive hurdle that might deter Americans from going to Guanajuato or Querétaro, where English is less prevalent.

More Americans also means more American food, more American sports on TV, and more spaces designed to make Americans feel comfortable. Jewish delis, burger joints and microbreweries covered with TVs are easy to find — and they are harder to come by in Guanajuato or Querétaro. More places for Americans will always lead to more Americans.

The invention of social media has also greatly benefited San Miguel’s tourism industry. The Parroquia de San Miguel Árcangel — with its towering spires and jaw-dropping pink facade — looks glorious in an Instagram story. The courtyards and gardens throughout the town also make for great photos, and some have called San Miguel’s local Starbucks the most beautiful in the world.

Once San Miguel was named the best city in the world by Travel and Leisure magazine, more visitors than ever began to arrive.

San Miguel is also small and relatively relaxed. It’s dense and walkable, to the point that residents do not need a car to get around. It has a large local bar scene, but not many clubs. The weather is consistent and relatively mild year-round. All of these — along with cheaper prices than the United States — have made San Miguel a picture-perfect place for American retirees looking for something different late in life. With retirees generally less motivated to learn Spanish, the influx of English-speakers forced business to cater to that demographic.

While San Miguel is definitely popular, it still is not widely known in the United States. When most Americans think of tourism in Mexico, they imagine the picturesque beaches of Cancún, Los Cabos or Puerto Vallarta. Mexico City is rapidly growing as an international tourist destination and those seeking more of an adventure have probably heard of Oaxaca. Despite the high volume of arrivals, San Miguel de Allende does not have the same level of international recognition as other Mexican destinations.

And it shouldn’t. San Miguel is a small city that has already been drastically gentrified. Homes throughout Centro have been replaced by shops and restaurants, the cost of living continues to climb, and there is a lack of jobs outside of the tourism industry.

So what sets San Miguel apart? It’s at the top of tourism rankings, while other beautiful Bajío towns receive less attention. It has splashes of Mexican culture while still feeling comfortable for Americans.

Does that make San Miguel better than other cities? Yes and no. It feels more Americanized, which makes it attractive to American tourists. But the vibe isn’t just American — it’s international. Expats mingle with locals, and travelers from all over the world visit the cobblestone streets. It’s a destination for a reason, but a lot of those reasons can be found in a lot of other cities in the region — without the crowds, or price tag, that have followed San Miguel’s fame.

Jared Tucker is a summer intern at Mexico News Daily in San Miguel de Allende and a rising senior at the University of Washington in Seattle, where he is the sports editor for The Daily UW. He was previously a fellow at TheFulcrum.us, where he covered public participation in American democracy.

World.title: Seaweed diplomacy: Mexico and Japan to tackle sargassum crisis in new joint program
World.content:
The Foreign Ministry has announced that Japan will be participating in the development of a joint program to address the massive influx of sargassum on Mexico’s shores.

Japan — which has been actively collaborating with Caribbean nations to tackle the sargassum problems plaguing the region — will offer ocean-monitoring technology, specialized equipment including robotics and sensors and financial cooperation.

Additionally, Japan will provide sargassum-collecting ships and vessels adapted for the collection of the macroalgae at sea in order to strengthen Mexico’s capacity to address the situation along its Caribbean beaches.

The collaboration will also feature satellite monitoring, biological decomposition technologies for sargassum and technical training programs through Japan’s International Cooperation Agency, in coordination with Mexico’s Agency for International Development Cooperation.

The project will include academic research, as well as business-oriented research and development. This work will focus on processes for converting the sargassum, as a raw material, into commercially viable products, such as fertilizer, biofuels, building materials and soap.

The goal is to boost marine and nearshore coastal conservation efforts, support integrated coastal management actions and mitigate negative impacts on sectors such as fisheries, public health and tourism.

The announcement came during an Aug. 3 meeting between Foreign Minister Roberto Velasco and his Japanese counterpart, Toshimitsu Motegi, in which they agreed to establish a working group to advance new areas of collaboration to strengthen bilateral relations in the political, economic, scientific and technological spheres.

In a joint statement to the media, they announced the launch of a high-level economic dialogue to boost bilateral trade, which, from January to May this year, amounted to US $9.9 billion, a 4% increase compared to the same period last year.

A few days earlier, President Claudia Sheinbaum pledged 2 billion pesos in federal funds (US $115 million) to battle an influx of sargassum in the state of Quintana Roo.

These funds will be directed toward sargassum control efforts spanning roughly 30 miles of beachfront spanning resorts including Cancún, Playa del Carmen, Puerto Morelos, Tulum and Mahahual.

El secretario de Relaciones Exteriores, Roberto Velasco (@r_velascoa), recibió a su homólogo japonés, el ministro de Asuntos Exteriores de @MofaJapan_en, Motegi Toshimitsu (@moteging), quien realiza una visita de trabajo a nuestro país. En reunión bilateral, ambos titulares de… pic.twitter.com/iaZwAhBjjV — Relaciones Exteriores (@SRE_mx) August 3, 2026

In October, Cancún will host the international EU-Caribbean Global Gateway Conference on Sargassum, with the aim of articulating joint strategies for the containment and management of biomass and sargassum.

The conference is expected to focus on regional cooperation, circular economy solutions and sargassum-harvesting technology.

With reports from Excelsior and MVS Noticias

World.title: The Mexican peso hits its strongest level against the dollar in 6 months
World.content:
Mexico’s currency gained 0.12% vs the U.S. dollar in Thursday trading, extending its rally to 10 straight days after the central bank left interest rates unchanged at its Aug. 6 monetary policy meeting.

The peso closed Thursday at 17.21 to the US dollar and dipped below 17.14 in early trading on Friday, an additional 0.58% gain and its strongest level against the U.S. dollar since Feb. 23.

Forbes México attributed Friday’s early action to a negative U.S. jobs report and said the peso is on pace to appreciate by 1.3% by the end of the week.

Mexico’s currency was also boosted by the central bank’s unanimous decision on Thursday to hold its benchmark rate at 6.50% for a second consecutive meeting, while hinting that rates would remain at the current level for the foreseeable future.

In a statement, Banxico’s board of governors said “headline and core inflation are expected to decline throughout the forecast horizon, albeit more gradually than previously anticipated.”

Headline inflation slowed in July for a fourth consecutive month though the central bank does not expect it to converge to its 3% target until late next year.

In a social media post, Gabriela Siller, director of analysis at Grupo Financerio BASE, said the peso is also appreciating “due to the carry-trade,” a strategy whereby an investor borrows money in a currency with a low interest rate and invests those funds into higher-yielding assets or currencies.

Siller said large global investors are borrowing in the U.S. and Japan, then investing in Mexico, indicating that the peso continues to benefit from a wide interest rate differential (Mexico’s 6.50% policy rate compares favorably to the U.S. Federal Reserve’s 3.50%-3.75% target range).

The newspaper El Economista said the U.S. jobs report (which noted that U.S. nonfarm payrolls fell by 23,000 jobs last month, following a downwardly revised increase of 20,000 jobs the previous month) prompted the market to reduce bets that U.S. interest rates will rise.

Monex Grupo Financiero concurred, saying in a statement that the peso’s advance against the dollar is “driven by the weakness of the dollar and a readjustment of expectations on the direction of the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy” at its next meeting in September.

With reports from El Economista and Forbes México

World.title: After crushing Panama, Mexico’s Under-20 team looks to clinch Olympics berth
World.content:
Close on the heels of El Tri’s impressive World Cup performance, Mexico’s Under-20 men’s squad has qualified for next year’s U-20 World Cup and is on the verge of earning an invitation to the 2028 Olympics.

At the same time, El Tri’s U-23 team has reached the final of the Central America and Caribbean Games where it will face Venezuela on Friday evening in Santo Domingo, the capital of the Dominican Republic.

México vs Panamá | 2026 Concacaf Men's Under-20 Championship Quarterfinals

Watch this video on YouTube

Coach Alex Diego’s U-20 team faces Canada on Friday night in Puebla with a spot in the final on the line. The winner will face either Costa Rica or Team USA who play earlier Friday.

Team Mexico earned its berth in the semifinals by manhandling Panama 4-0 on Wednesday, its fourth straight shut-out in the tournament, which features 12 teams from the Concacaf region competing for four tickets to the World Cup.

All four semifinalists automatically secured invites to the U-20 World Cup, so now the battle is for the lone remaining Concacaf berth in the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.

As the host nation, the U.S. receives one of the two Olympics spots reserved for Concacaf teams.

That means if Team USA defeats Costa Rica and Mexico gets past Canada, El Mini Tri will have clinched a trip to the Olympics regardless of the outcome in Sunday’s final. However, if Costa Rica upsets the Stars-and-Stripes, then Mexico would have to win the final to earn a spot in the Olympics.

Of course, coach Diego’s goal is to hoist the trophy on home soil, but to do so, El Tri will have to overcome a pair of key injuries and the suspension of its first-choice goalie.

Attacking midfielder Santiago Sandoval required surgery after breaking a finger during the team’s 2-0 victory over Costa Rica in the team’s second group stage match, ending his participation in the tournament.

Of equal concern is the status of winger Hugo Camberos, a rising star who has attracted attention from English Premier League clubs.

Camberos has scored in each of Mexico’s matches thus far, but limped off the pitch late in Wednesday’s match and his availability for the semifinal is in question.

The situation in goal for Mexico is of lesser concern since back-up goalie Cristo Navarrete kept a clean sheet in both starts since first-choice keeper Juan Liceaga was shown a red card in El Tri’s second match.

With reports from ESPN, FIFA, N+ and Concacaf

World.title: Meet the woman bringing adobe back to a Maya village
World.content:
Recently, on a trip to Valladolid, I met a woman named Debi Morris, who is bringing adobe back to the Maya village of Ek’ Balam by building a community center out of the all-natural, sustainable material.

Morris fell in love with Ek’ Balam years ago after a taxi dropped her off in the middle of town rather than at the Ek’ Balam ruins. She was captivated by the warm, welcoming people, the laughing children and the surrounding smiles. So she decided to give back using adobe.

What is adobe?

Adobe is a highly durable, all-natural building material that, with proper maintenance and moisture protection, can last for centuries. The proof is still standing in Yotzil, a tiny village in Yucatán. Other historic structures, such as New Mexico’s Palace of the Governors, built in 1610, still stand strong, proving adobe’s longevity.

Made of locally sourced natural materials, adobe recipes vary slightly from place to place depending on the soil and sand. In Ek’ Balam, it is made of high-clay red dirt, sand, dried grass, agave fiber, water and horse manure. Dried beforehand, the manure carries no odor. Builders also added a layer of fermented cactus juice, called baba de nopal, to waterproof the exterior walls.

Adobe also offers high thermal mass, making it ideal for escaping the heat of a Yucatán summer. Because of this thermal efficiency, adobe is growing in popularity as people look for ways to adapt to rising temperatures and reduce air conditioning usage.

Key characteristics of adobe

Composition: Typically consists of blended clay, sand, silt, a fibrous binder (such as chopped straw or agave fibers) and water to bind the mixture and prevent cracking.

Thermal mass: Thick adobe walls absorb heat during the day and slowly release it at night, providing natural climate control in hot, arid environments.

Sustainability: Sourced directly from the earth, adobe is non-toxic, biodegradable and fully recyclable.

Durability: Traditional adobe lasts for centuries but remains susceptible to water erosion, and so requires regular maintenance.

Adapting adobe to local soil

“You’re going to need patience. This is trial and error. There is no specific formula,” an expert advised Morris when she began.

She learned through trial and error that everything depends on local materials. For example, a builder cannot use the same formula in Mérida, even though it is in the same state of Yucatán, because the soil composition differs. In Ek’ Balam, one plot may have red dirt, while a neighboring plot contains entirely different mineral compounds.

“That was an eye-opener,” Morris said.

Not all red dirt works; the clay content must be tested first. “Thank God ours did, so that was a big blessing,” she said. Each layer requires experimentation.

Building in Ek’ Balam

Construction begins with the frame: two layers of wood with a layer of rock in between. Once the frame is set, builders apply the first layer of adobe — a mixture of red dirt, water and dried zacate, a local grass found in surrounding fields. The mixture is combined using hands and feet.

Next comes the layering process: rock, adobe, rock, adobe. After drying for two days, the structure is ready for a second layer consisting of red dirt, sand, water and dried grass. For this layer, the grass is treated with borax to repel insects.

The third layer contains red dirt, fine double-sifted sand, sifted horse manure and agave fibers, which are also treated with borax and cut into 1- to 2-centimeter pieces.

Finally, builders add baba de nopal, or prickly pear cactus extract. The extract is made by removing spines from cactus paddles, chopping them and fermenting them in water for at least 24 hours before straining.

Once the third layer is completed, it is sprayed with water several times a day for five days to retain moisture. On the eighth day, smoothed cracks are treated with warmed cactus extract for waterproofing. Before hurricane season, a final layer of natural linseed oil is applied for additional weather protection without compromising thermal performance.

Reviving an ancient practice

In 2004, Ek’ Balam consisted primarily of traditional palapas. Today, concrete homes have become common, but they trap heat, leading residents to joke that they feel like pizza ovens. Adobe offers a solution rooted in local heritage.

Although adobe construction was an ancient Maya technique, the knowledge was lost generations ago. Morris visited several villages asking abuelitos (grandfathers) if they knew how to make adobe. The answer was almost always, “My grandfather did.” In one nearby village, centuries-old adobe walls are still standing, proving the material’s regional durability.

As a result, Ek’ Balam has welcomed the return of this traditional building method.

Mexico Correspondent for International Living, Bel is an experienced writer, author, photographer and videographer with 500+ articles published both in print and across digital platforms. Living in the Mexican Caribbean for over seven years now, she’s in love with Mexico and has no plans to go anywhere anytime soon.

World.title: Estadio Azteca owners lost an estimated $47M on FIFA’s most profitable World Cup ever
World.content:
Grupo Ollamani, which owns the iconic Estadio Azteca, is perhaps one of the big financial losers of the World Cup after the release of a new financial report, cited by El País, that reveals a multi-million dollar loss.

The holding company, which also owns the publishing subsidiary of Grupo Televisa, reported to the Mexican Stock Exchange (BMV) a net loss of 557.2 million pesos (US $32.2 million) in its second-quarter financial results, primarily associated with the cost of the World Cup.

Led by media mogul Emilio Azcárraga Jean, Grupo Ollamani also estimated an additional financial impact of 255.9 million pesos (US $14.9 million) in July, when the stadium also hosted World Cup matches.

Combined, the total impact would amount to 813 million pesos (US $47.4 million) covering the costs of what’s been described as FIFA operations.

These operations include making Estadio Azteca (also known as Estadio Banorte) available to host five matches and organizing tournament-related activities in Mexico City.

Cause of losses

Ollamani said the reported financial loss was partly due to payments related to a dispute over the use of the stadium’s premium seats and box seats.

In the lead-up to the event, people who owned boxes and premium seats inside the stadium demanded those seats for World Cup matches. But FIFA ultimately required full control. A legal dispute was eventually resolved, whereby Ollamani had to pay FIFA 1 billion pesos (US $58.3 million) so the owners could use their seats.

The company noted that the negative financial impact did not reflect the ordinary course of its operations and stems from extraordinary circumstances related to the World Cup.

“At the same time, investments were made to prepare and modernize Banorte Stadium — representing long-term improvements to its infrastructure, functionality, operational capacity, and digitalization — the benefits of which will extend beyond the World Cup period,” the company said in a statement cited by El País.

Ollamani’s report adds to a broader picture that confirms the World Cup did not generate the expected economic impact. The results were particularly disappointing for the hospitality sector.

In stark contrast, FIFA emerged as the tournament’s biggest financial winner, reportedly generating a record US $15 billion in revenue, which far exceeded its US $11 billion forecast. This performance was mainly fueled by the sale of licensing, broadcasting and hospitality rights, as well as sponsorships and ticketing sales.

With reports from El País, The Guardian and Infobae

World.title: Mexico reestablishes diplomatic relations with Peru: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📉 Inflation falls to 3.12%: Sheinbaum highlighted INEGI data showing headline inflation dropped to 3.12% in July from 3.37% in June, calling the decline “very important.” It’s the lowest rate since May 2020.

Sheinbaum highlighted INEGI data showing headline inflation dropped to 3.12% in July from 3.37% in June, calling the decline “very important.” It’s the lowest rate since May 2020. ✈️ Bettsy Chávez arrives in Mexico: Sheinbaum announced former Peruvian PM Bettsy Chávez was “about to land” in Mexico, after months of asylum at Mexico’s Lima embassy under Brazil’s protection following Peru’s diplomatic break with Mexico last November.

Sheinbaum announced former Peruvian PM Bettsy Chávez was “about to land” in Mexico, after months of asylum at Mexico’s Lima embassy under Brazil’s protection following Peru’s diplomatic break with Mexico last November. 🇲🇽 🇵🇪 Mexico and Peru to restore relations: Sheinbaum said President Keiko Fujimori’s new government granted Chávez safe passage as a “good will” gesture, and announced Mexico and Peru would reestablish diplomatic ties. She reaffirmed support for ousted ex-President Castillo.

Sheinbaum said President Keiko Fujimori’s new government granted Chávez safe passage as a “good will” gesture, and announced Mexico and Peru would reestablish diplomatic ties. She reaffirmed support for ousted ex-President Castillo. ⚖️ Ex-Guerrero governor’s arrest “not political”: Asked about Thursday’s arrest of Ángel Aguirre over alleged concealment of Ayotzinapa-related video evidence, Sheinbaum denied any political motive.

Asked about Thursday’s arrest of Ángel Aguirre over alleged concealment of Ayotzinapa-related video evidence, Sheinbaum denied any political motive. 🚫 No fracking in Tampico-Misantla basin: Sheinbaum reaffirmed her government would follow the expert committee’s recommendation against fracking there, citing Indigenous peoples, rich biodiversity and serious potential environmental impacts.

Sheinbaum reaffirmed her government would follow the expert committee’s recommendation against fracking there, citing Indigenous peoples, rich biodiversity and serious potential environmental impacts. 🥑 Officials to discuss avocado certification suspension: Sheinbaum said Mexican officials would meet U.S. Embassy representatives Friday morning to address security concerns behind the suspension, aiming to resume Michoacán avocado exports. Why today’s mañanera matters

Today’s mañanera was important as President Claudia Sheinbaum spoke about a wide range of significant topics.

They included inflation, diplomatic relations with Peru, the arrest of a former governor, fracking and the suspension of U.S. avocado certifications in Michoacán.

Sheinbaum acknowledges decline in inflation

At the very start of her press conference, Sheinbaum highlighted that Mexico’s headline inflation rate fell to 3.12% in July, per data published by the national statistics agency INEGI on Friday.

She noted that the headline rate fell to that level from 3.37% in June, and described the decline as “very important.”

The inflation rate in July — just above the Bank of Mexico’s 3% target — was the lowest rate since May 2020.

Sheinbaum announces arrival of Bettsy Chávez to Mexico

Sheinbaum told reporters that former Peruvian Prime Minister Bettsy Chávez was “about to land in Mexico.”

She noted that Chávez, who briefly served as prime minister during the presidency of Pedro Castillo, stayed in Mexico’s Embassy in Peru for several months. Last November, the government of Peru severed diplomatic relations with Mexico after Chávez, who was accused of rebellion, was granted asylum at the Mexican Embassy in Lima.

“This embassy had to close because Peru broke off relations with Mexico and she remained [in the embassy] under the protection of Brazil, to whom we are very grateful,” Sheinbaum said.

The president said that Chávez was granted “safe passage” to travel to Mexico by the new Peruvian government, led by President Keiko Fujimori. She said that a Mexican Air Force plane traveled to the South American country to collect the ex-prime minister and bring her to Mexico.

Sheinbaum: Mexico and Peru to reestablish relations

Sheinbaum said that the granting of safe passage to Chávez was an act of “good will” from the government of President Fujimori “toward Mexico.”

She subsequently announced that Mexico and Peru would reestablish diplomatic relations.

“I don’t know if I can announce it now or not, but I’m going to announce it. With this [act of good will], relations with Peru are going to be reestablished,” Sheinbaum said.

“And we, as always, as we have done, are going to continue defending President Castillo,” said Sheinbaum, who last September described the 2022 ousting of the ex-president by the Peruvian Congress as a “coup.”

“… The new government of Peru knows that,” she said.

Sheinbaum: Arrest of ex-governor of Guerrero has nothing to do with politics

A reporter asked the president about the arrest on Thursday of former Guerrero Governor Ángel Aguirre, who is alleged to have ordered the concealment of security camera video footage that showed the bus on which students from the Ayotzinapa Rural Teachers College were traveling at the time it was stopped by police in Iguala, Guerrero, on Sept. 26, 2014. Forty-three students were abducted and presumably murdered after the bus was stopped.

Sheinbaum said that the arrest of Aguirre — governor of Guerrero between 2011 and 2014 — was the result of months of work by the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR). She said that the FGR has adopted “new ways of investigating” the Ayotzinapa case.

“It may be the same evidence, but now they’re deepening [the investigation] through different mechanisms, many of which involve scientific analysis,” Sheinbaum said.

Asked whether the arrest of Aguirre had a “political background,” the president responded: “It has nothing to do with a political issue. It’s part of an investigation.”

As governor, Aguirre represented the Democratic Revolution Party, or PRD, but he was previously affiliated with the Institutional Revolutionary Party, or PRI, for decades. Mexico’s president at the time of the students’ disappearance was Enrique Peña Nieto, who represented the PRI both as president between 2012 and 2018 and governor of México state between 2005 and 2011.

Sheinbaum explains why there will be no fracking in the Tampico-Misantla basin

Sheinbaum reiterated that no final decision has been taken regarding the commencement of large-scale fracking in two shale basins in northern Mexico.

Subsequently, a day after an expert fracking committee publicly announced its recommendation against fracking in the resource-rich Tampico-Misantla basin in Veracruz and Tamaulipas, the president reaffirmed that her government would heed that advice.

“In the Tampico-Misantla basin, [there will be] no [fracking] there,” Sheinbaum said.

“Why? Because there are Indigenous peoples, because the nature is very rich, because the environmental impacts would be very serious,” she said.

Despite those remarks, Sheinbaum has asserted that the use of “new technologies” can make fracking a sustainable practice that doesn’t harm the environment.

Mexican and US officials to discuss suspension of avocado certifications

Sheinbaum told reporters that Mexican officials would meet with U.S. Embassy officials on Friday morning to discuss the U.S. government’s suspension of avocado certifications in Michoacán due to security concerns.

She said that the “objective” of today’s meeting is to address the U.S. government’s concerns with a view to resuming avocado exports to the United States.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: Costa Rica Prices Fall Again as Inflation Remains Below Zero
World.content:
Consumer prices in Costa Rica fell again in July, reversing two months of increases and keeping the country in a prolonged period of negative inflation. The Consumer Price Index fell 0.47% in July compared with June. That followed monthly increases of 0.27% in May and 0.71% in June. For the first seven months of 2026, prices are now down 0.40%, while the year-over-year inflation rate stands at -0.28%.

Costa Rica has now recorded negative year-over-year inflation for 15 consecutive months, dating back to May 2025. Inflation also remains well below the Central Bank’s 2026 target of 3%, with a tolerance range of 2% to 4%. July’s decline was broad enough to affect eight of the 13 major categories used to calculate the index.

Transportation prices fell 0.89%, while food and nonalcoholic beverages declined 0.78%. Recreation, sports and culture recorded the largest percentage decrease among the major categories, falling 1.50%. Information and communication prices declined 0.93%. Some of the sharpest price drops involved travel.

International airline tickets fell 16.69% during the month, while overseas tourism packages declined 7.75%. Egg prices dropped 11.90%, taxi transportation fell 8.02%, and mobile telephone services decreased 1.04%. Not everything became cheaper. Housing rent increased 0.16%, tomatoes rose 3.51%, gasoline increased 0.23%, and sweet peppers climbed 6.11%. Shampoo and hair conditioner prices rose 1.17%.

Overall, 42% of the 293 goods and services tracked in the index became cheaper in July. Another 33% increased in price, while 25% remained unchanged. The July figures are also important because they are the first calculated under Costa Rica’s updated Consumer Price Index methodology.

The new index uses June 2026 as its base month and tracks 293 goods and services, compared with 289 under the previous system. The weight assigned to different household expenses was updated using information from the 2024 National Household Income and Expenditure Survey, allowing the index to better reflect how Costa Rican households currently spend their money.

The new methodology does not itself cause prices or inflation to rise or fall. Historical data have been linked to the new index so that major inflation trends can continue to be compared over time. One important distinction in the latest figures is that although prices fell sharply from June to July, the annual inflation rate actually became slightly less negative. Year-over-year inflation moved from -0.32% in June to -0.28% in July, meaning it edged closer to zero.

The stronger downward movement is visible in the monthly figure and in year-to-date prices, which shifted from a 0.08% increase through June to a 0.40% decline through July. Costa Rica’s extended period of unusually low inflation has also become an important issue for monetary policy. The Central Bank cut its policy interest rate by 0.25 percentage points in July to 3.00%, with inflation remaining below its target range as economic growth showed signs of slowing.

For consumers, falling prices in areas such as food, transportation and travel can provide immediate relief. But a prolonged period of economy-wide deflation is different from simply having cheaper individual products. Persistent negative inflation can become a concern if it coincides with weaker demand, slower business activity and slower economic growth.

The next monthly inflation report will provide another indication of whether July’s decline was temporary or whether consumer prices are entering another sustained period of contraction.

World.title: Costa Rica Approves New Rules for Nighttime Ambulance Flights
World.content:
Costa Rica has approved a national protocol governing nighttime air ambulance flights, closing out roughly ten months of uncertainty that began when Civil Aviation barred the practice at most of the airfields last October. Under the framework, night medical flights are permitted at six locations: the airfields at Limón, Palmar Sur and Coto 47 near Ciudad Neily, along with Tobías Bolaños in Pavas, Daniel Oduber in Liberia and Juan Santamaría in Alajuela.

Juan Santamaría must now serve as the arrival point for every nighttime medical flight in the country. The selection came down largely to which fields have runway lighting and a permanent police presence, both treated as prerequisites for safe operations after dark. Coto 47 has both, including a base of the Air Vigilance Service, and Palmar Sur received substantial state investment in lighting and security in recent years.

Left off the approved list are several airfields serving high-traffic tourist areas, among them Tamarindo, Quepos and Puerto Jiménez. Pilots had also identified Cóbano and Nicoya as essential for reaching patients in coastal and peninsular communities far from major hospitals.

The protocol restricts these flights to patients in critical condition whose lives are at immediate risk and who cannot safely wait for daylight. It sets out an eleven-step process that begins when the Costa Rican Social Security Fund identifies an emergency case, moves through coordination with the Air Vigilance Service and Civil Aviation, and ends with a private operator carrying out the flight once conditions and authorization align.

Officials say exceptions outside the formal protocol will still be permitted when a patient’s life is at stake. The rules were drafted jointly by the Ministry of Health, Civil Aviation, the Social Security Fund and the Air Vigilance Service, and are to be reviewed annually.

The finalized protocol ends a dispute that began with a directive issued on October 9 of last year, which prohibited takeoffs and landings between sunset and sunrise at uncontrolled airfields nationwide. Civil Aviation argued the flights had operated for decades without a formal regulatory framework and that medical operations must meet the same technical and legal standards as any other flight.

Transportation Minister Efraím Zeledón Leiva and Social Security Fund president Mónica Taylor defended the restriction at a press conference in February, characterizing the volume of genuinely urgent flights as minimal. Taylor said many transfers went to private hospitals and involved minor complaints. Zeledón referred to irregular commercial arrangements around the flights at Tobías Bolaños, and maintained that extreme emergencies were still being authorized.

That position drew immediate pushback from pilots, ambulance operators and physicians inside the Social Security system. The Fund’s own emergency and disaster center warned the restriction was delaying transfers of patients who needed higher-capacity hospitals, and the hospital in Ciudad Neily fell back on ground transfers with police escorts to speed the run into the Central Valley.

Ricardo Hernández, a paramedic and operations manager at the air and ground transport company SAAT, said roughly 700 people a year need urgent air transport in Costa Rica for medical reasons, and that close to half of all transfers happen at night. Operators separately reported hundreds of night ambulance flights annually before the restriction took effect, and said the country had recorded no accidents in night operations at uncontrolled airfields in eighteen years.

An analysis presented by pilots counted 3,130 nighttime ambulance flights over the previous decade, an average of about 285 a year, without a serious incident. Pilots also noted that the October directive landed at the start of high tourist season, when visitors are more likely to be injured in remote or coastal areas.

For anyone traveling to the more remote parts of the country, including popular surf and beach towns that are not on the approved list, the practical effect is unchanged. A serious nighttime medical emergency in those areas will still mean a lengthy ground transfer rather than an air evacuation, because every flight must now either originate or terminate at one of the six designated locations.

Civil Aviation issued temporary technical standards for qualifying airfields earlier this year while the permanent framework was being finalized. Those interim rules are now replaced. Whether additional airfields can be brought onto the list will depend on lighting, perimeter security and staffing upgrades that have not yet been funded or scheduled.

World.title: Costa Rica Investigates Fernández and Chaves Over Police Director Appointment
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Attorney General’s Office has opened a criminal investigation involving President Laura Fernández and Finance Minister Rodrigo Chaves over the appointment of the head of the Policía de Control Fiscal, or Fiscal Control Police. The investigation centers on the June appointment of Katherine Tenorio Ruiz as director of the police, which operates under the Ministry of Finance and is responsible for combating tax evasion, customs violations and contraband.

Prosecutors opened the case following a complaint questioning whether the government legally changed the requirements for the position shortly before Tenorio was appointed. To be clear, the opening of a criminal case does not mean Fernández or Chaves committed a crime. Prosecutors are now examining whether any actions connected to the regulatory change and appointment violated Costa Rican law.

At the center of the dispute is a requirement contained in Costa Rica’s General Police Law. The law establishes that directors of police forces must hold at least the police rank of comisionado, while deputy directors must hold at least the rank of comandante. That requirement had previously been examined by Costa Rica’s Procuraduría General de la República, the government’s legal advisory authority.

In a 2021 ruling requested by the Ministry of Finance, the Procuraduría determined that directors and deputy directors of police under the Executive Branch must meet the minimum police-rank requirements established by law. The ruling specifically addressed the application of those requirements to bodies such as the Fiscal Control Police.

The controversy intensified because of a regulatory change approved shortly before Tenorio took office. On June 9, Fernández and Chaves signed an Executive Decree changing the regulations governing the Fiscal Control Police. The decree established professional and technical qualifications for the director and deputy director positions, but also explicitly stated that appointments to those posts would not require possession of police ranks.

The decree was published in the official government newspaper La Gaceta on June 18. Four days later, on June 22, the Ministry of Finance announced Tenorio as the new director. The legal question now facing investigators is whether the Executive Branch could use a decree, which is a lower-level regulation, to remove a qualification established by national law.

The complaint that prompted the investigation was filed by Frente Amplio lawmaker Antonio Trejos. It asks prosecutors to examine the actions of Fernández, Chaves and any other officials involved in preparing, reviewing or approving the decree and Tenorio’s appointment. It also asks authorities to determine whether Tenorio held the required rank of comisionado when she took office.

Tenorio’s official government biography does not identify her as holding that rank. However, that absence alone does not establish that she does not hold it, and prosecutors have not announced a conclusion on that question. Tenorio has substantial professional experience relevant to the work of the Fiscal Control Police. She is an attorney, notary and criminologist and holds a master’s degree in Law and International Business.

She previously worked as an investigator with the Fiscal Control Police and as a criminologist in investigations involving the Panama Papers and complex fraud. She has also worked as a legal adviser in the Vice Ministry of Telecommunications and in the Arms and Explosives Control Department of the Ministry of Public Security.

The controversy therefore focuses primarily on the legal requirement for police rank rather than Tenorio’s academic or professional credentials. The government’s June decree said the new requirements were intended to ensure that the Fiscal Control Police is led by qualified professionals capable of handling its specialized responsibilities involving tax, customs and financial investigations.

The investigation comes at a politically sensitive moment for the Fernández administration, as tensions between the Executive Branch and Costa Rica’s judicial institutions have escalated in recent weeks. Thousands of people demonstrated in San José and other parts of the country on Thursday in support of the Judiciary and Costa Rica’s system of checks and balances following disputes over judicial funding, court decisions and the authority of different branches of government.

The investigation into the Fiscal Control Police appointment is still at an early stage. Prosecutors have not announced charges against Fernández or Chaves, nor have they determined that the appointment or decree was unlawful. As of this morning, no new public explanation from the government had been located addressing the Fiscalía’s decision to open the case.

World.title: Costa Rica Offers Panama Two-Part Plan to End Trade Block
World.content:
Costa Rica has presented Panama with a two-part proposal aimed at ending a seven-year agricultural trade dispute that has blocked meat, dairy products, fruit and other Costa Rican goods from entering the neighboring country. Foreign Trade Minister Indiana Trejos sent the proposal Wednesday to Panama’s minister of commerce and industries, Julio Moltó. The plan combines practical steps to address Panama’s export concerns with international arbitration to resolve the legal case stalled at the World Trade Organization.

The first part would establish a memorandum of understanding covering products Panama wants to export to Costa Rica. Under the proposed agreement, Costa Rica would process Panama’s export applications with the assistance of an international organization. The outside participation is intended to make the process more transparent and give Panama greater confidence that its requests will receive fair treatment.

The second part would send Panama’s appeal in the agricultural dispute to a special WTO arbitration process. Both countries would agree in advance to accept the arbitrators’ decision, providing a way around the prolonged shutdown of the WTO’s regular appeals system. The WTO Appellate Body has been unable to hear cases since December 2019 because it lacks enough appointed members. Panama appealed the ruling against its restrictions in February 2025, effectively leaving the case unresolved despite Costa Rica’s earlier victory.

The dispute began between January 2019 and June 2020, when Panama stopped allowing imports of several Costa Rican agricultural and food products. The restrictions have affected strawberries, fresh pineapples, bananas, plantains, dairy products and meat from Costa Rican cattle, pigs and poultry. Sixteen Costa Rican meat and dairy facilities lost access to the Panamanian market after their sanitary approvals were not renewed.

Panama defended the measures as necessary to protect public health, agriculture and local producers.Its concerns included pesticide residue detected in strawberry shipments, a pest associated with pineapples and the potential regional threat from a banana disease. Panama also required Costa Rican meat and dairy exporters to restart parts of the sanitary approval process.

Costa Rica argued that the restrictions were not supported by adequate scientific evidence and were more restrictive than necessary. After consultations failed, Costa Rica formally brought the case to the WTO in January 2021. A dispute panel was established later that year, although staffing shortages, the complexity of the case and translation requirements delayed the final decision.

The panel’s report was released in December 2024 and largely supported Costa Rica’s position. It found that several of Panama’s measures were not based on sufficient scientific evidence and that less restrictive alternatives were available. The panel also found that Panama had treated some Costa Rican products differently from comparable imports allowed from other countries.

The ruling recommended that Panama bring its restrictions into line with international trade rules. Panama appealed, but the inactive WTO appeals system prevented the ruling from becoming a final, enforceable resolution. The new arbitration proposal is designed to break that deadlock without requiring either government to abandon the formal trade process.

The conflict became more politically tense after President Laura Fernández took office in May. Fernández ordered Costa Rica’s foreign ministry to pursue international action over the restrictions, arguing that farmers and food producers had been harmed by years of blocked exports.

Panamanian President José Raúl Mulino responded by suspending planned electricity sales to Costa Rica and accusing the Costa Rican government of escalating the dispute publicly rather than resolving it through direct talks. The Costa Rican Electricity Institute said at the time that the country was not buying electricity from Panama and did not expect to do so during 2026.

The two governments later reopened diplomatic contact and discussed a broader agenda including trade, security, migration, customs and regional cooperation. Costa Rica’s latest proposal represents the clearest attempt so far to convert those discussions into a formal settlement.

The plan offers Panama a supervised process for its own export requests while giving Costa Rica a path toward a binding decision on the restrictions affecting its agricultural products. A settlement would reopen a nearby market for Costa Rican farmers and food companies while giving Panamanian exporters a clearer route into Costa Rica.

The proposal now depends on whether Panama accepts the two agreements or requests changes before moving forward.

World.title: Election Season Starts – Poll of UDP convention in the Culture Capital this weekend
World.content:
Election Season Starts – Poll of UDP convention in the Culture Capital this weekend

The views expressed in this article are those of the writer and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News

By Dr. Philip Castillo: Municipal elections are eight months away and the first steps start with party conventions to select Mayoral and councilor candidates. The Opposition UDP will hold its convention this weekend on August 9. The convention will feature two candidates vying for Mayor, and each candidate has his/her respective slate of six councilor candidates. Hence the ballot will have a total of 14 candidates. Only 7 can win.

Castillo Poll # 3 of 2026 presents the findings of a poll conducted in Dangriga over the weekend of August 1st to 3rd. For a municipal election, the target population is the registered voters of that municipality. However for a party convention, that target population deliberately excludes known members of the other party. So for the upcoming UDP convention, the party will not allow known PUP members to vote. That presents a major challenge since ascertaining who is a “known PUP” is a subjective endeavour. This also means that for polling purposes, the actual target population is unknown.

The above, notwithstanding…here goes:

Table 1 – Mayor

Source: Castillo Poll #3 of 2026 (August, 2026)

Table 2 – Councilors

Source: Castillo Poll #3 of 2026 (August, 2026)

A poll is a sample randomly drawn from a given population. I’ve already noted the challenges of identifying the target population. Yet another challenge undertaking any poll is that there WILL always be a margin of error. The margin of error relates to the extent to which the mean or the average of the sample (which is known) varies from the mean or the parameter of wider population (which is unknown). This degree of variance is expressed as a plus (+) or minus (-) because the variation can go in either direction. Polling organizations generally use a margin of error of +/- 3 percentage points. This poll had a margin of error of +/- 9%.

Another statistic that must be noted is the degree of confidence. This refers to the extent to which if you draw repeat samples you realistically expect the same results. For this poll the degree of confidence was at 90 %. This means that if the sample was drawn a hundred times, in ninety out of those one hundred times, the expected result would be the very same. Polling organizations generally use a degree of confidence of 95%.

From my projections, I estimate the voting population on Sunday August 9th 2026 to be around 695 voters. However accounting for the margin of error, the voting population could be as low as 9% less than 695. Or as high as 9% above 695. The actual ranges are 633 to 757 .

Tables 1 and 2 above are redone using these numbers to estimate actual votes.

Table 3 – Mayor

Source: Castillo Poll #3 of 2026 (August, 2026)

Table 4 – Councilors

Source: Castillo Poll #3 of 2026 (August, 2026)

Accounting for the margin of error, Dayton Sabal, Jamall Swaso and John Sabal are still EXPECTED to win. Elsworth Magdaleno and Albourne Mashall are LIKELY to win. For the sixth and final council seat, probabilistically and because the numbers fall within the range of the margin of error, Marsha Mejia and Cindy Fajardo are favorites BUT Steven Laurie and Francis Marin have a punchers chance.

Dr. Philip Castillo is a development economist and an independent pollster. Send comments to [email protected].

World.title: Santander responds to Belize River fish kill, says factory does not routinely discharge process water into river
World.content:
Santander responds to Belize River fish kill, says factory does not routinely discharge process water into river

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Santander Sugar Group (SSG) has issued a statement amid concerns over the recent loss of aquatic life in the Belize River Valley, saying it is cooperating fully with an ongoing investigation by the Department of the Environment (DoE) and other government agencies.

In a statement issued Friday, August 7, Santander said it is “deeply saddened” by the reported loss of aquatic life and has granted authorities unrestricted access to its facilities and operations. The company did not accept responsibility for the fish kill, and said it welcomes the completion of the government’s investigation.

Santander said its processing facility operates as a closed-loop system in which process water is recovered, cooled where necessary and reused. According to the company, there is no continuous process effluent stream or routine discharge of high-temperature process water from its factory into the Belize River.

The company also stressed that its canals are not connected to Labouring Creek and said its operations account for approximately 12 percent of the agricultural land within the broader watershed.

Santander has faced environmental scrutiny in the past. In 2012, the company’s development was linked to the dredging of a large canal through the Labouring Creek Jaguar Corridor Wildlife Sanctuary, and in 2016 government authorities cited Santander for breaches of its Environmental Compliance Plan following investigations into activities affecting environmentally sensitive areas.

The present investigation, however, remains ongoing, and authorities have not publicly established that Santander caused the reported aquatic deaths. Santander says it will review any findings and recommendations issued by regulators and remains committed to environmental compliance and protection of the Belize River watershed.

World.title: NICH supports 2nd National EdTech Summit
World.content:
NICH supports 2nd National EdTech Summit

By Zoila Palma: The National Institute of Culture and History (NICH) participated in the 2nd National EdTech Summit, highlighting the importance of preserving Belize’s culture and identity as technology continues to transform education.

NICH said its participation reflected the guiding principle of Minister of Education, Culture, Science and Technology, Hon. Francis Fonseca, that “Culture is WHO and WHAT we are.” The institute said this principle continues to guide its efforts to ensure Belize’s heritage, creativity and identity remain central to the country’s digital transformation in education.

During the summit, NICH showcased exhibits and initiatives from the Institute of Archaeology, USpaces, Houses of Culture in Orange Walk, Corozal and Benque Viejo del Carmen, as well as the Belize Music Project. These initiatives demonstrated how culture can enrich learning, encourage innovation and inspire future generations.

NICH said it is working with the Ministry of Education, Culture, Science and Technology to promote a future where technology strengthens education while culture remains central to Belize’s national identity.

World.title: Kingston Container Terminal employees arrested as police probe $1 billion cocaine bust
World.content:
file photo

KINGSTON, Jamaica — A major multi-agency operation is underway at the Kingston Container Terminal after police uncovered a suspected cocaine smuggling network linked to the facility.

The operation, led by the Firearms and Narcotics Investigation Division (FNID) and the Jamaica Customs Agency, with support from the Specialised Operations Branch, follows the seizure of cocaine valued at approximately $1 billion earlier this week.

Several employees at the terminal have been arrested as investigators probe their alleged involvement in a drug trafficking syndicate operating from the facility.

Authorities said the investigation is ongoing and further updates will be provided soon.

World.title: Surviving burn victims from Guardsman fire return home
World.content:
Fabian Brown, one of the two surviving men of four initially injured in a fire returns home after treatment in the US alongside his wife Myeisha (out of frame)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Two of the four men injured in an explosion at a garage adjacent to Guardsman Group-Beryllium Limited headquarters, on South Camp Road, have returned to Jamaica following intensive burn treatment overseas.

Fabian Brown was one of two airlifted back to Jamaica on Friday in the company of his wife, Myesha, who spoke to Observer Online.

“The journey, I must say, has been rough. It has been hard,” she said.

Despite this, Myesha had high praise for those involved in her husband’s care, including the staff of Wellstar Cobb Burn Centre and Trinity Airlines as well as the Burn Foundation of Jamaica and their Crisis Support Charity arm.

She issued an urgent call to corporate Jamaica to put their support behind the foundation.

“I encourage Jamaica, corporate Jamaica, to support the Crisis Support Charity…it’s not just supporting the survivors. It’s not just burned people alone. But overall, if you look at what they have done, they’ve been doing good. And if it wasn’t for them, we would not have been able to leave here and for him to get that thorough care that he needs.”

Guardsman had committed to supporting the men who were injured in the May 27 incident, which firefighters said happened before 9:00 am while welding work was being done on the property.

Brown was airlifted along with Damian Walters and a third man for care overseas after the incident. The fourth man passed away at a local hospital before he could be airlifted. Walters also passed away while undergoing treatment overseas.

READ: Employee injured in Guardsman fire succumbs to injuries

Meanwhile, as Myesha expressed her sorrow at the two deaths, she and Fabian are now preparing for a life that may look significantly different.

“The journey is just beginning. People might think, oh, you get burned, you’re healed. This is a life-changing experience. People need to understand that when you experience burns and you’re recovering, it takes years, and your life will never be the same. The sun, something that we take for granted, you can no longer go in that,” she said.

Despite the challenges, she expressed faith in God and gratitude for her husband’s life.

“Not until you have someone who has been affected severely by burns can you know what that journey is, and I’m thankful, grateful that Fabian is still here with us,” she said.

World.title: 3-year-old dies in suspected drowning in Westmoreland
World.content:
WESTMORELAND, Jamaica — Westmoreland police are investigating a suspected drowning following the death of a three-year-old child at a popular attraction in Little Bay, Westmoreland, on Independence Day.

The deceased has been identified as Kayson Barrett of an Ocean Pointe address in the parish of Hanover.

Reports from the police indicate that around 2:45 pm, the child, his mother, and another relative were at the attraction when he reportedly wandered away unnoticed, prompting his parent and the relative to launch a search.

Barrett was later found in a swimming pool on the property and taken to the lifeguard on duty, who immediately attempted to administer cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR).

The child was subsequently rushed to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

The police were unable to say if any charges are pending.

— Anthony Lewis.

World.title: Card, Douglas win silver in 100m at World U20 Championships
World.content:
Jamaica's Shanoya Douglas parades with the Jamaican flag after winning the silver medal in the women's 100m on Thursday's second day of the 2026 World Athletics Under 20 championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon. Douglas, the world leader was beaten by American Maria Maxwell. (Photos: Paul Reid)

OREGON, USA — Jamaica’s Gary Card and Shanoya Douglas won silver medals in the men and women’s 100m on Thursday night at the World Athletics Under-20 Championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon.

It was the first medals for Jamaica at the championships, putting them in ninth position on the medals tables.

Americans Tate Taylor and Mia Maxwell delighted the home fans by winning the double, only the second time athletes from the same country had taken both gold medals at the same under-20 championships after Americans Noah Lyles and Candace Hill achieved the feat in 2016 in Bydgoszcz, Poland.

Card got off to a fast start but was chased and caught by Tate who passed him to win in a personal best 9.94 seconds (0.1m/s), the Jamaican second in 10.05 seconds. South Africa’s Marko Ferreira took the bronze with 10.16 seconds.

Maxwell got the edge over Douglas at the start and held off the Jamaican to the tape, running 11.14 seconds (-0.1m/s). Douglas finished second in 11.17 seconds with Italy’s Kelly Ann Maevane Doualla Edimo third in 11.27 seconds. Theianna-Lee Terrelonge was sixth in 11.37 seconds

It was the first time in 10 years an American won the women’s 100m and snapped the four-championships winning streak by the Jamaicans – Briana Williams in 2018, Tina Clayton in 2021 and 2022 and Alana Reid in 2024.

Also on Thursday, thrower Able Mills failed to record a legal throw in both the women’s discus and shot put finals that were held within two hours of each other.

Mills had thrown distances close to her lifetime bests to qualify for both finals but failed to make a legal mark in either.

Jamaica also failed to qualify any runner in the 400m finals set for Friday afternoon, all four failing to get past their semifinals.

Jabari Matheson who was running his fourth 400m race in two days, placed sixth in his semi-final in 47.29 seconds, the first time he failed to go under the 47.00 second mark at the championships.

Jason Pitter failed to get up to his high standards, and was sixth in his semi-final in 46.50 seconds after he advanced on time from the first round.

Daniellia Dixon was fifth in her semi-final in 53.77 seconds and Shameika McLean, who had run three times since the start of the championships, just failed to get into the final after placing fourth in her semis in 54.24 seconds.

-Paul A Reid
