World.title: Fingers crossed for ganja
World.content:
Walter Melbourne, director of licensing and applications at the Cannabis Licensing Authority, speaking at this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

THERE is no indication when Jamaica could see its first cannabis company registered on the local stock market, but key players in the sector are hopeful it will happen soon.

As global powers equivocate with the classification of the weed, leaders at Jamaica’s Cannabis Licensing Authority (CLA) are keeping their fingers crossed that the tight hold on the plant will be relaxed to allow the medical and commercial industry to grow.

During this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange the top brass of the CLA pointed to the recent indication by the United States (US) that cannabis could be moved from a Schedule I drug to Schedule III.

That announcement earlier this year was welcomed by players in the industry; however, months later it is not clear where cannabis will sit on the US drug scheduling list as US lawmakers continue debate on the matter.

According to CLA Chief Executive Officer Farrah Blake, “rescheduling of ganja would answer a lot of questions” in relation to access to the banking system and eligibility for grants for farmers and businesses in the industry.

As it relates to Jamaica possibly seeing its first regulated marijuana company hit the stock market, chair of the CLA Dr Nadeen Spence said, “We have to keep our fingers crossed” that marijuana will in fact be reclassified to reflect a Schedule III status.

It would, she argued, “translate into something that reassures the banking sector that ganja is not as risky as it currently is”.

Although uncertainty looms over ganja’s position on the list, Walter Melbourne, director of licensing and applications at the CLA, said there nevertheless needs to be an appreciation for the progress being achieved by the entity.

“Wherever we are now, it is a metamorphosis, a giant leap. In the 1970s, if you were caught with even a small amount it was a mandatory prison sentence. Some of our prominent people in society have had trouble. There was a lot of persecution and prosecution. Where we are now is really a massive step. I am making the point to say, who knows. Let’s keep going and we might very well see it there one day,” said Melbourne.

The US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) describes Schedule I drugs as substances or chemicals with no currently accepted medical use and have a high potential for abuse, such as heroin and ecstasy.

Schedule III drugs are substances or chemicals with a moderate to low potential for physical and psychological dependence. The DEA states that drugs listed under Schedule III are considered to have less potential to be abused than Schedule I and II drugs.

The US Department of Justice has already officially reclassified cannabis as less dangerous, marking a major shift in that country’s drug policy.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche changed the classifications of products containing marijuana that are covered by the Food and Drug Administration or that have received a state medical marijuana licence.

They will move cannabis from a Schedule I narcotic like heroin to a Schedule III drug — on par with Tylenol with codeine.

Marijuana remains illegal at the federal level. Despite the federal ban, most US states have legalised the medical or recreational use of marijuana, and many have shops where it can be purchased legally.

World.title: Come Alive delivers!
World.content:
H.U.M.B.L.E (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

The East Lawns of King’s House became more than a venue on Saturday night. For several hours it was transformed by a sea of worshippers into a space of praise.

It was the perfect start to the month in which Jamaica celebrates its 64th year of Independence as hundreds gathered for the second staging of the Come Alive Gospel concert.

Dubbed a national call to worship, it became evident from the very first note that this was no ordinary musical showcase. It was an invitation — one that patrons answered with lifted hands, tear-filled eyes, and hearts fully surrendered to praise.

Christian worship, often confined to church walls, spilled freely across the grounds as saints gave their whole beings to the moment, proving that praise can command the same passion and intensity as any secular spectacle.

Yet, unlike the fleeting excitement of entertainment, what unfolded at King’s House was rooted in something deeper — an encounter with the divine.

The group H.U.M.B.L.E opened the main event with a spirited rendition of the Jamaican National Anthem, their harmonies echoing across the venue before they returned with a medley of old-time gospel favourites that ignited a revival spirit which lingered for the remainder of the programme.

That spirit only intensified when Petra Kaye took the stage. With a commanding voice that carried effortlessly across the lawns, the singer brought a fervency reminiscent of the “old-time religion” of generations past. Songs such as Crown Him, I Can Recommend My God, and the beloved Sovereign God Medley became more than performances. Attendees sang along with conviction, their praises rising heavenward like incense.

Johnmark Wiggan followed with a deeply personal set, sharing snippets of a testimony marked by trials that, by his own admission, should have destroyed him had it not been for the hand of God. As he delivered songs including Still Deh Yah, Because You Are Good, Run Me Dung, and Testimony, an intimate atmosphere settled over the audience. Eyes closed, hands lifted, and voices trembling with emotion, patrons appeared to journey back to defining moments in their Christian walk, as if remembering prayers answered, valleys crossed, and the faithfulness of God through every season.

The praise continued with Jermaine Edwards, whose set list included Peace In My Soul, Not Forget, Naa Bow, and Make You Smile. By the time he closed with his hit single Beautiful Day, the East Lawns had erupted into celebration.

Joy radiated from faces of attendance across the venue and, for a while, worries seemed to dissolve beneath the weight of worship.

Then came the evening’s international headliner, Michael W Smith.

Making a grand entrance, the singer’s band set the tone with a dramatic prelude before the legendary worship leader greeted the crowd.

“Jamaica, it’s so good to be here,” he said to great applause.

“We have a set list, but we might not stick to it,” he added, signalling that while plans had been made, the direction of the evening ultimately belonged to God.

Without hesitation, Smith launched into crowd favourites Open The Eyes of My Heart and Draw Me Close To You. The response was immediate. Worshippers surrendered themselves to the music.

Pausing between songs, Smith reflected on the immeasurable love of God; a love, he reminded the audience, that surpasses human understanding despite the Creator’s infinite power. He then transitioned into

Arms Around the Sun, a moving reminder of God’s unwavering affection for humanity.

Reflecting on his time in Jamaica, the singer shared that beyond the island’s beauty, it was the warmth and spirit of its people that had touched him most.

“Honestly, I love the people. I love your country, and I bless your country with all the promises of God,” he said before delivering favourites such as The Air I Breathe, Lord, I Give You My Heart, Above All, and There Is None Like You.

“Here is my prayer for Jamaica — at least one of them,” he said before leading the audience into

Let It Rain.

His set also included stirring renditions of Waymaker, Agnus Dei (Worthy Is The Lamb), Goodness of God, and Awesome God.

Had the curtains closed at that very moment, patrons would likely have left fulfilled, their faces glowing from an evening already overflowing with worship. But Come Alive still had one final offering.

Papa San emerged to deafening cheers, lifting the energy to even greater heights.

From the opening notes of Glory God, the veteran deejay had the audience captivated.

Songs like Hell Bruk Loose and Step Pan Di Enemy transformed the East Lawns into a grand dance floor as patrons abandoned their seats, dancing and rejoicing with uninhibited praise.

“I haven’t been here in a while ennu, so mek we go down memory lane likkle bit,” he told the crowd before launching into a nostalgic rendition of

Pop Style.

But amid the excitement, his message remained clear: “Worship should be a part of your life. Sing about what Jesus did for you,” he encouraged before performing Smile Again, a testimony of redemption and restoration.

Long after the final song faded, the message of the evening remained.

According to Eric Hosin, chairman of the Come Alive Collective, the success of the event was possible only because of God’s grace.

“We’re happy and giving God thanks and all the praises because this was only because of his goodness and his mercy,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

“People seemed to have enjoyed themselves. Papa San closing was just something else, and we’re giving God thanks. We saw worship taking place with Michael W Smith, Jermaine Edwards, Johnmark Wiggan, Petra Kaye, and H.U.M.B.L.E, who started out with that lovely rendition of the national anthem. It was an amazing night.”

He added: “It was a national call to worship. We answered a call from the Lord, where He said He was seeking true worshippers. Persons even came with their tambourines for worship and we thank the Lord.”

World.title: FLOW’S US$25-M REBUILD
World.content:
Flow Jamaica has spent more than US$25 million on the Hurricane Melissa rebuild efforts. .

FLOW Jamaica has spent more than US$25 million ($3.90 billion) restoring its network after Hurricane Melissa, including US$12 million ($1.87 billion) during the second quarter as it continued reconnecting fixed-line customers in western Jamaica.

Balan Nair, chief executive officer of Liberty Latin America Limited (LILA), disclosed the expenditure during the company’s earnings call on Thursday, while discussing recovery work in Jamaica.

“The actual business operations itself is improving, and we are getting very close to getting back to full strength. As a matter of fact, our mobile business has improved coming out of this, and our market share has improved coming out of this. Our ARPU (average revenue per user) has improved coming out of this,” Nair said of the recovery effort.

Liberty’s Caribbean segment added 11,000 postpaid subscribers during the second quarter ended June 30, with 6,000 subscribers coming from the Jamaican market. Revenue from Jamaica was down US$3.1 million or three per cent to US$101.6 million ($15.86 billion) for the second quarter. Liberty’s quarterly filing with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission noted that Hurricane Melissa had a negative impact of US$8 million on revenue.

“We continue to see negative headwinds from Hurricane Melissa in Jamaica, the effect is clearly diminishing,” Nair said.

However, the recovery in Jamaica continues to be impacted by the pace of infrastructure restoration in western Jamaica. LILA noted that approximately 38,000 RGUs (revenue generating units) in the Jamaican market remained offline at the end of the quarter. This comprised 19,000 broadband internet units, 15,000 fixed-line telephony and 4,000 video subscribers.

“I think there are some homes that we will not rebuild back to, and it’s just gone. For the most part, we think we can get back to a pretty high level of penetration,” Nair noted as the company brought 48,000 RGUs back online during the first six months of 2026.

Liberty’s Jamaican operation, led by Flow Jamaica, reported a US$5.2 million or two per cent reduction in six-month revenue to US$204.8 million.

The hurricane had a US$20 million negative impact to Liberty’s revenue and a US$22 million impact on its operating income before depreciation and amortisation.

Nair credited the recovery trajectory to the work of the company’s teams in Jamaica and Miami, including the managers overseeing its Jamaica operations.

Despite the headwinds it experienced from Hurricane Melissa, Flow Jamaica continues to expand its offerings to the Jamaican market. Flow launched the 5G network on June 11 providing coverage to approximately 70 per cent of Jamaica’s population. This service is available to residential and enterprise postpaid subscribers.

Flow also launched the ‘Unbeatable’ Network campaign as it pushes fixed mobile convergence which bundles fixed and mobile services. The fixed broadband service is backed by the ability to switch from home Wi-Fi to the mobile network during power outages. Mobile connectivity is, in turn, supported by satellite through Flow’s Starlink DTC partnership.

“The Unbeatable campaign is now live in Jamaica and Cayman and coming soon to other Liberty Caribbean markets, as well as being deployed across the broader LLA group. In the Caribbean, it encompasses the unique concept of an always-on network, both in fixed and mobile,” Nair said during his presentation.

The Category 5 hurricane and the recent El Niño phenomenon prompted analyst Matthew Harrigan to ask about the availability of parametric insurance in the Caribbean.

LILA Chief Financial Officer Chris Noyes said the company had parametric insurance coverage for the hurricane season.

Parametric insurance has helped Jamaica rebuild and recover from the last two major hurricanes, with a US$81-million payment from weather derivatives received in 2025.

“I think we are one of the key global issuers of the parametric. We were able to do it even with the event we had in Jamaica, with a very cost-effective cover similar to prior years,” Noyes told Harrigan.

Nair said the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) website has become a permanent monitoring tool for his team since July.

He added that LILA’s leadership team would visit NOAA’s headquarters in Boulder, Colorado, to meet climatologists and hurricane experts.

LILA’s consolidated revenue increased one per cent to US$1.10 billion for the second quarter, US$10 million above analysts’ estimates.

Due to lower impairment and restructuring charges, LILA reported an operating profit of US$181.2 million compared to an operating loss of US$333 million. LILA’s adjusted OIBDA grew five per cent to US$436 million.

With a 34 per cent reduction in non-operating expenses to US$157.2 million, LILA reported a profit before tax of US$24 million versus a loss before tax of US$570.8 million.

However, higher taxes resulted in LILA reporting a consolidated net loss of US$10.6 million, with a US$24-million loss attributable to shareholders.

LILA’s consolidated revenue for the six-month period edged up to US$2.19 billion, while the company reported an operating profit of US$326.4 million, compared with an operating loss of US$204.9 million.

The net loss attributable to shareholders improved to US$46.7 million from US$559.7 million.

LILA’s asset base stood at US$12.23 billion, including US$3.78 billion in property and equipment and US$714.1 million in cash. Total liabilities stood at US$11.23 billion, while equity attributable to shareholders was US$528.1 million.

LILA’s Class C shares traded at US$8.54 on Thursday, while its Class A shares traded at US$8.66. The company has repurchased US$60 million of its common shares and has US$140 million remaining under its share-repurchase programme.

“As we look to [the] rest of 2026, we intend to build upon our H1 operational progress and lap the October 2025 Jamaica hurricane, all of which should set us up for a strong fourth quarter and positive momentum leading into 2027,” Nair said.

World.title: Germany’s gas gamble puts Europe’s winter at risk
World.content:
The low reserves have already added to the increased pressure on gas prices linked to renewed tensions around the Strait of Hormuz, with the European natural gas benchmark now consistently higher than it was for the first four months of the Iran war.

The European Commission, the EU’s executive arm, has said the bloc faces no winter supply risks. But a report by energy analytics firm Rapidan projects that reserves will rise to only 65 percent of total storage capacity by November, arguing that hitting the EU's target by winter won't be possible without "materially higher prices."

That risk has been exacerbated, analysts say, by the bloc’s move in recent years to replace its long-term supply deals with Russia with short-term purchases of globally traded liquefied natural gas. These seaborne cargoes are highly mobile and go to the highest bidder — leaving buyers more exposed to volatility on international markets, especially in the wake of the loss of key supplies from Qatar and rising demand in Asia.

A tanker passes through the Strait of Hormuz on Feb. 25, 2026. | Fadel Senna/AFP via Getty Images

Germany, the bloc's largest gas consumer, has seen its reserves fill up even more slowly than others, in part thanks to its more hands-off, market-led approach to restocking than many of its neighbors. As a result, reserves stood at only 47 percent of national capacity in August, according to the latest data — the lowest fill level since records began. That's especially worrying as the country's reserves are important for the bloc as a whole, representing over 20 percent of the EU's storage capacity.

Nevertheless, Berlin is staying the course. While its energy ministry has acknowledged the country's historically low reserves, it has refused to intervene to direct its main state-controlled gas buyers, SEFE and Uniper, to buy gas at current prices to ensure its targets are met, instead of waiting for market conditions to improve.

"It is the responsibility of companies and traders to fill the storage facilities for the winter," a spokesperson for the German energy ministry told POLITICO. "Government-led filling of the storage facilities would further constrain the gas market and drive prices even higher. The supply situation over the coming months would actually deteriorate."

World.title: Italy says it won’t take orders from Spain on border checks
World.content:
Earlier in the day, the Spanish government had threatened to take “proportional measures” if Rome did not stop its reintroduced border checks and temporary suspension of the Schengen Agreement by Aug. 9.

In its statement, Rome said it would keep these controls in place “at least until August 15 and, in any case, until security and terrorism risks to Italy can be completely ruled out,” adding that a new “migratory wave” is expected in Ceuta on that date.

“Only when it is certain that there will be no security or terrorism risks for Italy, that there will be no new wave and that there are no irregular migrants heading toward European territory will it be possible to reconsider what has already been decided,” said the document.

World.title: EU adds 5 people to Russia sanctions list after latest deadly attacks on Ukraine
World.content:
Russia this week carried out one of its deadliest barrages on Kyiv, killing 17.

The EU has added five individuals to its Russia sanctions list. The move was driven by Moscow’s “intensified strikes deliberately targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure” in Ukraine, according to a press release.

The press release does not refer to a specific attack, but earlier this week Russia carried out one of its deadliest barrages on the Ukrainian capital, killing 17. In July, a similar attack in Kyiv killed 12.

Among those included in the new sanctions is Ramil Badgutdinov — the head of a company that helps produce the Iskander-M ballistic missiles — and Aleksandr Dyukarev, head of the KrasMash plant that produces Sarmat ballistic missiles. Russia has not yet used Sarmat missiles in Ukraine, but Moscow has been testing them.

World.title: Madrid threatens retaliation if Italy keeps border controls on travelers from Spain
World.content:
In addition to slamming Rome for imposing border controls that inconvenienced thousands of passengers by creating legal uncertainty in the middle of the summer holiday season, Madrid also took Italy to task for criticizing Spain’s handling of migrants while failing to protect its own borders.

Even though “Italy is the EU member state that has recorded the highest number of irregular crossings in recent years, with figures that have at times been twice those of Spain … Spain has never introduced controls on travelers from Italy,” the Spanish government said.

Madrid has now given the Italian government two days to either lift the border controls or face reciprocal measures that aim to “protect the interests and dignity” of Spanish citizens.

“Governments should work to promote understanding between countries and serve the general interests of their populations, rather than create divisions and pointless conflicts driven by domestic electoral considerations,” the statement said.

“We trust that Europeanism, common sense and good faith will prevail.”

World.title: Musk says French Greens’ presidential candidate should be ‘shut down’
World.content:
“I’d rather be accused of defending democracy than of trying to buy it.”

Musk, who is a former adviser to U.S. President Donald Trump, has regularly weighed in on European politics and thrown his support behind far-right candidates and parties — and France is no exception.

In July, Musk said far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen was “France’s last hope,” but her National Rally party was quick to downplay his backing to avoid being associated with the controversial owner of Tesla and SpaceX.

Hard-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon also slammed Musk’s attacks against Tondelier on Thursday, before accusing the French government of not doing enough to fight foreign interference.

“The French presidential election is an open bar for all the manipulators in the world,” he wrote — a criticism Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot promptly rejected.

Earlier this week, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the government was boosting efforts to detect and punish foreign interference in the upcoming 2027 election, while presidential candidates Gabriel Attal and Édouard Philippe, as well as likely candidate Raphaël Glucksmann shared they had been victims of Russian disinformation campaigns.

World.title: Week Ender: Verhofstadt on “Trumpism”, plus summer must-reads
World.content:
It’s August in Brussels, which means it’s vacation time.

Whether you’re heading off to the beach or holding down the fort in town, this episode is brimming with book recommendations from our newsroom and from you, our listeners. Whatever your genre preference, from true crime thrillers to deep political dives, we’ve got your summer holiday covered.

But this installment is not just a book chat.

We’re also tackling the rise of populism and the crises facing liberal democracies around the world. That’s the topic of “Defeating Trumpism,” a new book by former Belgian Prime Minister and European Parliament Member Guy Verhofstadt. The book is a self-diagnosis from one of Europe’s most passionate centrists about the failures of his movement. And his prescription? A new political paradigm he calls “Citizenism.”

World.title: L’Europe veut sortir de sa dépendance à Palantir
World.content:
"Soyons honnêtes, le produit de Palantir est très bon et addictif, c’est un peu comme le sucre dans le Coca", reconnaît le député MoDem Philippe Latombe, défenseur français de la souveraineté numérique. "Palantir est capable de traiter d’énormes quantités de données avec une grande précision et, grâce à son expérience, l’entreprise a eu le temps d’améliorer ses algorithmes auprès de nombreux clients et de les adapter à de nombreux cas d’utilisation."

Pourtant, la volonté de se libérer de Palantir gagne tout le continent : de Madrid, où le gouvernement de Pedro Sánchez a ordonné aux entreprises publiques d’exclure Palantir des futurs marchés publics, jusqu’aux services de renseignement intérieurs français (DGSI), qui ont préféré l’entreprise française ChapsVision à Palantir. Au Royaume-Uni, le prochain test pourrait avoir lieu en février 2027, lorsque le nouveau gouvernement travailliste d’Andy Burnham devra décider s’il met fin au contrat de 330 millions de livres sterling conclu avec Palantir pour la plateforme fédérée de données de la Sécurité sociale (NHS).

La décision prise le mois dernier par les services de renseignement français et allemands d’opter pour ChapsVision a porté un double coup dur à la direction de Palantir. Le PDG du géant américain, Alex Karp, est toutefois resté sûr de lui après ce revirement soudain, affirmant qu’il ne s’inquiétait pas de la concurrence européenne. "Nous avons un exemple de ce qui ne fonctionne pas", a-t-il ironisé la semaine dernière sur Fox Business. "Ça s'appelle l'Europe."

Alex Karp, PDG de Palantir, est l'invité de l'émission « The Claman Countdown » aux studios de Fox Business Network. | John Lamparski/Getty Images

Olivier Dellenbach, fondateur et PDG de ChapsVision, concède à POLITICO que son entreprise avait tiré profit de ce qu’il qualifie de "rejet viscéral de Palantir" en Europe.

Il refuse toutefois que ChapsVision soit réduit à une simple alternative anti-Palantir. La souveraineté numérique, affirme-t-il, restera une formule creuse si les gouvernements ne la transforment pas en politique industrielle. "Il faut plus de commandes publiques", estime Olivier Dellenbach.

La Belgique, l'Allemagne, le Luxembourg, la Roumanie, les Pays-Bas et le Canada ont déjà manifesté leur intérêt pour le système d'IA "Artemis" de l'armée française, selon Patrick Moreau, l'un des architectes de cette solution développée par l'entreprise française d'aérospatiale et de défense Thales.

World.title: US Senate approves sweeping Russia sanctions bill targeting energy income
World.content:
The US Senate has overwhelmingly approved a sweeping sanctions package targeting Russia's energy revenues, including Russian officials, oligarchs, financial institutions and the so-called shadow fleet.

 

The bipartisan legislation, which passed the Senate 86-11, would allow US President Donald Trump to set tariffs of up to 500% on Russian imports, including gas and oil.

It would also penalise countries that continue to buy Russian oil, gas and other exports, allowing Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods from major purchasers of Russian oil and gas, including countries such as China and India.

US sanctions would also expand to target older, reflagged oil tankers that Russia uses to circumvent existing US sanctions on Russian oil and energy revenues.

The legislation now heads to the House of Representatives, though a vote there will not take place until at least early September due to the congressional summer recess.

If adopted into law, Putin himself would be among those targeted by the sanctions, as well as other top officials.

The negotiated bill also includes waiver authority for the president, allowing the White House to waive sanctions or restrictions if the president certifies to Congress that the waiver is in the national interest.

The show of force from the Senate is the most substantial move yet during Trump’s second term to shift the dynamic of the more than four-year war. Congress has struggled to ensure US funding and munitions flows to Ukraine, but Trump has given a nod to the sanctions package, putting pressure for the House to take it up for a vote and send it to the White House for his signature.

The bill was named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, who died on 11 July after spending more than a year building support for it.

Shortly before his death, Graham announced he had reached an agreement with the White House on a revised version of the text, including the extension of existing sanctions authority aimed at restricting funding for Iran's energy and weapons sectors.

World.title: Paris: nearly 100,000 signatures against new National Assembly pavilion
World.content:
For almost two years this saga, full of twists and turns, has pitted and involved several players: the National Assembly and its president Yaël Braun-Pivet, Paris City Hall and the association Sites & Monuments.

 

The project to build a new reception pavilion for the National Assembly has proved highly divisive. Championed by the president of the institution, Yaël Braun-Pivet, it involves replacing the historic stone pavilion, dating from 1888, with a contemporary glass structure. The future building is to house a shop, a cafeteria and educational spaces, functions which the Sites & Monuments association considers secondary for a parliament.

"The problem is that this building would break that symmetry and introduce a large quantity of new material, namely glass", explains to Euronews Julien Lacaze, president of Sites & Monuments. He recalls that the project is to be built within a Remarkable Heritage Site (SPR) in the 7th arrondissement, in an area listed as a UNESCO World Heritage site.

In his view, the architectural project disrupts the historic harmony of the Seine embankments on several levels: it breaks the symmetry between La Madeleine and the colonnade of the Palais-Bourbon, introduces glass on a massive scale into an ensemble dominated by stone, and undermines both the horizontality and the architectural unity of the site.

"What is most serious is destroying a historic building. Once you have demolished something and put up something that is not in harmony with its surroundings, it is final. It cannot be reversed", laments the president of this association, founded in 1901, recognised as being in the public interest since 1936 and accredited for environmental protection. Sites & Monuments specialises in the defence of heritage.

We want to preserve a site that belongs to the whole world.

In the association president's view, other solutions exist, more respectful of the building's original architecture, and deserve to be examined.

He cites in particular the proposal by the Japanese firm SANAA, a Pritzker Prize laureate, which suggested keeping the existing 1888 pavilion while adding a contemporary stone extension, rather than glass as in the approved project. In his view, this proposal would have met the Assembly's functional needs without fundamentally transforming the architectural landscape.

A construction cost deemed excessive

Beyond the aesthetic and historical issues which Julien Lacaze believes are under threat, the project has also drawn criticism over its cost. The announced budget of 52.8 million euros strikes him as too high in a context of budgetary constraints, all the more so as the final bill could rise during the works. Although the project will be self-financed by the National Assembly, he argues that: "It is the French people's money. At a time when people are being asked to tighten their belts, spending 53 million euros on a building with a shop and a cafeteria is questionable."

Since the project was announced, the association's president says he has identified several elements in the way the case has been handled which he considers problematic. According to him, no information on the progress of the project was released for almost a year after the competition. A first planning application is said to have been submitted in contradiction with the Preservation and Enhancement Plan (PSMV) for the 7th arrondissement, notably because of the excessive height of the building, its footprint on protected areas and the impact on heritage gardens and courtyards.

Faced with the risk of legal challenges, the permit is said to have been withdrawn. He says the authorities then initiated a targeted amendment of the PSMV in order to make the project compatible with planning rules.

"It is a question of ego"

This architectural project has been driven by the president of the National Assembly, Yaël Braun-Pivet, since 2025.

Julien Lacaze accuses her of wanting to leave her mark on her term of office through an architectural statement intended to symbolise the institution's transparency.

"What you can criticise [Yaël Braun-Pivet] for is not a lack of architectural culture. It is not listening."

There are very prestigious advisory commissions, associations recognised as being in the public interest, architectural historians: they all say this project should not go ahead. It is a question of ego.

Asked by Franceinfo, the president of the National Assembly said she was "overwhelmed by criticism of a project people do not know".

In its campaign, the Sites & Monuments association enjoys the support of several political figures, notably from Les Républicains (LR) and La France insoumise (LFI), as well as former presidential candidate Ségolène Royal.

Launched just over a year ago on the Change.org online platform, the petition has seen renewed interest in recent weeks. It is approaching 100,000 signatures at the time of publication of this article.

Contacted by Euronews, the National Assembly did not respond to our requests for comment.

For its part, Paris City Hall told us by email that "this project, which aims to modernise and strengthen conditions for receiving the public at the Palais-Bourbon by increasing the areas dedicated to them" must now be "the subject of a planning application, which will be examined by the state, during which the City will be consulted in an advisory capacity".

"False", retorts the president of the association, who claims, with evidence to support him, that the City has already taken a position in favour of the project, since the Council of Paris approved the amendment to the Preservation and Enhancement Plan (PSMV), needed to bring the project into line with planning rules.

"There was a decision by the City of Paris approving the draft amendment (...) on 16 July," he says. In his view, the municipal majority has therefore indeed thrown its weight behind the project.

"Emmanuel Grégoire is taking up the cause for the project. Despite strong opposition, the City of Paris has given its approval."

According to Julien Lacaze, the project is also backed by part of the government, as he notes that the request to amend the PSMV originates from the regional prefect and the Paris police prefect, which in his view means that the Ministry of Culture also supports the project.

"We will do everything that is legal. We have the right to launch petitions and we will challenge the permit in court," he says.

"If this building is constructed, it will be a sign of the lack of sensitivity, the obstinacy and the outsized egos of some of our leaders in Paris."

The association plans to continue collecting signatures for the petition, to take part in the public inquiry into the PSMV amendment and, finally, to file a legal challenge against the future planning permission.

World.title: Household income plunges in Greece, Austria despite overall OECD growth
World.content:
Household budgets across the OECD are barely keeping pace with inflation, as fresh data reveals income growth has slowed sharply just as GDP ticks higher, a divergence that is playing out very differently from one country to the next.

 

Real household income per capita in OECD countries increased by 0.2% in the first quarter of 2026, slowing from the 0.6% rise recorded in the fourth quarter of 2025.

Over the same period, real GDP per capita grew by 0.3%, edging up from 0.2% in the final quarter of 2025.

While GDP growth captures changes in overall economic activity, growth in household income reflects changes in the income households receive, that is, the income available for consumption or saving.

Of the 21 countries for which data are available, 13 recorded an increase in real household income per capita, while the remaining 8 saw a decline.

How G7 economies compare

Among G7 economies, real household income per capita rose by 0.2% in the first quarter of 2026, although developments varied from country to country.

In Italy, real household income per capita bounced back after a 0.9% fall in the fourth quarter of 2025 and increased by 0.8% in the first quarter of 2026.

The rebound was driven mainly by higher employee compensation, linked to a slight drop in the unemployment rate (from 5.7% to 5.4% in the first quarter of 2026), which offset a decline in social benefits.

At the same time, growth in real GDP per capita held steady at 0.3%.

In Canada, Germany and the United States, real household income per capita increased by 0.2%, compared with 0.0%, 0.1% and -0.2%, respectively, in the fourth quarter of 2025.

By contrast, in the United Kingdom real household income per capita fell by 0.8% after a 1.1% increase in the previous quarter. This drop reflects a higher tax burden on income and wealth, partly due to the reduction in the capital gains tax allowance, combined with lower net social benefits and stronger inflationary pressures.

Meanwhile, real GDP per capita in the United Kingdom rose by 0.6%, following two consecutive quarters of zero growth.

A slight decrease was also recorded in France, where real household income per capita edged down by 0.1% after a 0.3% increase in the fourth quarter of 2025.

Among the other OECD countries, the largest increases in real household income per capita were recorded in Hungary and Chile.

In Hungary, a 6.3% rise in employee compensation led to an acceleration in real household income per capita, from 1.7% in the fourth quarter of 2025 to 6.0% in the first quarter of 2026, far outpacing the 0.9% increase in real GDP per capita.

In Chile, higher compensation for employees and the self-employed, together with an increase in net property income, resulted in a 4.8% rise in real household income per capita in the first quarter of 2026, after no change in the previous quarter.

Conversely, the sharpest declines in the first quarter of 2026 were recorded in Greece and Austria, where real household income per capita contracted because of falls in net property income and social benefits, dropping by 3.6% and 2.8%, respectively.

What happened in Greece in the first quarter of 2026

Real household disposable income per capita fell by 3.6% compared with the previous quarter, the steepest drop among OECD countries.

According to the OECD, the decline is mainly due to two factors: a reduction in net property income, such as interest, dividends and investment income, and a reduction in net social benefits to households.

World.title: Exclusive: Euronews ‘extremist’ label is Lukashenka’s revenge, Tsikhanouskaya said
World.content:
Belarus’ decision to classify Euronews as “extremist” is an act of revenge for its reporting on the country’s disputed 2020 election, political prisoners and Russia’s war against Ukraine, opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya said on Friday.

 

In an exclusive interview with Euronews, Tsikhanouskaya said the move showed that Aliaksandr Lukashenka’s government remained afraid of independent information six years after the mass protests that followed the presidential election.

“It is revenge - revenge by the regime for Euronews’ reporting,” she said.

“Euronews covered the 2020 protests, it covered the election, which Lukashenka lost. It covered the stories of political prisoners and the war, which started from Belarus.”

Belarusian information ministry placed Euronews’ website on its "Republican List of Extremist Materials," according to Belarus-based media. The ruling is subject to immediate execution under Belarusian civil procedure rules.

The decision means access to the Euronews website will now be restricted in Belarus, while readers could face administrative penalties for storing or distributing its content.

Euronews’ television broadcast was already banned in Belarus in 2021.

Tsikhanouskaya noted called the decisions “hypocritical” given that Lukashenka himself gave an interview to Euronews before.

“Now even watching them can be considered a crime in Belarus".

She warned that the designation could turn viewing and sharing independent news into a pretext for repression.

“Watching Euronews or reading the Euronews website can land you in jail. Sharing Euronews news can become a crime.”

The ruling gave the regime and its law enforcement agency KGB “another excuse to prosecute people who are simply looking for information”, Tsikhanouskaya said, adding that journalists, contributors and those assisting news organisations could also be at risk.

FILE: FILE - Protesters with old Belarusian national flags march at an opposition rally in Minsk, Belarus, on Sept. 6, 2020. AP Photo

Her comments come ahead of the sixth anniversary of the August 2020 election, which was followed by an unprecedented wave of peaceful demonstrations against Lukashenka’s declared victory.

The opposition, the EU and many western governments rejected the result as fraudulent.

The authorities responded with a sweeping crackdown on protesters, activists, independent media and civil society.

Tsikhanouskaya said repression had become the operating principle of the state because the government feared that a relaxation could trigger another public uprising.

“If it stops, people will rise up again,” she said. “Constant, systemic repression has become the modus operandi of the entire system.”

She added that arrests continued daily and that the true scale of the crackdown remained unclear because many detainees were not publicly identified.

“Under such terror, visible protest is almost impossible. It has gone underground,” she said. “But I know that people haven’t given up. They are waiting and preparing for new momentum.”

FILEL: Police officers detain Nina Bahinskaya, 73, during an opposition rally to protest the official presidential election results in Minsk, Belarus, Sept. 19, 2020. AP Photo

The opposition leader, who lives in exile, argued that control of information was central to the government’s survival. Millions of Belarusians still follow independent outlets covertly, she said, using virtual private networks and other tools to bypass censorship.

“Independent media are the backbone of our movement,” Tsikhanouskaya said.

She stated that independent reporting had helped ensure that many Belarusians understood the reality of Russia’s war in Ukraine, despite official propaganda, and that most supported Ukraine.

But she warned that the state was adapting as quickly as citizens. “The KGB often uses tech platforms to track, identify, and prosecute opponents,” she said, adding that her team was working with companies including Meta and Alphabet to ensure their platforms were not used to facilitate persecution.

Tsikhanouskaya advised people in Belarus to make digital security a priority, including by using VPNs, keeping separate devices for accessing independent media and avoiding contact with unknown accounts that could be linked to security services.

Related Belarus ban of Euronews sparks debate and support for press freedom across Europe

She said Belarusians were also advised to regularly clear their phones, use pseudonyms online and avoid responding to unknown contacts, which could be attempts by the KGB to recruit or blackmail them. Some independent outlets use accounts that are not branded as “extremist”, she said, allowing audiences to continue accessing information under difficult conditions.

“Difficult conditions force us to be creative,” she said. “That is the only way to survive under a dictatorship.”

She said the “extremist” designation should not deter Euronews from continuing its work.

“Euronews can take this designation as a badge of honour,” Tsikhanouskaya said.

“Many decent people and organisations have been declared ‘extremist’ by the dictator. It means your work matters.”

Despite the crackdown, she urged Belarusians not to see the democratic movement as defeated.

“Our struggle has not ended. It has simply taken a different form,” she said. “It is no longer a sprint, but a marathon.”

Tsikhanouskaya said a strong Ukraine and a weakened Russia could create an opening for democratic change in Belarus, arguing that Lukashenka’s government depended on the Kremlin’s support.

“Without Russian support, Lukashenka’s regime will not survive,” she said. “That is why so many Belarusians hope for Ukraine’s victory.”

Vladimir Putin and Aliaksandr Lukashenka pose for a photo during their meeting in St. Petersburg, Russia,Dec. 21, 2025. AP Photo

Tsikhanouskaya urged western partners to see Belarus “not only as a problem, but also as an opportunity”, arguing that democratic forces must be ready to seize any opening created by a shift in the regional balance of power.

“Dictatorships often collapse when no one expects it,” she said.

Belarusians wanted peaceful change through free elections, without violence, and a future in Europe rather than under Russian control, she said.

“A free, democratic and independent Belarus would make Europe much safer for everyone.”

World.title: US employers slash 23,000 jobs amid ongoing Iran war pressure
World.content:
US employers unexpectedly cut 23,000 jobs last month, and Bureau of Labor Statistics revisions shaved 103,000 jobs off payrolls in May and June. This was in sharp contrast with analyst expectations of an almost 100,000 spike in jobs in July.

 

However, the unemployment rate eased slightly to 4.1% in July, down from 4.2% in June, mainly due to more people leaving the labour market.

The July jobs numbers from the Bureau of Labor Statistics on Friday marked a sharp reversal for the domestic labour market and a political setback for President Donald Trump less than three months before his Republican Party seeks to keep full control of Congress in the midterm election.

Local public schools reduced 50,000 jobs last month, whereas 26,000 jobs were shed from restaurants and bars and 19,000 from retailers.

July's unemployment rate was the lowest since June 2025, as 264,000 people dropped out of the labour market. The share of those working or looking for work fell to 61.4%, the lowest since February 2021.

The Trump administration, which has imposed massive tariffs in an attempt to create manufacturing jobs, noted that jobs were up 22,000 at construction companies and 5,000 at factories.

“The Trump industrial resurgence is on schedule. Manufacturing and factory construction jobs grew again in July even as government payrolls continued to significantly shrink,’’ said White House spokesman Kush Desai.

Hiring had rebounded this year from a lackluster 2025 in the face of the conflict in the Persian Gulf that has sent energy prices surging and put a strain on family budgets. Job growth had been solid, if unspectacular. Some businesses are having trouble filling vacancies, while others are using technology to replace human labour.

The rise of the 'no hire, no fire' economy

Americans who have jobs are enjoying unusual job security. Layoffs are low by historical standards. This is mainly due to companies being unwilling to risk giving up the staff they have, following the surprise labour shortages following the pandemic.

But Americans who have lost their jobs — or are seeking to enter the job market for the first time — are struggling to catch a break.

Economists have used the term "no hire, no fire'' to describe the unusual job market conditions.

So far this year, employers are adding 61,000 jobs a month, up from 9,700 in 2025, the weakest outside a recession since 2002.

The United States does not need as many jobs as it used to to keep the unemployment rate from rising.

Trump’s immigration crackdown and the ongoing retirement of baby boomers mean fewer people are competing for work. So the “break-even’’ rate of monthly hiring, 155,000 in 2023-2024, has dropped, perhaps to nearly zero, according to a Federal Reserve study.

“There are just fewer people available to hire,’’ said Sal Guatieri, senior economist at BMO Capital Markets. For some, labour shortages translate into higher wages.

The payroll processor ADP reported Wednesday that people who changed jobs last month pocketed a 7% raise, the biggest year-over-year gain in almost a year and a premium over a 4.4% increase for workers who stayed where they were.

At the same time, companies have become more productive in recent years, using technology to do the work that humans used to do. “We are seeing companies produce more with their current staff,’’ Guatieri said. “So there’s less need to take on new workers.’’

Shortages of available workers and rising productivity, he said, “will keep the lid on the rate of hiring and monthly job growth.’’

Moreover, the outlook for hiring is clouded by the ongoing fighting in the Persian Gulf, which has pushed up energy prices and squeezed family budgets, and by the rise of artificial intelligence, which could either make workers more efficient and better paid — or take their jobs.

In a report out this week, researchers Ingrid Chen, Marianna Kudlyak and Riva Mikhlin of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco found that landing a job has gotten tougher in the past couple of years — surprisingly so.

Normally, this deep into an economic expansion (it has been more than six years since the last recession), employers would need workers so badly that they would be taking chances on young people and on those with less education. Not this time.

“Instead of being pulled in, the pipeline into employment is shrinking such that the recovery is no longer reaching workers at the margins,’’ Chen, Kudlyak and Mikhlin write.

Moreover, the unemployed people who normally get back to work the fastest — those in their prime working years, ages 25 to 54, and with college educations, are struggling to find new jobs.

The San Francisco Fed researchers are not sure what is making the job search so tough.

They suspect it might have to do with the immigration crackdown, hiring slowdowns specifically at tech companies and government contractors, uncertainty over the direction of government policy or “early signals of broader labor market deterioration."

World.title: From the Hundred Horse Chestnut to the ancient olive tree: where to see Italy's oldest trees
World.content:
Some people travel hundreds of kilometres to admire a breathtaking view, and others, instead, to visit a tree. Not just any tree, but a giant that has spanned centuries, and in some cases millennia, becoming a silent witness to Italy's history.

 

From the Hundred Horse Chestnut on Etna to the thousand-year-old wild olive in Sardinia, via the Witches' Oak in Tuscany, our country is home to genuine living monuments which are now even more numerous: the Agriculture Ministry has in fact updated the national list of monumental trees with 82 new entries.

These trees tell stories and legends, have inspired writers, withstood earthquakes and tragedies, and offered protection to travellers and emperors. A unique natural heritage well worth discovering on a real tour among Italy's green giants.

Monumental trees: what they are and why they are protected

"These green giants are not just trees, they are part of our land, our culture and our history", said Agriculture Minister Francesco Lollobrigida about the tenth update of the national list of monumental trees (source in Italian).

The trees recorded in the inventory are selected for their extraordinary biological, landscape and ecological value. Some are exceptional in size, others belong to rare species, and still others have become symbols of communities, sacred places or the backdrop to historic events. In many cases, it is precisely their bond with the local area and popular traditions that makes them unique.

Where to see Italy's most beautiful centuries-old trees

From Abruzzo to Sicily, via Veneto, Tuscany, Sardinia and Calabria, these trees are among the most fascinating nature destinations in the country.

Pescara is home to the famous "reclining" Aleppo pine, a tree which, instead of breaking after a landslip, settled on the ground and carried on growing. For scientists it is an incredible example of adaptation, while tradition has it that it bent down to listen to the song of sea nymphs.

In the heart of the Umbra Forest in Puglia grows the Ancient Yew, a millenary tree that for the ancients was at once a symbol of death and of immortality. Its poisonous leaves fed superstitions and tales, but its ability to regenerate has turned it into a symbol of rebirth.

The Witches' Oak and trees steeped in legend

If there is one tree that more than any other fires the imagination, it is the Witches' Oak in the province of Lucca. Its huge branches, which stretch almost parallel to the ground for more than forty metres, are said to have hosted witches' sabbaths on nights of the full moon.

But legend gives way to literature as well. It is said that Carlo Collodi found inspiration under its canopy as he dreamed up the adventures of Pinocchio, making this oak one of Italy's most iconic trees.

In Umbria too, nature meets myth. The great Roverella di Nottoria is at the centre of an ancient legend according to which it even managed to defeat the Devil, keeping its leaves through the winter and thus preventing the wood from becoming completely bare.

Monumental trees that tell Italy's history

Not all these giants are home only to fantastical tales. Some have become witnesses to events that have marked the country's history.

One such case is the Vajont Sequoia in Longarone, which survived the 1963 disaster. On its trunk you can still see the scar left by the wave that devastated the valley, killing almost two thousand people. Today that tree is one of the most powerful symbols of Italy's collective memory.

In Lazio, meanwhile, the Manildo Oak owes its survival to an act of courage. In 1968 the farmer Manildo Lombardelli opposed its felling, allowing this majestic Turkey oak to go on living and become one of the most admired natural monuments in the Viterbo area.

From the Hundred Horse Chestnut to the Luras wild olive: the patriarchs of nature

Among the true patriarchs of Italy's botanical heritage stands the famous Hundred Horse Chestnut in Etna Park. At around 2,200 years old, it is one of the oldest trees in Europe. Legend has it that a queen, caught in a violent storm, found shelter together with her retinue of one hundred horsemen beneath its immense canopy.

Even older is thought to be the Luras wild olive in Sardinia, which is believed to be around 3,000 years old. Considered the oldest tree in Italy and among the oldest on the continent, it continues to amaze with the size of its trunk and the vitality of its crown.

In Calabria, by contrast, the Curinga Oriental plane offers a truly unique experience: its enormous hollow trunk is so large it can accommodate up to ten people at the same time, giving the feeling of literally stepping inside a natural monument.

A tour of monumental trees is a journey through nature, history and legend

The latest update to the national list confirms that Italy is rich not only in art cities and spectacular landscapes, but also in genuine living monuments. Visiting these trees means travelling through centuries of history, immersing yourself in local traditions and discovering places where nature, myth and memory still live side by side.

For many they are just trees. For those who encounter them up close they become much more: guardians of time, symbols of resilience and perfect stops on a journey that is anything but ordinary, made up of silence, wonder and deep roots.

World.title: Wildfires continue to rage as Europe swelters under extreme heat
World.content:
Firefighters continued battling multiple wildfires across Serbia on Friday, as temperatures continue to soar.

 

In the northeast of the country, firefighters battled a wildfire in a nature reserve, deploying both ground crews and helicopters.

Local authorities said the flames had scorched at least 700 hectares of land in the Deliblato Sands special natural reserve, located roughly 50 kilometres east of Belgrade.

Meanwhile, near the town of Kraljevo, several blazes also continued to burn, forcing residents of nearby villages to evacuate.

Local residents said more than 150 acres of pine wood forest had been destroyed in just a couple of days.

"The damage is huge. It's a young pine wood forest, these pines were planted during the '80s," one resident told press agency The Associated Press.

On Thursday, another major fire swept through the Ibar valley in central Serbia. Assisted by water-bombing aircraft, firefighters tackled the rough terrain to protect nearby villages.

Serbia was not the only country affected. Days of extreme heat, with temperatures reaching 40 degrees Celcius, fuelled wildfires across several Balkan countries on Thursday.

Europe's extreme summer weather has also taken a toll on the continent's rivers, with parts of the Danube falling to record-low water levels.

While it is not unusual for river levels to decrease during the summer months, this year's drop has been unprecedented.

A boat laying on a dry bank in front of Djerdap II, a large dam on the Danube River, between Romania and Serbia, near Prahovo, Serbia, Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026. AP Photo/Darko Vojinovic

In Hungary, the Danube's exceptionally low water levels triggered an energy crisis, forcing the country to shut down its only nuclear power plant, which relies on water from the river for cooling.

Last week, Serbia also had to reduce its power generation from hydroelectric plants, with its two biggest plants having been reduced to an output just 20 and 30 percent of their capacities.

Southeastern Europe also continues to swelter under extreme heat.

In the northern Italian region of Emilia-Romagna, a wildfire broke out in a remote area of Vedriano. Firefighting efforts have been underway since Thursday afternoon.

Italy has placed all its major cities under the highest heat alert.

In neighbouring France, a major wildfire in the southern Var region is no longer spreading, but firefighters maintain a large presence because of the risk of flare-ups.

"It's a fire that can last over long periods of time. In the mornings, for example, it’s about setting up because (fire) risks with winds and rising heat increase in the afternoon," Chief Sergeant Anthony from Marseille Naval Fire Battalion said.

The fire, which started on July 20, burnt more than 60 square kilometers, marking the largest blaze recorded in the region in recent decades.

Europe is the world's fastest-warming continent, according to their European State of the Climate 2025 report, with temperatures rising at around twice the global average.

It warned heatwaves are expected to become more frequent, more intense and occur later and earlier in the year as the climate continues to warm.

World.title: Ceuta: Spain sets up border controls on travelers from Italy
World.content:
Spain had warned Italy it would impose entry checks on visitors unless Rome halts its controls by Sunday. Even though they don't share a land border, the countries entered a spat after the Ceuta border rush.

Spain's government on Friday moved to impose reciprocal entry checks on people traveling from Italy. The Spanish government had warned that it would do so unless Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's governemnt lifted the border measures it has implemented against Spain.

Italy's right-wing government announced the checks at the height of the social media panic as tens of thousands of people gained entry into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta bordering Morocco last week.

The checks are essentially symbolic, given that Ceuta is not on the European mainland and Italy and Spain do not share a land border, meaning that the vast majority of people potentially affected are tourists on planes.

Nevertheless, the issue has turned into a point of dispute between two governments of different ideological persuasions with contrasting messaging priorities on migration policy.

Did Morocco instigate the Ceuta migrant incident? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did Spain say about checks on travelers from Italy?

The border controls on Italy will go into effect from midnight ‌on ⁠Saturday ⁠until September 7, the Spanish government said. Border agents will check passport, nationality and visas for Italian passengers and visitors from other ​countries arriving from Italy.

Spain had called Italy's decision to impose checks on people arriving from Spain "unjustified, contrary to the interests of the European Union and discriminatory against ​the Spanish population."

Madrid said there was no real risk of people who overwhelmed Ceuta's border controls reaching the European mainland, let alone Italy. It pointed to the vast majority of the estimated 72,000 people returning to Morocco within days. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez also drew attention to the higher numbers of irregular migrants reaching Italian than Spanish territory in recent years.

"If [Italy] fails to [remove the entry checks] before Sunday, August 9, Spain will be forced to adopt proportionate measures to protect the interests and dignity of its citizens," the government said.

Italy replied later Friday that it would not accept "ultimatums ⁠or ⁠impositions" from Madrid, and that it would maintain the suspension of Schengen rules for non-EU nationals arriving from Spain until at least August 15.

Despite Spain's objections, an array of European countries, including Germany, and the European Commission all made comments about the importance of border security to the open-border Schengen Zoneamid the public uproar. Italy was among comparatively few to go so far as to frame the issue as "suspending" Spain's Schengen status, however.

Italy first made the announcement as images and footage of the border breach were going viral online Image: Atlas/REUTERS

What do we know about Italy's checks on travelers from Spain?

Details on precisely what checks, if any, Italy has actually implemented over the past week have been thin on the ground.

Migration analyst Gerald Knaus told DW earlier this week that the move was "pure populism" and a "completely bizarre" measure.

"They don't have a border, so it's only for a few flights," Knaus said. "It makes no sense in the high tourist season. And as Giorgia Meloni indicated, it shouldn't inconvenience travelers."

Knaus said the decision could only be understood in the context of domestic political appearances, not foreign policy realities.

"I think to understand it, you must understand that on [Meloni's] right, there is a radical right party in Italy that puts pressure on her. And so politicians everywhere in Europe, when they see these images which create fear, are looking for something to say — something to do that makes them look tough."

EU defends border response after Ceuta crossing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Meloni and Sanchez: A clash of styles on migration

At least in terms of their stated positions and approaches, Italy and Spain have quite different stances on the issue of migration.

Meloni came to power in 2022 in Italy, after several years of much higher irregular migration rates and asylum applications caused in large part by the wars in Syria and Ukraine. She promised a tougher line on migration into one of the most common landing points in southern Europe.

Sanchez, meanwhile, has championed a more pro-migration stance during his two terms in office. He argues that Spain's economy needs migration and offered an amnesty and temporary residency permit process earlier this year to irregular migrants already in the country. Sanchez said it was better to grant residency and start collecting taxes than to keep people out of the formal labor market.

Migration expert Knaus, however, warned against overstating the practical differences between the two countries, saying Meloni faced similar economic requirements and was actually pursuing comparable policies — only with much less public fanfare.

"Italy is doing something very similar. Hundreds of thousands of people are brought in or are already in the country and are regularized for the Italian labour market under Giorgia Meloni," Knaus said. "And 1.6 million people were regularized under various Italian governments in the last 20 years."

World.title: Colombia: Trump ally De la Espriella takes office
World.content:
Conservative Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in as Colombia's president, promising to crack down on armed drug gangs.

Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in as Colombia's president on Friday, promising to boost ties with the United States and tackle armed groups linked to the drug trade.

The 48-year-old ex-lawyer lurches the Andean nation to the right, taking office after winning a close June 21 runoff against Sen. Ivan Cepeda, an ally of outgoing President Gustavo Petro.

Security was stepped up in case armed groups ambushed the occasion Image: Luis Acosta/AFP

What happened at the inauguration?

In a speech shortly after his swearing-in, De la Espriella vowed once again to wipe out "narcoterrorism" in the South American country.

"The option of dialogue is completely exhausted," he said, referring to his predecessor, who had promoted a peaceful resolution to the crisis.

De la Espriella then promised to restore "order, authority and freedom" to the South American nation.

"There will be no room for maneuvers that undermine the stability of the nation," said the hardline leader, who has spoken of opening mega-prisons to house captured rebels and drug dealers.

Instead of the capital Bogota, the inauguration took place at a university in the southwestern city of Cali.

Colombia’s third-largest city is located near major drug-trafficking corridors and the Pacific coast, and is a regular scene of violence by rival groups.

Among the VIP guests were King Felipe VI of Spain, acting US Attorney General Todd Blanche, FIFA President Gianni Infantino and Latin American presidents, including Argentina's Javier Milei, Ecuador's Daniel Noboa and Chile's Jose Antonio Kast.

Outgoing president Petro declined to attend the ceremony and called for mass protests Friday, claiming election fraud without providing evidence.

After the swearing-in, the new president was due to address troops at a military barracks Image: Matias Delacroix/AP Photo/picture alliance

Who is Abelardo de la Espriella?

The 48-year-old is a former lawyer and businessman who has never held public office.

He funded his campaign with the profits from his law firm and other business ventures in the agri-food, real estate and fashion sectors.

The self-styled "El Tigre" (The Tiger) plans to forge a military alliance with the US and Israel to aid his war on rebel groups, including remnants of the FARC guerrillas, who waged an armed conflict that peaked in the 1990s and 2000s.

De la Espriella won the backing of US President Donald Trump after committing Colombia to a US-backed coalition to fight drug trafficking, dubbed the "Shield of the Americas."

He has also offered to launch joint military operations with Washington and even host US troops on Colombian soil.

The millionaire has also announced plans to resume diplomatic relations with Israel and sever them with Cuba and Nicaragua.

De la Espriella's win is another point for right-wing politics in Latin America, after electoral victories from Chile to Costa Rica, having also promised to crack down on security issues.
