World.title: Pentagon ploughs $560 million into ‘world-first’ Australian mining project
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaCritical minerals Pentagon ploughs $560 million into ‘world-first’ Australian mining project Michael Koziol August 8, 2026 — 9:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: The Pentagon will invest more than half a billion dollars in a “world-first” mining project in central western NSW that produces scandium, a rare critical mineral used in fighter jets, spacecraft and other tools of war. The $US400 million ($560 million) loan is intended to expand production at Sunrise Energy Metals’ Syerston Scandium Project near Fifield, south-west of Dubbo, as the US seeks to urgently diversify its supply chain for rare earths. Sunrise Energy Metals’ Syerston scandium project in NSW. Last year, Sunrise announced a deal for US weapons contractor Lockheed Martin to buy up to 15 tonnes of scandium oxide over five years. The move came just days after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and US President Donald Trump signed a critical minerals deal in Washington. Scandium – used to strengthen aluminium – is already used widely for defence, aerospace and energy applications, but nearly all supply comes from China, Russia and Ukraine.



The US has not mined scandium since 1969. The Pentagon said foreign competitors accounted for about 80 per cent of global scandium production and nearly 100 per cent of processing. Trump announced the Pentagon’s investment on Friday (Washington time) during a televised roundtable with mining executives at the US State Department. The White House described the Sunrise venture as “the world’s first primary scandium mine”. The US Department of Defence said the conditional loan from its Office of Strategic Capital would build a “complete, US-aligned value chain from mine to finished metal”, securing a vital supply of scandium for the US defence and commercial industrial base. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said: “We’re going to make sure the United States – not our adversaries – controls the supply chains of power and critical minerals.”



Representatives of Australian mining giants BHP and Rio Tinto, who have proposed and planned an underground copper mine in Arizona called Resolution Copper, also attended Friday’s roundtable. When realised, it is forecast to meet about a quarter of US copper demand. “Mr President, you have brought mining back to America single-handedly,” said Resolution Copper president Vicky Peacey at the roundtable. “We started permitting in 2005 … we finally got it over the line earlier this year.” President Donald Trump holds a solid gold replica of a deep sea nodule he was gifted during a roundtable on American mining on Friday. AP Photo/Allison Robbert BHP’s North America president Jessica Farrell and vice president for international affairs Dominic Perrottet – the former NSW premier – also attended. Resources Minister Madeleine King said the Pentagon’s loan was a significant vote of confidence in Australia’s critical minerals sector and its capacity to supply the minerals the US and its partners needed.



Scandium had a range of aerospace, defence and clean energy applications, King noted. “No one country alone can create secure, end-to-end supply chains in critical minerals and rare earths.” Albanese announced last year that Australia would create a $1.2 billion strategic reserve of critical minerals to purchase and hold minerals such as lithium, rare earths, nickel, cobalt and graphite via special agreements with local producers. Resolution Copper president and general manager Vicky Peacey (far left) with US Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. AP Photo/Allison Robbert The deal signed by Albanese and Trump last October set out that the countries would provide at least $US1 billion for critical minerals projects in each country. According to a federal government fact sheet, NSW has the highest concentration of scandium in the world. Those deposits have rapidly come to the interest of the US government.



Sunrise Energy Metals secured a $US67 million debt financing letter of interest from the US Export-Import Bank last year. Related Article Mining Why are Australia’s rare earths ‘crucial for the world’? Joe Hockey has an idea The Syerston project is also benefiting from a program unveiled by the NSW government last month that allows it to defer royalty payments for five years. “The Syerston Scandium Project has been identified as a project of strategic importance under the US-Australia critical minerals partnership,” the NSW government said. “This support further reinforces the strategic necessity of bringing Syerston online as rapidly as possible.” Another company, the Canada-listed, Nevada-headquartered Scandium International Mining Corp, is also developing a scandium mine near Nyngan, NSW and a nearby scandium exploration site known as Honeybugle.

Speaking on Friday in Europe (Friday night, AEST), he said that Madrid was prepared to respond with a tough approach of its own. Hours later, it did just that. This is now a major headache for the European Union. And travellers from Australia. Loading Italy has suspended the usual rules for travellers from outside the European Union who arrive from Spain, declaring that it needs the stronger safeguards until at least August 15. Spain has decided to do the same for those who arrive from Italy. This applies from midnight on Saturday – 8am on Sunday, AEST – at Spanish borders. So, officials will conduct passport, nationality and visa checks for Italian passengers and visitors from other countries arriving from Italy.



Australians travelling between the two countries will need to be on guard for additional controls. Related Article Analysis

Immigration How the storming of Ceuta shifts Europe to the right What began as a diplomatic dispute about Ceuta is turning into a test of the Schengen Agreement that was signed in 1985 to waive passport checks on travellers moving across the internal borders of most EU member states. At its best, the Schengen Agreement allows the citizens of 29 member countries to move easily across their borders without a passport check, visa or electronic travel authority. For visitors from Australia and other countries, it also ensures relatively seamless travel across those internal EU borders. Once the traveller arrives at the first Schengen member state and clears passport control, there is usually no need for any other passport check when moving to other member states inside the Schengen zone.



This has been so successful that the initial agreement of 1985 was codified in a convention in 1990 and extended many times to the point where the Schengen zone now has a population of 450 million people. The latest expansion came last year when Romania and Bulgaria joined in full. Related Article Aviation ‘Bring food and water’: Australians face six-hour lines for Euro summer For Australians on longer journeys, the only challenge with the Schengen zone is making sure they don’t visit for more than 90 days in any 180-day period – the basic rule that often leads to side-trips to non-Schengen states such as Britain or Ireland. (While Ireland is in the EU, it never joined Schengen.) But now, Schengen is under some strain. The argument between Italy and Spain comes amid other tensions at European borders. The new digital Entry/Exit System, or EES, has led to long queues at passport control for non-EU nationals, who must be registered with the new system.



Travellers have missed flights because of sluggish checks at border control kiosks, where officials gather fingerprints and photographs to enter each person into the vast new database. It is an operational failure. The workaround at some airports is to halt the EES for a period and return to old ways of clearing queues. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez with his Italian counterpart, Giorgia Meloni, in 2023. Bloomberg The new argument about Schengen, however, is foundational. It is about whether Schengen has become a point of weakness for Europe when so many are concerned about illegal arrivals and asylum seekers. Political leaders are responding to clear signals that voters want lower migration. Spain insists that the concern is overblown. Its latest estimate is that 72,000 people entered Ceuta from Morocco in the final days of July. It says almost all of them returned to Morocco. Crucially, Ceuta is not in the Schengen zone. Adult migrants who get to Ceuta have to clear other checks before they can reach the European mainland.



Thousands of the migrants are still in Ceuta, though. Spanish authorities have confirmed about 1100 unaccompanied minors are still in the enclave and have a legal right to remain. They are likely to be transferred to Spain. Even so, Italy will not drop its concern about illegal migrants getting to Spain and taking advantage of easy travel across borders into Italy. So Spain has chosen to retaliate. A 12-year-old who crossed into Spain is escorted by a Spanish soldier to the Spain-Morocco border this week, as the child begs not to be sent back to Morocco. AP In practical terms, this means Italian officials check passports for non-EU citizens arriving from Spain. Since there is no land border between the two, it entails checks on flights from Madrid, Barcelona, ​​Ibiza, Valencia and other Spanish locations, as well as some ferries. Italy appears to have an agreement with France to have stronger checks on land border crossings, but it is not clear what difference this makes.



The Spanish response appears likely to mean additional checks on all travellers arriving directly from Italian airports. Related Article Immigration ‘I don’t know why they let us through’: How 50,000 people surged into a Spanish exclave Travellers moving through other Schengen states should not see any change – not for now, at least. But everything depends on whether the argument between Italy and Spain spreads to their neighbours. What if other countries decide they too want to erect barriers against arrivals from Spain because of the anxiety about migrants in Ceuta? As right-wing leaders in Europe demand bigger and stronger borders, it will be tempting for governments to toughen their policies, even if Spain insists that it has the problem under control.



For the moment, Italy and Spain are set to intensify their fight over national pride and border policy by making queues longer at their airports. And by punishing travellers. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ‘The club went too far’: AFL chairman apologises over concussion contract saga
World.content:
AFL Commission chairman and former Geelong president Craig Drummond has apologised for “the mistakes made in this very complex situation” amid the fallout from the league’s concussion contract saga.

On Friday, Geelong premiership defender Jake Kolodjashnij identified himself as the player at the centre of a secret concussion deal with the club, which was scrapped this week after the AFL said it did not approve it.

AFL Commission chairman and former Geelong president Craig Drummond. Luis Enrique Ascui

Kolodjashnij didn’t directly address signing any document pertaining to his playing contract but said he “participated fully” in the AFL’s concussion panel process and is insisted he is fully healthy and fit to play at the highest level.

On Saturday, Drummond, who was the Cats’ president when the deal was signed, said in a statement that despite getting agreement from Kolodjashnij for the secret deal, “the club went too far in adding a waiver into an informed consent document and it will be removed”.

World.title: ‘Massive loss’: Roosters enforcer weighs in on Panthers’ injury blow
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘Massive loss’: Roosters enforcer weighs in on Panthers’ injury blow Christian Nicolussi August 8, 2026 — 10:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Isaah Yeo has been described as the “heartbeat” of the Penrith Panthers by Spencer Leniu, who won premierships alongside the lock forward – but will now try to heap more misery on his old mates on Thursday night. What was shaping as one of the NRL games of the year – and a potential grand final preview – between the Panthers and Sydney Roosters at CommBank Stadium has lost a superstar in Yeo because of a suspected pectoral injury. Isaah Yeo could be out for the remainder of the season for the Panthers. NRL Imagery Yeo flew back to Sydney with his teammates on Saturday morning following the 28-12 loss to the Warriors at Go Media Stadium in Auckland where he lasted 33 minutes. The co-captain immediately winced in pain and grabbed at his right pec before he made his way from the field.



Penrith coach Ivan Cleary confirmed after the game: “It doesn’t look great.” The 31-year-old is expected to undergo scans on Sunday, with the worst-case scenario to end Yeo’s season – and more than likely his dreams of captaining Australia to a World Cup win on home soil. Loading Leniu was saddened to hear the Yeo news when informed in the sheds after the Roosters’ gritty 20-18 win over Canterbury on Friday night. “No way. That’s a massive loss – he’s the heartbeat of their team,” Leniu said.



“Knowing Penrith, they’re a world-class team, and they’ll have that next-man-up mentality. “They’ve done it the last couple of years, they fill those voids when it comes around, and it will be no different next week if he’s out. Loading “He’s the captain, and when a lot of experience like that goes off the field, you definitely notice it. “But Penrith are a well-oiled machine. With that next-man-up mentality, if you get the tap on the shoulder, you’ve got a duty to perform and wear the jersey with pride.



“That’s been the Penrith Panthers the last few years. That’s why they’ve been such a great team. Another perspective Opinion

NRL 2026 These are the forbidden phrases the NRL won’t let you hear Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author “They’ll still be pushing for that premiership at the end of the season. Next week will be another day in the office.” The Panthers won 40-4 against the Roosters in round three when Tom Jenkins raced in four tries. But the Roosters have won their past seven games, and are building momentum at the right time. They are also set to welcome back skipper James Tedesco from an ankle injury. “I’ve got a lot of confidence in this team, the boys inside the four walls have confidence in each other, it was a scrappy win [against the Dogs], but we got the win,” Leniu said.



Naufahu Whyte has been a standout for the Roosters, and in Leniu’s opinion is on track to be crowned one of the Dally M props of the year. “He’s a no-nonsense player, he comes into training, if you ask him how he’s going, he’ll tell you, ‘same old, same old’,” Leniu said. “That’s who he is. He goes about his business, he doesn’t try to be anyone else but himself, and flourishes when he goes out there.”

World.title: The new Wallabies coach has copped an early hospital pass
World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionWallabies The new Wallabies coach has copped an early hospital pass Paul Cully August 8, 2026 — 9:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Les Kiss’ first Test as Wallabies coach could easily turn into the shocker in Osaka. The heat and humidity they are likely to encounter is one factor, but aside from that, Japan are a competitive Test side underpinned by an improving domestic competition filled with high-quality coaches from around the world. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Les Kiss chat at training ahead of Saturday’s match against Japan. Getty Images The Brave Blossoms were messed around by Ireland’s recent refusal to travel to Japan in the Nations Championship, but they have won the scheduling battle for this two-Test series against the Wallabies. Kiss would have copped the odd hospital pass as a player. Now, as a coach, he’s got a high ball well above his shoulders with Eddie Jones steaming in from 20 metres away.



The Wallabies could lose this Test. The bar for success in Kiss’ debut as coach is a win of any nature: get the job done and get out of there. It is a Test with a high-risk profile, and Kiss was never going to be able to fully mitigate that risk, no matter how he selected his team. Loading However, his 23-man squad and the make-up of the bench have increased the likelihood of Japan getting away to the fast start they desperately want. Josh Canham and Miles Amatosero are a young pairing, and they will face Warner Dearns, the best second-rower in Super Rugby Pacific this season, while prop Aidan Ross is more solid than spectacular and certainly won’t offer the same mobility around the field as Angus Bell.



Jones has prioritised speed from the outset, preferring Jack Cornelsen in the second row ahead of Harry Hockings, and Amatosero is going to be tested by the speed of the game if Japan get the quick ball they want. Clearly, the Wallabies’ strategy is to finish the Test strongly with their stacked bench, but they won’t want to be chasing the game with the combative Hockings and that old warrior Michael Leitch providing serious nuisance value off the bench for Jones. Eddie Jones and Japan will be ready for the challenge posed by the Wallabies. Getty Images The Wallabies must have considered the opposite approach – trying to overwhelm the Japanese early. That is something the French did well in June. Japan probably don’t even know themselves what a good side they are, but their self-belief will soar if they start well and exert scoreboard pressure on the Wallabies.



A Japan XV side put themselves in a great position against the Maori All Blacks in late June, racing into a 24-7 lead at halftime during their game in Nagoya, before that lack of self-belief kicked in. They were chased down and lost 38-31. But they will have learnt something from that defeat and young No.10 Ryunosuke Ito probably banked some valuable lessons as he continues his crash-course introduction to Test rugby. Loading The other player to look for is Japan No.6 Ben Gunter, who is on a big collision course with Wallaby Rob Valetini. Gunter, who grew up in Australia, has arguably the biggest shoulders in Test rugby and is not afraid to use them. He has snuck under the radar this week with all the focus on Hockings, but Gunter is the better player. He is an old-fashioned hitman who will also be lining up Harry Wilson if the Wallabies captain comes off the back fence.



The Jones factor is also inescapable, and the former Wallabies coach will have some clear views on how and where Kiss’s side can be vulnerable. Related Article Australian rugby Hoop dreams: How growing up on a court turned Josh into a Wallabies ‘baller’ But it’s a factor that is easy to overplay in a rugby world in which the degrees of separation between Australian rugby and Japan are decreasing anyway. For example, new Wallabies defence coach Scott McLeod almost won the Japan Rugby League One title in June (against Dave Rennie’s Kobe) as an assistant at Kubota Spears. In a classic clash of styles, Kubota employed a kicking and defence-based game plan, using the tactical nous of new/old Waratahs No.10 Bernard Foley.



Against Rennie’s ball-in-hand style – and Kobe superstar Ardie Savea – it almost worked too: Kubota might have won the game but for a knock-on by former Crusaders halfback Bryn Hall with the tryline in sight. That decider was a good showcase for the tactical variety and physicality of the Japanese game, and their players are increasingly well-prepared for the demands of Test rugby. Kiss, therefore, has been handed a tricky first assignment – and if he marks it with a victory, it is a bigger positive than he will get credit for. World.title: My daughter’s European backpacker odyssey is nothing like mine. That’s her loss
World.content:
NationalGen Z Opinion My daughter’s European backpacker odyssey is nothing like mine. That’s her loss Julia Baird Journalist, broadcaster, historian and author August 8, 2026 — 9:30am

August 8, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“I can’t believe,” says my daughter as I navigate our rented manual car around the narrow, cobbled streets of Nazaré, Portugal, “that you used to have to read maps to travel.” As the gears grind yet again under my rusty touch, I glance at her and laugh: “But we were using a whole part of our brain that you guys don’t touch now.” She shrugs, tapping on her phone. Illustration by Dionne Gain Remember maps? Calling from a phone box? Aerogram letters? Post-school travel for those born in the ’70s meant disappearing into Europe like a gumboot into quicksand, swallowed whole by different cultures. We were not being monitored, surveilled, tracked: we were finding our own paths, new ones. We didn’t have mobile phones with location data, downloadable maps, apps to make bookings. This, too, confounds my daughter: “But your parents wouldn’t know if you were dead.” I guess they just waved us off and hoped for the best. There was something delightful about the invisibility, being out of range and absolved of all responsibility. We were just gone, and we’d be back in a few months. Sure, I’d call home every week or two – collect, to the eye-rolls of my parents – and send the odd postcard, but that was it. We took photos on little cameras and mailed the film back home to be developed: they were unfailingly blurry, unflattering, often tilted or poorly framed. But it wasn’t about how we looked, it was about what we were looking at. There are few things as genuinely thrilling about entering and inhaling a new country for the first time. We took terrible risks, sleeping on beaches, train stations, boat shacks, all to save money, and relied on overnight train trips to get some rest, zigzagging around the continent with a heavily stamped Eurail Pass.



My daughter and her friends are too smart to do stupid things like sleep in public places. But I watch the reels and feeds of this Euro-generation, who save up and go year after year to the prettiest places in Europe, navigating swelling crowds, and I am gobsmacked. Julia Baird in Venice during her own backpacker adventure. First, they look so good. Polished and picture-perfect. I think I packed a hairbrush, but I can’t be sure. Maybe an eyeliner? Nothing more. I was gripped by an Oscar Wilde biography (the superb work by Richard Ellmann) and was somehow inspired by that to invest in several vintage Spanish brocade jackets which were hopeless in the cold and probably looked half mad, paired with scuffed Doc Martens and cut-off jeans. Today I scroll through Instagram and see a string of girls in bikinis and impeccable, tasteful clothes. Carousels of cute poses. Second, there is an ease to travel we did not know, facilitated by the phone and by the now-widespread fluency in English across Europe. If we didn’t make an effort to learn the local language, we were cooked: Google Translate didn’t exist. According to travel research group MMGY’s 2025 Portrait of European Travellers (surveying France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK), Gen Z (aged 14-29) is responsible for the travel boom in Europe, and is planning to spend more on global travel and take more vacations than any other age bracket. Unsurprisingly, Italy, Spain and Greece are considered the most desirable, while the US flags in popularity. They are using planning tools and AI to map out itineraries.



But tech isn’t just aiding travel, it’s shaping and changing it. The most picturesque, Insta-worthy places are swamped by young people looking for the perfect shot to post, much to the annoyance of locals. Sweating crowds in sweltering Europe jostle around landmarks and crowd the most photogenic vistas. Today in the centre of Lisbon, where I have come to research a book, on the way to the train station I wove past dozens of people in Instagram poses, hands on hips, laughing, tilting heads, pouting, flexing. What they are missing is the joy of not being seen. Of waking up on beaches with panda eyes, not worrying someone will take a shot and post it. I remember speaking a year ago to one teen who was preparing for a Mediterranean trip by having her eyelashes, nails and brows done: “No way am I going to be chopped [look unattractive] in Greece,” she said. The prevalence of social media has also led to milder behaviour, according to a 2024 survey by youth travel agency StudentUniverse. It found only one in five young Australians planned to party when travelling overseas: 84 per cent of Gen Z full-time students scheduled trips where there would be no drinking. Many parents would cheer, given the genuine concerns about drink-spiking and safety, but 27 per cent of Gen Z also said they just didn’t want to be snapped doing something embarrassing.



Related Article Opinion

Tourism Idiots are ruining travel for the rest of us Ben Groundwater Travel writer StudentUniverse’s Will Jones told Student Traveller this trend – of “dry-trippers” – had been rapid and widespread: “This is the first generation to be setting this trend. I’m a Millennial and I remember when I was their age having holidays focused on drinking and partying. So it is amazing how much, and how quickly, this has changed. “Australians used to be seen as big party people, but this Gen Z is the first global generation. Because of social media, they all seem to be following the same trends and doing the same things.” This is a generation that is having less sex, drinking less and reading fewer books (although they are reading in digital formats). But they are travelling more often. War or global instability haven’t deterred them, with only 1.5 per cent of Australians under 30 cancelling trips to Europe in 2026. Home ownership is hard, almost impossible; holidays are within reach.



In 2023, The Guardian declared “gritty gap years” were out and “grand tours of Europe’s charisma” were in. Is it weird to be nostalgic about the grit? A time when we could run wild, unobserved, learning how to fend for ourselves? When we could just have fun – or not – instead of feeling like we also had to look like we were having fun? I realise this makes me seem ancient. I also feel like I’m describing the daily life of ancient explorers. But in trading concealment for convenience, evaporation for ease, surely we are in danger of losing the pleasure of forgetting ourselves and truly paying attention, marvelling. Julia Baird is a journalist, author and regular columnist. Her latest book is Bright Shining: How grace changes everything. World.title: Pentagon ploughs $560 million into ‘world-first’ Australian mining project
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaCritical minerals Pentagon ploughs $560 million into ‘world-first’ Australian mining project Michael Koziol August 8, 2026 — 9:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: The Pentagon will invest more than half a billion dollars in a “world-first” mining project in central western NSW that produces scandium, a rare critical mineral used in fighter jets, spacecraft and other tools of war. The $US400 million ($560 million) loan is intended to expand production at Sunrise Energy Metals’ Syerston Scandium Project near Fifield, south-west of Dubbo, as the US seeks to urgently diversify its supply chain for rare earths. Sunrise Energy Metals’ Syerston scandium project in NSW. Last year, Sunrise announced a deal for US weapons contractor Lockheed Martin to buy up to 15 tonnes of scandium oxide over five years. The move came just days after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and US President Donald Trump signed a critical minerals deal in Washington. Scandium – used to strengthen aluminium – is already used widely for defence, aerospace and energy applications, but nearly all supply comes from China, Russia and Ukraine.



The US has not mined scandium since 1969. The Pentagon said foreign competitors accounted for about 80 per cent of global scandium production and nearly 100 per cent of processing. Trump announced the Pentagon’s investment on Friday (Washington time) during a televised roundtable with mining executives at the US State Department. The White House described the Sunrise venture as “the world’s first primary scandium mine”. The US Department of Defence said the conditional loan from its Office of Strategic Capital would build a “complete, US-aligned value chain from mine to finished metal”, securing a vital supply of scandium for the US defence and commercial industrial base. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said: “We’re going to make sure the United States – not our adversaries – controls the supply chains of power and critical minerals.”



Representatives of Australian mining giants BHP and Rio Tinto, who have proposed and planned an underground copper mine in Arizona called Resolution Copper, also attended Friday’s roundtable. When realised, it is forecast to meet about a quarter of US copper demand. “Mr President, you have brought mining back to America single-handedly,” said Resolution Copper president Vicky Peacey at the roundtable. “We started permitting in 2005 … we finally got it over the line earlier this year.” President Donald Trump holds a solid gold replica of a deep sea nodule he was gifted during a roundtable on American mining on Friday. AP Photo/Allison Robbert BHP’s North America president Jessica Farrell and vice president for international affairs Dominic Perrottet – the former NSW premier – also attended. Resources Minister Madeleine King said the Pentagon’s loan was a significant vote of confidence in Australia’s critical minerals sector and its capacity to supply the minerals the US and its partners needed.



Scandium had a range of aerospace, defence and clean energy applications, King noted. “No one country alone can create secure, end-to-end supply chains in critical minerals and rare earths.” Albanese announced last year that Australia would create a $1.2 billion strategic reserve of critical minerals to purchase and hold minerals such as lithium, rare earths, nickel, cobalt and graphite via special agreements with local producers. Resolution Copper president and general manager Vicky Peacey (far left) with US Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. AP Photo/Allison Robbert The deal signed by Albanese and Trump last October set out that the countries would provide at least $US1 billion for critical minerals projects in each country. According to a federal government fact sheet, NSW has the highest concentration of scandium in the world. Those deposits have rapidly come to the interest of the US government.



Sunrise Energy Metals secured a $US67 million debt financing letter of interest from the US Export-Import Bank last year. Related Article Mining Why are Australia’s rare earths ‘crucial for the world’? Joe Hockey has an idea The Syerston project is also benefiting from a program unveiled by the NSW government last month that allows it to defer royalty payments for five years. “The Syerston Scandium Project has been identified as a project of strategic importance under the US-Australia critical minerals partnership,” the NSW government said. “This support further reinforces the strategic necessity of bringing Syerston online as rapidly as possible.” Another company, the Canada-listed, Nevada-headquartered Scandium International Mining Corp, is also developing a scandium mine near Nyngan, NSW and a nearby scandium exploration site known as Honeybugle.

World.title: New Zealand places further sanctions against Russia supporters
World.content:
New Zealand has placed another round of sanctions targeting those supporting Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

The latest package targets 33 individuals and groups, with a particular focus on cyber actors, and those involved in the forced relocation, abduction and re-education of Ukrainian children.

The sanctions also target people supporting Russia's military-industrial complex, political figures, and North Koreans and Iranians providing support to Moscow.

Foreign Minister Winston Peters said New Zealand remained concerned about the treatment of Ukrainian children.

"Children should never be used as instruments of war," he said. "New Zealand remains deeply concerned by efforts to abduct and re-educate Ukrainian children through co-ercive state-directed programmes."

The package also targets malicious cyber actors and people involved in spreading anti-Ukraine propaganda aimed at legitimising Russia's invasion.

Peters said cyber activity could have real-world consequences, including helping Russia gather intelligence, evade sanctions and disrupt opponents of its war.

"New Zealand stands with our partners in calling out Moscow's use of these actors."

This is New Zealand's 36th round of sanctions against Russia, since the Russia Sanctions Act came into force in March 2022.

World.title: Beloved Nelson cafe forced to close after landlord dispute and roadworks woes
World.content:
A popular Nelson cafe and gallery has announced its closure, after a dispute with the landlord and ongoing roadworks made it untenable to continue.

Red Art Gallery & Café owners Ant and Suzi Stevens say after nine years in business, its closure was forced after the landlord chose not to renew the lease, a devastating blow after months of roadworks on the two adjacent streets had seriously impacted revenue.

The work, part of the $78 million Bridge to Better project, has seen water pipes and other infrastructure along the the length of Bridge Street replaced, causing disruption to a number of businesses since it first began last year.

The couple said the decision to close in September was not the outcome they wanted, especially on the back of a tough few years,

"It's just heartbreaking, I just feel like I'm losing a child to be honest, it's just been my baby for so long," Suzi said.

The business had survived a global pandemic, a recession and roadworks which effectively left them an island, with the cafe and gallery entrance hidden behind fences, trucks and diggers.

Bridge Street and Haven Road either side of the business have been closed for months while the roads are ripped up and pipes replaced, with customers having to walk down narrow, uneven gravel paths between temporary fences to reach the business.

The gallery represented about 60 artists, most of them from Nelson and Tasman, and they had taken on more after the Suter Art Gallery made the decision to stop stocking the work of around 40 local artists, after getting advice from external retail specialists.

Roadworks in Nelson are taking a toll on local businesses. Samantha Gee/RNZ

Since announcing the closure on social media, the couple had received hundreds of comments in support.

The cafe was full on Friday morning when RNZ visited. Within an hour, it had made as much money as it had over the previous two days combined.

"We knew there would be strong support, but not the way it's been with the messages, with the people coming in," Ant said.

"Love and compassion and heart will beat greed any day."

He said the council told the couple they would be the "most impacted business" given their proximity to the roadworks, but there had been "zero talk of compensation or help in any way", except to be asked whether they had two hard years in them until the upgrade was complete.

"It'll be wonderful for someone else, but it won't be us," Ant said.

Council agrees to defer rates if landlords come to the party

Nelson mayor Nick Smith previously said he had met with a number of "very distressed" business owners who were feeling the pressure of the ongoing roadworks.

Staff had gone to "tremendous effort" to try and minimise disruption in the city by promoting businesses, he said.

Smith acknowledged the work was "incredibly disruptive" but said it was essential to renew and upgrade infrastructure that, in some places, was over 100 years old.

Once complete, Bridge Street was tipped to be a "people-focused corridor" with utility services capable of supporting inner city development.

At a council meeting on Thursday, elected members agreed to allow affected businesses to defer rates from the current year, with repayments split over the next three years, if landlords agreed to provide the equivalent financial relief to the tenant.

Nelson's mayor says council staff are trying to minimise disruption in the city by promoting businesses. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Nelson Tasman Chamber of Commerce chair Venus Guy said it was disappointing to see the closure of long-standing local businesses.

"Red Gallery has been part of our city centre, and our thoughts are with the owners and everyone affected by this decision."

She said while the Bridge to Better project was an important investment in Nelson's future, the major infrastructure work placed very real pressures on businesses during construction.

"It is essential that we continue working together to minimise disruption, support affected businesses and remind our community that our city centre remains open for business.

Central city businesses feeling the hurt

Longstanding cafe and food store Prego Mediterranean Foods & Comida Cafe shut its doors in June, and the owners said at the time that the [https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/business/625679/road-closures-and-rising-costs-force-closure-of-nelson-businessongoing ongoing roadworks were one of the factors in its closure].

Further down Bridge Street, Pizzeria Bella owner Yusef Corten said he thought more could be done to support businesses affected by the infrastructure works.

At lunchtime on Friday, his restaurant was empty and the noise of roadworks outside made it hard to be heard when speaking.

He had organised a meeting with about 30 Bridge Street business owners that were also struggling around two months ago.

He said the rates deferral scheme made little difference. It gave relief of about $80 per month, but would have to be paid back in the years to come.

Pizzeria Bella owner Yusef Corten sits in front of his restaurant and behind a fence while work is done on Bridge Street. Samantha Gee/RNZ

Corten, who had owned and operated hospitality businesses in Nelson for more than a decade, said he bought Pizzeria Bella a year ago. He started out with nine employees, but was now down to three. Only he and his son were working full-time, with debt that kept rising.

Pizzeria Bella's revenue was down 80 percent since the roadworks began. On Tuesday, Corten made $300 between the lunch and dinner services. His accountant had told him he needed turnover of $2000 a day to survive.

"Every day I am more negative, more negative."

Corten said two businesses had closed and it was possible that more would follow.

World.title: New healthcare-focused school subject could jump start next generation of workers - doctor
World.content:
A new healthcare-focused high school subject could jump start the next generation of medical professionals, a Northland provider says.

The government has announced nine new secondary school subjects to be developed by industry groups.

That included a course on "health services and care", which Ngāti Hine Health Trust clinical advisor Dr Mataroria Lyndon said would be a great opportunity to attract youngsters to the sector.

"I came through as a doctor and did my training but never had the opportunity to be exposed earlier, especially at high school," Dr Lyndon said.

"Part of the learning will be around understanding care situations, communication... And then expose them at an earlier stage to the different types of health roles, whether that be medicine, nursing, community carers, mental health workers."

He said students would have a chance to observe different types of health roles in real world settings, which he hoped would include Ngāti Hine clinics.

"As a subject now going forward it'll help young people see a place for themselves in healthcare and in the community workforce," he said.

"Traditionally we might think of health workers as doctors and nurses, but those at the Ngāti Hine Health Trust for example... There are community carers, there are podiatrists, nutritionists, community health workers, health promotion, it's just a good opportunity to have those pathways into the health workforce much earlier."

He hoped students would feel inspired to enter the health workforce at a time when it was facing severe shortages.

"We're among the largest providers in Northland, so hopefully we can grow our own workforce to have more students in Northland studying earlier," Dr Lyndon said.

World.title: Am I too old to be more aggressive? - Ask Susan
World.content:
Got questions? RNZ has a podcast, 'No Stupid Questions', with Susan Edmunds.

We'd love to hear more of your questions about money and the economy. You can send through written questions, like these ones, but even better, you can drop us a voice memo to our email questions@rnz.co.nz.

You can also sign up to RNZ's new money newsletter, 'Money with Susan Edmunds'.

A stupid question but is 46 too old to change to aggressive for my KiwiSaver?

This isn't personalised advice but in general, I wouldn't think so. It depends on a lot of factors like your personal risk tolerance and your investing timeframe.

Aggressive funds are among the most volatile options in KiwiSaver, and have even more exposure to growth assets than growth funds. They invest in things like equities that can fluctuate in value a lot, and you need to have time to ride out any downturns which could see your fund losing up to about 30 percent in a year. But over the long term, taking more risk tends to pay off. Morningstar data shows aggressive funds have returned an average 10.3 percent a year over the past 10 years, the best of the KiwiSaver bunch.

People are usually told they shouldn't be in an aggressive fund if they don't have 10 to 15 years to stick with it.

That said, even if you were a bit older than you are now, it could work. You don't have to pull all your money out at 65, and you may want to keep some exposure to growth assets at that point to help your investment grow.

I would talk to an adviser.

I've just read your response to a question on whether an individual should put their money into a managed fund or KiwiSaver. Your comment was that it's ultimately up to them but in your response you state that "Once you reach 65, a KiwiSaver fund is much the same as any other managed fund, because there are no restrictions on access to your money".

I've recently been told by a financial adviser that this isn't correct and that if you leave your money in a KiwiSaver fund beyond the age of 65 and the government then change the eligibility age for superannuation, this money is then locked into the KiwiSaver fund until you reach that age. Is this correct?

Technically, yes. But in practice I don't think this is something you need to worry about.

At the moment, access to KiwiSaver is tied to the age of eligibility for NZ Super, which is 65.

So if the age were to be increased, at the moment the law would mean the age of access to KiwiSaver would increase, too.

There are already discussions happening, though, about whether that's appropriate. I would expect access to KiwiSaver to be addressed alongside any plans to increase the NZ Super age.

I know some people think having access to KiwiSaver earlier than NZ Super could be a way to help people who want to stop working earlier, if the pension age rises.

I would also note that even if the age was pushed up without any change to the KiwiSaver rules, it would not be something that would affect you as a recently retired person. These sorts of changes are usually signalled well in advance to take effect over a period of time, usually for future generations.

I'm a real layman in regard to financial matters, and am completely lost - perhaps you could illuminate me a little. Now retired, I contributed to a retirement fund (not KiwiSaver) and recently asked them whether PIE (like in my KiwiSaver) was automatically paid across to IRD.

Their reply as I understood it stated that they pay a base fund 28 percent to IRD - but that PIE does not apply in the instance of retirement funds. I was informed that if I withdraw funds/close my account, then I need to inform this via my IR3 and I will be taxed accordingly at my 17.5 percent rate. My quandary is, does IRD make me pay tax on the entire retirement fund amount, or just on the "growth" aspect which has occurred across the years of investing contributions into that fund, the Teachers Retirement Savings Scheme.

Also, am I better off to perhaps withdraw my retirement scheme funds and have them invested together with my other funds which I have in KiwiSaver?

Very quickly, when you're invested in KiwiSaver you're usually paying tax on the income that your investments make, not the growth in the value of the investments themselves. (There are some complexities around this for foreign investments.)

You don't pay tax on withdrawal, except where there could be a "square up" to do on the tax you would normally pay in the year. You aren't going to be charged tax on the total withdrawal amount, or the growth you've had on your investments while you've been investing, or anything like that.

As for the PIE rate, Dean Anderson at Kernel says it's possible that the fund you're in has a fixed PIE rate of 28 percent. In that case, it could be beneficial for you to move to a multi-rate PIE that could allow you you pay tax at a lower rate.

He says it could be that you can now find a fund that's a better fit for your goals, or you might want to consolidate your money into your other investments. "For someone who's now retired, if you're on a lower tax rate then looking for a multi-rate pie is probably a good option because then they tax is automatically at the correct PIR and does not involve any tax filing.

"One of the benefits at the moment of the New Zealand regime is the fact that for an investor in retirement, why PIRs are really good is there is no capital gains tax, there's no other complexity to worry about. You can get into the right risk profile and then say, 'hey I want to sell down $100 or $1000 or I want to take out some holiday money or create a regular income' and there's nothing they have to think about from a tax perspective, it's all going to get handled."

World.title: 'Māori data in Māori hands': Experts want Google to adhere to data sovereignty principles
World.content:
Māori tech experts have renewed calls to adhere to Māori data sovereignty principles after a first of its kind partnership with tech giant Google.

In July, Google and Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori (the Māori Language Commission) launched an AI-powered text-to-speech (TTS) model for Google Maps that could correctly pronounce cities and towns with te reo Māori names.

In a statement Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori said all Māori data from the model was placed under the kaitiakitanga of Te Taura Whiri.

"Google has a license to use this data for the purposes of this text-to-speech model. The long-term view remains to establish a consortium of interested groups as long term kaitiakitanga.

"The goal is to ensure Māori academics, researchers and communities who are looking to improve speech or similar technology, would have the ability to access this data, share the benefit and contribute to the evolution of this kaupapa."

University of Waikato computer science professor Te Taka Keegan told RNZ any data generated around reo Māori, tikanga Māori, must stay in Māori hands.

"This was one of the first times where Google has ever produced something where that's been the case. So the IP for the data, not the IP for the actual tool and the technology, the techniques, the algorithms, but the IP for the actual data itself remains with Te Taura Whiri."

Keegan said there were a few Māori organisations that would be suitable to take over guardianship in the long term.

"So what Te Taura Whiri needs to do, and they are aware of this and they should start working on it shortly, what they need to do is they need to find another storage avenue, where the data is held by Māori entities, because Māori entities will protect it, this government won't protect it. Te Taura Whiri is a government organisation."

Waikato University associate professor of Computer Science Te Taka Keegan. RNZ / Libby Kirkby-McLeod

Erena Mikaere (Tūhourangi) is the principal technician at Te Kāhui Raraunga, the operational arm of the Data Iwi Leaders group. She told RNZ in the short term, given that Te Taura Whiri had a duty of care for te reo, they probably came to the right arrangement.

Te Kāhui Raraunga released a Māori data governance model in 2023, aimed at a government audience to understand how to govern data in a way that adheres to a Māori worldview and that adheres to Māori data sovereignty principles, she said.

"We're talking about our reo data for now, which is some of our most precious data, absolutely. The Crown have so much of our data and our job is to advocate for that data to be available for iwi. Put iwi Māori data in iwi Māori hands, that is what we advocate for.

"So we have the tools, we have the resources, and we have the time to support and advise government agencies about how they could do that better. And we do think they need to do that better."

In May, Te Kāhui Raraunga launched its own decentralised data storage network, Te Pā Tūwatawata, and Mikaere said it would be open to having a conversation with Te Taura Whiri about the possibility of storing the Google Maps data set within it.

"Because we know it is the only large scale accessible, safe, sovereign storage solution available in Aotearoa owned by Māori. And we can support a governance model that in fact allows access to that data by the right people, the people who have affinity, who have connection and kinship to that data."

Since the launch of the platform Mikaere said it had been approached by a number private companies who saw that by adhering to the Māori data governance model, they were establishing ethical data governance models for their businesses and for their customers.

World.title: City Rail Link 'First Look' events begin
World.content:
Aucklanders have been getting their first chance to see inside the new City Rail Link, with a busy turnout for the first of a series of public open day events at new railway stations - this one at Maungawhau Station.

City Rail Link (CRL) is country's largest transport infrastructure project to date, with about three and a half kilometres of tunnels and costing $5.5b. It has been long-awaited and is scheduled to open on 13 September, with promises to speed up and modernise public transport in the sprawling city.

Auckland's first CRL station opens to the public Saturday Morning Download MP3 5m

But before it opens, a series of public 'First Look' weekend events are on offer in August, with the first at the new Maungawhau Station (formerly Mount Eden Station) between Mount Eden and Eden Terrace, on Saturday.

Food and activities were set up in the surrounding streets, with busking and community performances inside the train station. A steady stream of people had been coming in to have a look, Auckland Transport CRL communications manager Joel Rowan said, mid-morning on Saturday.

"There's a stage set up, we've got the local community really part of this. A local school kapa haka group has actually just been warming up. We've had heaps of interest in today, and everyone just seems to be just really enjoying it.

"I think people are relieved. Last night we had some of the locals and local businesses in here for a little preview of today's event. And they've really been hanging out - not just for today, but for the project to open.

"This station [has] been closed since 2020 for the construction. So I know that everyone's really looking forward to I guess getting the benefits when the opening finally does arrive on the 13th of September."

Maungawhau Station on Saturday RNZ/ Lucy Xia

West Auckland resident Harrison Fernandes-Burnard said he is expecting the CRL will take about 20 minutes off his daily commute.

"The old Mount Eden Station was quite basic, rustic you could say - but yeah it's amazing ... there's now four platforms and it's really spacious." It had changed a lot, and was a good  for the city, he said.

Irene Pang and her grandson Christian Yeung travelled from Meadowlands in East Auckland for the First Look event. Pang hopes there will be more frequent buses to Panmure Station from where she lives.

Yueng said he was excited about taking the train during school holidays and better connections to western parts of the city

Irene Pang and her grandson Christian Yeung, at the event at Maungawhau Station on Saturday morning. RNZ/ Lucy Xia

Before the old Mt Eden Station closed, the journey downtown from Maungawhau Station to what is now Waitematā Station (formerly Britomart) took about 20 minutes, travelling through Newmarket, Auckland Transport's Joel Rowan said.

It now takes about 10 minutes, or even less for either of the two new closer central stations: just a couple of minutes to Karanga-a-Hape Station, or about seven minutes to Te Waihorotiu Station near the Sky Tower. While people going to or from the westerns suburbs will find their trips much faster using the CRL, Rowan said.

At Maungawhau Station on Saturday Lucy Xia / RNZ

Many rehearsals and trials of the rail schedule had been carried out ahead of the full CRL opening, with big attendance expected from the first day.

Auckland Transport's website said the new Maungawhau Station was visually striking, and "combines world-class transport infrastructure with thoughtful design inspired by the surrounding volcanic landscape and deep cultural connections to nearby maunga."

"Its dramatic architecture, natural materials and spacious platforms create a station experience unlike anything else in Auckland."

Maungawhau Station on Saturday RNZ/ Lucy Xia

Ongoing CRL 'First Look' events are planned for Saturday 15 August at Karanga-a-Hape Station and Saturday 22 August at Te Waihorotiu Station, with a succession of one hour tours available on each day starting from 8am.

Auckland Transport said people planning to attend should apply ahead for tickets, which are free.

A new Journey Planner tool is also available online, to help Aucklanders plan for the new timetables when the CRL opens.

Maungawhau Station on Saturday RNZ/ Lucy Xia

World.title: Te Matatini o Ngā Taniwha 2027 draw announced
World.content:
The competition pool line up for Te Matatini o Ngā Taniwha 2027 where 57 kapa haka will compete for the national title has been announced.

Te Arikinui, Kuini Nga wai hono I te po, Patron of Te Matatini hosted the live draw on Saturday at Tūrangawaewae Marae in Ngāruawāhia.

Qualifying kapa haka representing 13 different regions have been allocated slots across four performance pools, Te Ihu, Te Haumi, Te Awa and Te Kei.

Three kapa from each of the four pool performance days will be selected to advance to Te Matangireia, the finals day where the next national champions will be named.

Te Matatini draw 2027. Te Matatini/Whakaata Māori

Te Matatini Chairman, Tā Herewini Parata congratulated all qualifying kapa haka, highlighting their dedication and commitment to championing te ao Māori.

"These qualifying kapa haka embody the very best of their hapū, marae and iwi traditional and contemporary performing arts. They captivate audiences here at home and around the world.

We've seen the influence on the world stage at the recent Commonwealth Games, for example, where our athletes celebrate with a haka following winning performances, where supporters wield poi, which shows our cultural tradition has become embedded in the psyche of Aotearoa New Zealand."

In 2025 Te Kapa Haka o Ngāti Whakaue from Te Arawa waka won the title of Toa Whakaihuwaka - the champions of Te Matatini.

Second place went to from Ngāti Rangiwēwehi - also from Te Arawa - while third went to Ngā Tumanako from Tāmaki Makaurau.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/te-ao-maori/543424/te-kapa-haka-o-ngati-whakaue-have-won-the-title-of-toa-whakaihuwaka-the-champions-of-te-matatini

Te Kapa Haka o Ngāti Whakaue at 2025 Te Matatini Festival at Pukekura/Bowl of Brooklands in New Plymouth Supplied / Te Matatini Enterprises

Parata also acknowledged the significant growth in popularity of the competition since its inception, 54 years ago.

"In 1972, the inaugural New Zealand Polynesian festival was held at Rotowhio, Rotorua with just 17 kapa haka teams taking to the stage. Over the decades, the festival has evolved in both name and stature and become what we know today as Te Matatini the largest celebration of kapa haka excellence in the world."

Te Matatini o Ngā Taniwha will be hosted by Tainui in the Waikato region in 2027 from Tuesday 23 February to Saturday 27 February.

World.title: NRL: What we learnt from NZ Warriors' stunning win over Penrith Panthers
World.content:
Analysis - And some wins are worth more than just two competition points.

Last month, NZ Warriors were lucky to survive a scare from NRL cellar-dwellers St George-Illawarra Dragons, a display that suggested they may struggle to retain their spot in the top four, let alone the top two, with the home playoff fixture that went with it.

Sure enough, seven days later, they were comprehensively outplayed and beaten by another team outside the post-season picture, Canterbury Bulldogs, to lose their grip on second - just the wake-up call their season needed.

This 28-12 win over top-of-the-table Penrith Panthers was the opposite of that.

"It always gives you confidence that you know you belong, but there's a lot of dips and turns, and the rollercoaster of the NRL over four weeks, lots of things will change, I'm sure," coach Andrew Webster reflected.

For the moment though, this result - and, more importantly, the performance - confirms the promise the Warriors showed through the first half of their campaign, when they shot out to a club record 9-2 start.

"I think it gives us confidence that we belong and we're going to have to improve," Webster assessed. "That's the best thing about tonight - there's still some improvement in us - but we definitely need to celebrate what we did well.

"I thought we played really good for 70 minutes, but there was a 10-minute period when we lost our way a bit. They were just throwing fearless footy at us, and we weren't really well connected and tried to solve it ourselves."

The pure theatre of Luke Metcalf's return to the halfback position and his huge influence on this contest already has many pointing the finger at Webster for not bringing his gamebreaker back to the line-up earlier.

Luke Metcalf's return to the Warriors line-up sparked a breakout performance against the Panthers. Brett Phibbs/Photosport

Metcalf's looming departure for the Dragons next season, after signing an extension with the Warriors and then backflipping, adds another dimension to this drama.

"At the end of the day, we're grown men," said co-captain Mitch Barnett. "All our halves have had to wait their turn and they've all taken their opportunity, when they've got it.

"You don't want injuries to happen to anyone, but it's pretty cool when Tanah Boyd takes an opportunity, he's our best player and gets injured, then Te Maire Martin gets an opportunity and now it's Luke's turn.

"It's good for him to get the performance out tonight and play the way he did. He will only gain more confidence from that, heading into next week."

An NRL season is a marathon, not a sprint, and sometimes having to wait for your chance is not a bad thing.

Here's what we learnt from the Warriors win over the Panthers.

Best players

Hard to go past Metcalf, whose two tries and five conversions were supplemented by 519 kicking metres, many of those contestable bombs.

He led all players in fantasy points, so well done to anyone who still had him on their rosters after all these weeks.

Leka Halasima showed exactly why his coach switched him to centre last week, dominating the left edge during the first half particularly. He didn't score, but he ran 21 times for a team-high 239 metres, including 73 after contact, broke 11 tackles and provided the assist to Chanel Harris-Tavita's first-half try.

Leka Halasima's move to centre may have taken the Warriors to the next level. Brett Phibbs/Photosport

"The best thing you can say about Leka is he's fearless," Webster said. "You can play him wing or fullback, he doesn't care, and I hope that doesn't change the older he gets and the more he understands things.

"Right now, he cares a lot, he wants to be in the team, he wants to contribute and he's learning all the time, but he's hard to handle."

Second-rower Jacob Laban continued his run of fine performances, leading the Warriors with 46 tackles in an 80-minute display.

Veteran front-rowers Mitch Barnett (163 metres, 37 tackles) and James Fisher-Harris (160 metres, 35 tackles) dominated the middle, while second-rower Kurt Capewell brought up his 50 games for the club in fine style, making the break that led to Metcalf's first try.

At fullback, Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad showed he wouldn't be handing back his No.1 jersey any time soon, scoring a try and running for 193 metres with two linebreaks.

Best try

Too many to choose from, but let's go with Harris-Tavita's effort just before halftime.

Halasima made the initially break, running 50 metres from his own goal-line over halfway on the first tackle.

Later in the same set, the Warriors shifted the ball back to his left edge, where Halasima took a pass from Harris-Tavita, bullied the last two defenders and offloaded to his five-eighth running the support line.

While Adam Pompey has been a reliable contributor to his team over several seasons, he simply doesn't have the x-factor that Halasima brings and that change may become Webster's masterstroke that takes the Warriors to the next level.

Key moment

With five minutes remaining, the Panthers had scored back-to-back tries and seemed to have another, when Nathan Cleary put up a bomb on the Warriors goal-line and wing Paul Alamoti gathered a loose ball to score.

Amid their celebrations, the try was reviewed by the bunker and second-rower Liam Martin was found to have strayed offside at the kick, before participating in the contest, so the try was overturned, much to the relief of every Warriors fan everywhere.

"You take those things, but if it had been onside and the try was scored, it would have been interesting to see how we handled that moment," Webster said. "That would have been a tough challenge.

"It was a big moment, but I still have the faith we would have come out fine."

Referee Gerard Sutton came under the spotlight for some of his decisions both ways. Brett Phibbs/Photosport

Moments later, Metcalf scored his second try to ice the win.

Key stat

The Warriors have now won 11/11 this season, when leading at halftime.

Referee blooper

I feel compelled to add this category, because it has become a real feature of the NRL this season.

Many fans across the Tasman are blowing up deluxe over Alamoti's sin-binning for a late, dangerous tackle on Halasima in the first half. The Warriors capitalised on his absence through Harris-Tavita's try.

Far worse was the blatant forward pass from prop Lindsay Smith, ruled backwards by referee Gerard Sutton, who was not helped at all by his touchies, as Penrith camped in the Warriors redzone. Webster later referred to this as the "second-worst forward pass I've seen in rugby league".

Presumably the worst is still the Reece Walsh shocker during the Warriors' 2023 preliminary final loss to Brisbane Broncos.

Injuries etc

The main setback occurred during the week, when Te Maire Martin tweaked a hamstring in training.

He had left last week's win over Gold Coast Titans early and was spotted icing a calf afterwards, so his absence wasn't totally unexpected, but the nature of the injury was.

Luckily, Webster had a readymade replacement chomping at the bit for a chance to step up. Martin is expected to be out 2-4 weeks, but will now have to earn a recall ahead of his replacement.

Hooker Wayde Egan went off for another concussion check, but passed it safely enough. If his team ever put some daylight between them and their nearest rivals, Egan could do with a week off to freshen up, after playing every game so far this season.

Te Maire Martin's misfortune has catapulted Luke Metcalf back into the Warriors line-up. NRL Photos/Photosport

Demitric Vaimauga still has no return date with tender ribs, although he trained in a non-contact vest during the week. His absence gave Eddie Ieremia-Toeava 47 more worthwhile minutes off the bench, while Englishman Morgan Gannon made a two-minute cameo at the end for his second NRL appearance.

His first ended with concussion after five minutes in March.

After missing just one game with a sprained foot, Taine Tuaupiki was back on the interchange, but wasn't needed and will now have to wait his turn behind Nicoll-Klokstad.

Penrith Panthers

This was a surprisingly muted display from the competition leaders, whose season is almost the mirror opposite of last year, when they started slowly and hit the bottom of the table, before bouncing back to reach the preliminary finals.

This year, they lost three from four during June/July and are now four from seven since that slump began, in grave danger of losing the minor premiership that once seemed theirs for the taking.

Their trajectory now has them heading in the opposite direction to the Warriors.

Nathan Cleary showed his class, but couldn't guide his team to victory over the Warriors. Brett Phibbs/Photosport

Halfback Cleary almost rescued the game in a five-minute period, when he sparked his own try with a long crossfield pass to create space down the left, before instigating a second with a masterful 40/20 kick.

Unfortunately, they also lost star lock Isaah Yeo to a shoulder injury that may prove a major blow to their season.

What does the result mean

The Warriors improve to 14-6 for the season, and now sit two points behind the Panthers and Sydney Roosters on the table.

They still lie third, but can fall further this weekend, if Cronulla Sharks can beat the Dragons by 66 points to overhaul the differential.

Most importantly for the Warriors, they are now eight points clear of the ninth-placed Bulldogs with four rounds remaining, so they're virtually assured of playoff footy, with a 288-point countback advantage.

What's next

Next Saturday, the Warriors return to Suncorp Stadium for a third time this season to face downcast champions Brisbane Broncos.

Like Luke Metcalf before him, Tanah Boyd suffered a season-ending knee injury at Suncorp Stadium. AAP / Photosport

Last time they met in 'Magic Round' - a Warriors home game - they prevailed 42-12 and the Broncos have lost 10 of their last 11 games. Ironically, their only win in that span was also against the Panthers.

The venue has turned into a Warriors stronghold, with amazing expat fan support expected, but it also holds some trepidation.

Last season, this was where Metcalf's Dally M Medal hopes came crashing down, when he tore the anterior cruciate ligament in his knee.

At Magic Round this year, his replacement, Tanah Boyd, suffered exactly the same injury on the same field, ending his campaign prematurely.

World.title: Surprise parents' visit inspires new leader in Tour de France Femmes
World.content:
Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney launched a decisive attack up Mont Ventoux to win the seventh stage of the Tour de France Femmes and take the overall lead from Marlen Reusser.

The 2024 champion was in tears as she put on the yellow jersey and now leads 2023 champion Demi Vollering by 15 seconds and Reusser by 39 with two stages left.

"I'm just so tired and so blown away with what just happened," Niewiadoma-Phinney said.

"When I started climbing I looked to the right and I saw my parents standing on the roadside. They came today by surprise. I saw my father yelling for me and I thought I had to make him proud."

Reusser and Vollering could not follow Niewiadoma-Phinney when she broke away about 9km from the top of Ventoux, one of the most iconic climbs in cycling with its barren, lunar aspect.

It was a first Tour stage win for Niewiadoma-Phinney, who won the 2024 edition without claiming a stage. Gritting her teeth in the final few hundred metres, the Polish rider dug deep and with the sun gleaming behind her, raised her arms after crossing the line.

She then almost lost balance through fatigue and had to be helped off her bike. Moments later, she was all smiles as she sat on the road and poured cooling water over her head.

"I never chase victories for the sake of winning, I target them because I like this beautiful feeling I have right now," Niewiadoma-Phinney said.

"I came here (before) to Mont Ventoux with my friends and my husband, and we rode up the climb three times.

"The feeling of reaching the top of this mountain was amazing. From that moment, I just wanted to experience that feeling again. The pure joy of riding, as if I was a kid."

Vollering dropped Reusser in the closing stages of the 15.7km ascent of Ventoux, which has featured several time on the men's Tour. In one of the darkest days in Tour history, British rider Tom Simpson died after collapsing during a tortuous ascent in 1967.

World time trial champion Reusser battled gamely but lost valuable time in the title fight. The Swiss rider finished the stage fourth as Vollering and two-time Giro d'Italia winner Elisa Longo Borghini of Italy both placed ahead of her.

There were three smaller climbs heading to Ventoux, which was ranked as a Hors Catégorie ascent — the hardest category — and had a gradient of nearly 9 per cent.

Vollering moved ahead first, and Reusser and Niewiadoma-Phinney joined her as others lagged behind. Niewiadoma-Phinney then attacked and, although Vollering stood up in her saddle to chase her the new race leader was riding a brilliant tempo and proved too strong.

"My idea was that I had to make it to Chalet Reynard on my own," Niewiadoma-Phinney said.

"Because from then on the headwind would be quite strong and the chasers would try to stay on each other's wheel for as long as possible."

The eighth stage is a flat 172km route for sprinters finishing in Nice, where the race ends after another mountain stage on Sunday night.

Stage nine features four sharp climbs of Col d'Èze, nestled in the hills overlooking the Principality of Monaco.

Two years ago, Niewiadoma-Phinney beat Vollering on the final stage to win the race by just four seconds.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.
